__Project.doc: Project is the root class representing the entire architecture of a software project in OpenAPPL. It sits at the top of the OpenAPPL ontology tree—a structured, semantic pattern definition scheme used to model projects. An OpenAPPL compiler leverages this ontology to generate applications (as microservices, a modular monolith or serverless functions, by the compiler's choice) by interpreting and compiling interconnected pattern objects. Each pattern object is defined as a class with typed properties, which can include both primitive types and references to other pattern classes. Projects are built as JSON instances that follow this schema, enabling AI agents and human architects to collaboratively define a system's structure, behavior, and deployment blueprint in a unified and machine-readable format.

Project.__projectSettings.doc: Defines the general configuration of the project. This includes fundamental attributes like project name, description, and environmental setup. Recommended as the first section to complete when initializing a new project.
Project.__authentication.doc: Configures the authentication and authorization mechanisms of the project. This module defines login models, session behavior, social logins, and access control. It is referenced by all services that require secure user management.
Project.__bffService.doc: Defines the Back-For-Front (BFF) service that serves as a frontend aggregation layer. It composes data from multiple services and presents them in optimized formats for the frontend.
Project.__notificationService.doc: Settings for configuring notification options at the project level so that a separte notification service can be used to send messages via email, SMS, or push notifications. This module defines the providers and event-driven behaviors for notifications.
Project.__library.doc: Represents the shared utility module of the project. It includes reusable components such as data objects, scripts, and helper functions accessible by all services.
Project.__services.doc: Defines the individual microservices within the project. Each service includes its own data model, logic, and CRUD capabilities. All services are listed as an array of Service objects.
Project.__agentHub.doc: Centralized AI agent management hub. Generates a dedicated service that hosts AI agents with cross-service tool access, runtime reconfiguration, and optional dynamic agent creation by end-users. Agents in the hub can use tools from any service in the project.
Project.__enterpriseHub.doc: Project-level enterprise-integration asset hub. Each EnterpriseModel binds to one connected enterprise platform (declared in projectSettings.enterpriseIntegrationsSettings) and catalogs the assets a designer works with — the external business objects, business events, and business actions — authored against the platform's metadata. Services then CONSUME these assets: a DataObject projects an enterpriseObject, a BusinessApi is triggered by an enterpriseEvent (via the SAP/AMQP→Kafka mirror), and an ExternalBusinessAction invokes an enterpriseAction. The mcpbff bridge is the runtime that talks to the platform; this hub is the design-time catalog. Peer of agentHub.

__Primitives.doc.#: These are the fundamental data types used across OpenAPPL patterns. They form the building blocks for defining properties in all pattern classes.
__Primitives.doc.String: Represents short text values, typically limited to 255 characters.
__Primitives.doc.Integer: Represents whole numbers, commonly stored as 32-bit integers in most databases.
__Primitives.doc.Double: Represents decimal numbers with high precision, commonly stored as 64-bit doubles.
__Primitives.doc.Boolean: Represents binary values: true or false.
__Primitives.doc.Text: Represents long-form textual content, suitable for descriptions or documents.
__Primitives.doc.Any: Represents a flexible type that can hold any kind of data — a primitive, an array, or an object. Use sparingly for dynamic or loosely-typed fields.

__MScript.doc:
Represents an OpenAPPL expression used for logic, validation, or configuration. Canonically an MScript is a **multilanguage object** — a per-language source map keyed by target language (`js`, `ts`, `python`, `go`, `java`, `csharp`, `php`, `rust`). Author the expression directly in one or more target languages, and/or supply a `js` source: codegen TRANSLATES the `js` form into the five languages that ship a translator — `java`, `python`, `csharp` (dotnet), `go` (golang) and `rust` — which is what makes a `js`-only MScript portable across service languages. Two keys are NOT translation targets: `ts` is linted but read by no compile target (the nodejs lane resolves `js` only), so a `ts`-only MScript is dead weight — neither run as-is nor translated; and `php` still has a translator but belongs to the frozen lane that is no longer reachable from a design. Each source must be a valid expression in its language; the `js`/`ts` source conforms to a JavaScript ExpressionStatement (a literal, identifier, expression, function call, or a `module.exports` assignment returning a valid object). A compile target prefers its own language's source when present and otherwise falls back to translating the `js` form; an MScript that offers a service's language neither its own source nor a `js` source is REFUSED at design time (`MSCRIPT_NO_SOURCE_FOR_TARGET_LANGUAGE`) rather than silently dropped from the generated service. The legacy plain-string form (a bare JS expression string) is deprecated: it is auto-migrated to `{ "js": "<expr>" }` by the legacy project migrator and rejected for new authoring. MScripts are parsed and analyzed by a specialized override class (`custom/MScript.ts`) that provides static checks and per-language compilation. This is the same `schema == code, per-language object` shape as `LibModuleBody`.

EMPTY vs AUTHORED. An MScript slot is EMPTY when no language source carries a non-blank string: `null`, the empty or whitespace-only string, `{}`, and the ALL-NULL envelope design tools scaffold for an untouched field (`{ "js": null, "ts": null, ... }`) all mean "nothing authored here". A slot declared `required` therefore reports `REQUIRED_FIELD_MISSING` for every one of those shapes, including the scaffold - which is a plain object, so truthiness used to call it authored and a design saved straight from the design tool's template validated as complete while the emitted action ran an empty script. A value of a shape an MScript slot cannot hold (a number, a boolean, an array, an envelope with a non-string source) is an `INVALID_FIELD_TYPE`, not a missing value.

MScript.__js.doc: JavaScript expression source — the reference form, and the only portable one. The nodejs lane consumes it directly; for every other service language codegen TRANSLATES it into that language — `java`, `python`, `csharp` (dotnet), `go` (golang), `rust` — whenever that language has no dedicated source below. `ts` is not a translation target, so `js` (never `ts`) is what makes an MScript portable.
MScript.__ts.doc: TypeScript expression source. Read by NO compile target today: the nodejs lane resolves the `js` source only, and no translator consumes `ts`. A `ts`-only MScript is dead weight — linted for syntax, then never emitted and never translated, and refused at design time. Author `js` for nodejs services.
MScript.__python.doc: Python-native expression source for python services.
MScript.__go.doc: Go-native expression source for golang services.
MScript.__java.doc: Java-native expression source for java services.
MScript.__csharp.doc: C#-native expression source for dotnet services.
MScript.__php.doc: PHP-native expression source for php services. Frozen lane — a PHP translator still exists but the lane is no longer reachable from a design. ARCHIVED: the php service lane was retired on 2026-07-31 (frozen) and php is no longer a selectable service language, so this key is never read by an active target. Kept so existing sources round-trip unchanged.
MScript.__rust.doc: Rust-native expression source for rust services.

__MScriptSourceKey.doc.#: The set of per-language source keys legal inside an `MScript` object — the target languages an MScript may carry native source for. Mirrors the `LibModuleBodyKey` precedent for `LibModuleBody`.
__MScriptSourceKey.doc.js: JavaScript expression source — the reference form, and the only portable one. The nodejs lane consumes it directly; codegen translates it into `java`, `python`, `csharp` (dotnet), `go` (golang) and `rust` for any of those targets that has no dedicated source.
__MScriptSourceKey.doc.ts: TypeScript expression source. Read by NO compile target today: the nodejs lane resolves the `js` source only, and no translator consumes `ts`. A `ts`-only MScript is dead weight — linted for syntax, then never emitted and never translated, and refused at design time. Author `js` for nodejs services.
__MScriptSourceKey.doc.python: Python-native expression source for python services.
__MScriptSourceKey.doc.go: Go-native expression source for golang services.
__MScriptSourceKey.doc.java: Java-native expression source for java services.
__MScriptSourceKey.doc.csharp: C#-native expression source for dotnet services.
__MScriptSourceKey.doc.php: PHP-native expression source for php services. Frozen lane — a PHP translator still exists but the lane is no longer reachable from a design.
__MScriptSourceKey.doc.rust: Rust-native expression source for rust services.

__DefaultFunction.doc.#: A DB-native default FUNCTION for a data property's column, authored abstractly and mapped by each generator to the correct per-engine spelling. Unlike `defaultValue` (a literal enforced verbatim at the DB level), a `DefaultFunction` names a computed default the database/ORM evaluates per insert. `defaultFn` and `defaultValue` are mutually exclusive.
__DefaultFunction.doc.now: The current timestamp at insert time. Maps to Sequelize `DataTypes.NOW`, Mongoose `Date.now`, SQL `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` (and each other target's equivalent). Only valid on a `Date` property. This replaces the legacy magic-string `defaultValue` sentinels (`new Date()`, `now()`, …).

__DataObjectName.doc: Represents a reference to a data object within the project. The value can be either a simple object name or a qualified reference in the format 'serviceName:objectName'. When using the qualified format, the part before the ':' specifies the service name, and the part after specifies the object name within that service. If only a single name is provided (without ':'), the system first searches for the object in the current service, then searches across other services in the project. As a best practice, when referencing data objects from other services, always fully qualified 'serviceName:objectName' format should be used to avoid potential naming conflicts. CASING: every part must be lowerCamelCase, exactly as the referenced data object's own `name` is stored (`orderItem`, `content:orderItem`). A part that is a single identifier starting with an uppercase letter is REWRITTEN IN PLACE, not rejected: the value saved into the blueprint is the canonical lowerCamelCase form and the response reports it as an applied autoFix, so `OrderItem` is saved as `orderItem` and `APIKey` as `apiKey` (acronym runs are folded, the same canonicalization the data object's `name` gets). Anything else is an error you must fix: separators or punctuation (`order-item`, `order item`), a leading digit (`9bad`), and UPPER_CASE constant spellings (`ORDER_ITEM`) - the last one because a data object named `ORDER_ITEM` keeps that exact name, so no lowerCamelCase reference to it can resolve.
__LocalDataObjectName.doc: Represents a reference to a data object within the same service. The value must be a simple object name; not a qualified reference in the format 'serviceName:objectName'. CASING: the value must be lowerCamelCase, exactly as the referenced data object's own `name` is stored (`orderItem`). A single identifier starting with an uppercase letter is REWRITTEN IN PLACE, not rejected: the value saved into the blueprint is the canonical lowerCamelCase form and the response reports it as an applied autoFix, so `OrderItem` is saved as `orderItem` and `APIKey` as `apiKey` (acronym runs are folded, the same canonicalization the data object's `name` gets). Anything else is an error you must fix: separators or punctuation (`order-item`, `order item`), a leading digit (`9bad`), and UPPER_CASE constant spellings (`ORDER_ITEM`) - the last one because a data object named `ORDER_ITEM` keeps that exact name, so no lowerCamelCase reference to it can resolve.
__PropRefer.doc: Represents a reference to a property of a data object, optionally renaming it in the current context. It is a string data, however can store string pairs joined with ':'.The first part is the name ofthe property and the second part after ':' mark is how it will be renamed in the context. If no second partis provided, the property is named in the context with its original name. Renaming is useful for mapping remote object properties to local aliases or transforming naming for aggregation.

__DataTypes.doc.#: These are the standardized data types used in microservice data models and BFF data views in OpenAPPL.
__DataTypes.doc.ID: Represents a unique identifier. Implemented as UUID in SQL databases and ObjectID in NoSQL databases.
__DataTypes.doc.String: Represents short text values, typically capped at 255 characters.
__DataTypes.doc.Text: Represents long-form text content suitable for descriptions or rich text.
__DataTypes.doc.Integer: Represents 4-byte integer values used for whole numbers.
__DataTypes.doc.Boolean: Represents logical values true or false.
__DataTypes.doc.Decimal: A FIXED-SCALE number. Use it for money and for every other quantity whose scale is part of its meaning (a rate, a weight on an invoice line): the column declares how many fractional digits it carries through `basicSettings.decimalScale` (default 2), and the framework ROUNDS every value to that scale, half-to-even, at each write boundary - every generated db-layer write helper (create, bulk create, update by id / id list / query, the doUpdate upsert), which business APIs, CRUD actions, seed data and custom dbLayer calls all write through, plus a request-parameter transform and an amount handed to a payment/invoice provider. Without it, binary floating point leaks into stored money: 3 x 16.10 = 48.300000000000004 reached a reservation amount, then the order intent, the payment provider, the invoice and the fiscal document, and every lane hand-rolled its own `Math.round((t + EPSILON) * 100) / 100`. STAGED: v1 stores the column as a Double and applies the boundary rounding above, which is what closes that hazard; v2 moves the SAME declaration to exact storage (PG NUMERIC, MySQL DECIMAL, Mongo Decimal128) with exact hydration, and needs no blueprint change when it lands. Columns bound to a payment/invoice/marketplace `amountProperty` REQUIRE this type. Declare the number in MAJOR currency units (250.00 TL, 10.00 USD), never minor units - adapters own each provider's wire encoding.
__DataTypes.doc.Short: Represents 2-byte short integers, useful for flags.
__DataTypes.doc.Object: Represents a generic JSON object, useful for flexible data structures.
__DataTypes.doc.Date: Represents date-time values, stored as ISO 8601 strings in UTC timezone.
__DataTypes.doc.Enum: Represents a fixed set of string values. Enum options are defined as an array of strings and internally stored as a short string.
__DataTypes.doc.GeoPoint: Repesents a geography point on the earth. It is a POINT GeoJson object storing lon and lat values.
__DataTypes.doc.GeoRoute: Represents a geography route on the earth. It is a LINESTRING GeoJson object, with an array of lon and lat pairs.
__DataTypes.doc.GeoArea: Represents a geography area on the earth. It is a POLYGON GeoJson object, with an array of lon and lat pairs. It hsould be closed as the last and first points should be equal. If not first point will be added automaticall as last point also.
__DataTypes.doc.Blob: Represents binary large object data. Stored as BYTEA in PostgreSQL or Buffer in MongoDB. Used for file content in database buckets.

__ProjectSettings.doc: Defines the core configuration of your OpenAPPL project, including metadata, environment preferences, and infrastructure settings. Use this section to set up the project name, description, Stripe payment settings, AI provider settings, CORS configuration, and custom CI/CD pipeline templates.

ProjectSettings.__corsSettings.doc: Defines CORS settings for service accesses. When enabled Cross Origins will be accepted according to the settings.
ProjectSettings.__basicSettings.doc: Defines the essential metadata for the project, including its name, full title, description, icon, and environment variables.
ProjectSettings.__aiProvidersSettings.doc: Settings for AI providers (LLMs + image / audio / video generators) used by AI agents (`agentHub.aiAgents`), `AiCallAction` business-API actions, and the mcpbff chat agent. Each entry is a named provider; service code resolves it by name at runtime through AI_PROVIDER_<NAME>_* environment variables. Mirrors the bucketProvidersSettings + notificationProvidersSettings shape — multiple entries can share the same provider type (e.g. two OpenAI accounts on different orgs).
ProjectSettings.__bucketProvidersSettings.doc: Settings for EXTERNAL cloud-storage bucket providers (S3, GCS, Azure Blob, R2, or any S3-compatible endpoint) used by RemoteBucket data. Each entry is a named provider; service code resolves it by name at runtime through BUCKET_<NAME>_* environment variables. Self-hosted storage needs NO provider entry — define `nativeBuckets` instead and the hosting platform provisions its own SeaweedFS (S3-API) store automatically.
ProjectSettings.__notificationProvidersSettings.doc: Settings for notification providers (email, SMS, push, Telegram, WhatsApp). Each entry is a named provider that can be referenced by EventNotification.providerName and send*Action.provider. The generator emits NOTIFICATION_PROVIDER_<NAME>_* environment variables per provider so service code can construct an SDK client at runtime without revisiting the project config. Mail has a BUILT-IN fallback: if a selected email provider's credentials are incomplete at runtime, the framework sinks the message into a mock SMTP endpoint rather than failing, so mail flows are exercisable in preview without a real mailbox. The sink is framework-owned — it is never declared in this list — so declare your real provider (or none) and add no placeholder entry. A message to a RESERVED non-deliverable recipient (an email domain under .invalid, .test, .example or .localhost, example.com / example.net / example.org, or a phone number in the fiction ranges +1 NXX 555-0100..0199 and +44 7700 900000..900999) is always stored in the channel's built-in sink and never handed to a real provider, on every deployment including production, so demo data cannot get a provider account flagged for bounces.
ProjectSettings.__paymentProvidersSettings.doc: Container for payment provider configurations — PSPs (Stripe, PayPal, iyzico, Adyen, Mangopay), merchant-of-record providers (Paddle, Lemon Squeezy), and custom adapters. Each entry is a named provider that can be referenced by DataObject `checkout` / `subscription` / `marketplace` opt-ins, by `PaymentAction.providerName`, `RefundAction.providerName`, `SubscriptionAction.providerName`, and `PayoutAction.providerName`. The generator emits PAYMENT_PROVIDER_<NAME>_* environment variables per provider so service code can construct an SDK client at runtime. Mirrors the aiProvidersSettings / bucketProvidersSettings / notificationProvidersSettings shape — multiple entries can share the same provider type (e.g. one Stripe account for one-time charges + a second Stripe Connect account for marketplace payouts).
ProjectSettings.__invoiceProvidersSettings.doc: Settings for invoice providers — the backends that issue, number, finalize and collect invoices for invoicing-enabled data objects. Invoicing is a SEPARATE axis from payment: a PaymentProvider moves money, an InvoiceProvider produces the billing document (InvoiceProvider: sap + PaymentProvider: stripe is a supported combination). Each entry is a named provider referenced by DataObject `invoicing` opt-ins. NATIVE brands (internal, stripe, logoIsbasi, mikro, parasut, custom) carry credentials in their configuration[] and the generator emits INVOICE_PROVIDER_<NAME>_* environment variables per entry; BRIDGE brands (sap, dynamics365, netsuite, logoTiger) instead name an enterpriseIntegrationsSettings entry via `integrationName` and reach the platform through the mcpbff bridge — they carry no credentials of their own. The `internal` brand needs no entry at all: a data object whose invoicing.configuration.providerName is null binds the framework-native invoicing implicitly. Mirrors the paymentProvidersSettings shape — a named array; multiple entries can share the same provider type.
ProjectSettings.__fiscalProvidersSettings.doc: Settings for fiscal providers — the integrators that submit documents into a government's fiscal infrastructure (e-invoice, e-archive, real-time reporting) for fiscalization-enabled data objects. Fiscalization is a SEPARATE axis from both payment and invoicing: an InvoiceProvider is the commercial system of record, a FiscalProvider is the regulatory transport (InvoiceProvider: logoTiger + FiscalProvider: foriba is a supported combination, and so is fiscalization with no invoice provider at all in reporting-only regimes). Each entry is a named provider referenced by DataObject `fiscalization` opt-ins; `provider` selects the adapter (v1 Turkey-first: elogo, foriba, nilvera, izibiz and uyumsoft all ship adapters; plus mock and custom), `network` names the government infrastructure it serves (GIB, SDI, KSeF, ...). Credentials live in configuration[] and the generator emits FISCAL_PROVIDER_<NAME>_* environment variables per entry. There is NO internal brand — fiscalization always goes through an integrator or the mock adapter. Mirrors the invoiceProvidersSettings shape — a named array; multiple entries can share the same provider type.
ProjectSettings.__decisionProvidersSettings.doc: Settings for calibrated decision providers — System One models that answer TYPED questions about a piece of state with a calibrated probability instead of generating text (docs/ADR-decision-layer-system-one.md). A decision layer is a SEPARATE axis from AI: a decision provider has no prompt, its answers are typed (noul probability / choice / score), and its output tokens are free, so the aiProvider surfaces (AIPromptTemplate, responseFormat, two-sided token budgets, the model price table) would state false things about it — that family split is ADR Decision 1. Each entry is a named provider referenced by decision-consuming patterns (DecisionAction, FuzzyDomainFilter, DataProperty.decisionSource); service code resolves it by name at runtime through DECISION_PROVIDER_<NAME>_* environment variables. Brands: typesafe (Jev), custom (a TypeSafe-wire-compatible endpoint, or the same interface emulated over an OpenAI/Anthropic structured-output call), and mock — a REAL keyless transport answering all three question types deterministically, so a build never blocks on a missing credential and CI never reaches the network (the payment MOCK_TRANSPORT_BRANDS precedent). NO authorization decision may ever come from a decision provider — a noul standing in for permissionCheck/membershipCheck/absoluteRoles is validation ERROR DECISION_ON_AUTHZ_SURFACE. Mirrors the bucketProvidersSettings shape — a named array; multiple entries can share the same provider type.
ProjectSettings.__computeSettings.doc: Project-level compute-layer settings (see docs/ADR-calculation-layer.md §10). Governs the bounded compute pool and queue that the compute-worker controller drains for any rust/python service that declares `computeJobs`. Mirrors the sibling settings blocks (bucketProvidersSettings, etc.) — it is a single configuration object, not a provider list. Controls global concurrency, queue depth, the default ComputeResourceProfile applied to jobs that don't set their own, the opt-in Python free-threaded toggle, and whether GPU scheduling is enabled.
ProjectSettings.__graphProvidersSettings.doc: Settings for graph-database providers (Neo4j first; the surface is provider-agnostic — see docs/ADR-graph-database-layer.md §1/§11). Each entry is a named graph connection that DataObject `objectSettings.graphProjection`, property `graphEdge`, `service.graphLayer` (edges/queries/resources), `GraphQueryAction.provider`, and `ComputeJob.graphIO.provider` reference by name. The generator emits GRAPH_<NAME>_* environment variables per provider so service code resolves the Bolt driver pool at runtime without revisiting the project config. Mirrors the bucketProvidersSettings shape — a named array. No separate graph system service (consistent with the buckets-have-no-service precedent).
ProjectSettings.__bigLoadProvidersSettings.doc: Settings for big-load datastore providers used by the big-load pattern family — the hot/cold/analytics stores behind an `EventStream`. Each entry is a named store; service code resolves it by name at runtime through BIGLOAD_<NAME>_* environment variables. Mirrors the bucketProvidersSettings / graphProvidersSettings shape — a named array. Engines: `cassandra` (write-optimized hot/time-series store), `clickhouse` (columnar OLAP analytics store), `s3Parquet` (cold columnar archive / data lake). An `EventStream`'s hotStore / coldSink / analytics bindings reference these by name.
ProjectSettings.__chatProvidersSettings.doc: RETIRED (patterns 1.60.0). Chat bots are gone: an aiAgent chat surface (`agentHub.aiAgents[].endpointSettings.chatSurfaces[].provider`) and an mcpbff chat exposure (`mcpbffSettings.chatSurfaces[].provider`) bind DIRECTLY to a channel provider, a `notificationProvidersSettings.notificationProviders[]` entry of kind `whatsapp` (Meta Cloud, provider `whatsapp`) or `telegram`, which owns every credential of the channel (WhatsApp: access token, phone number id, API version/base, app secret, verify token; Telegram: bot token, webhook secret). A blueprint still carrying this section loads: each bot is converted on load (a WhatsApp bot to its `whatsappProvider`, a Telegram bot to the telegram provider whose bot token names the same env var, else to a generated provider named after the bot), the surfaces and the mcpbff exposure are re-pointed to the provider, the bot credential fields are dropped, and validation warns per converted bot (CHAT_BOT_CONVERTED) until the converted blueprint is saved. Nothing reads CHAT_PROVIDER_<NAME>_* any more.
ProjectSettings.__amqpProvidersSettings.doc: Settings for external AMQP brokers the project mirrors Kafka topics with (external AMQP broker integration). Each entry is a named broker; the mcpbff KafkaAMQPMirror discovers the entries from the blueprint and runs the bridging — regular services stay pure Kafka and never open AMQP connections. The `provider` brand decides which AMQP protocol the mirror speaks: `rabbitmq` / `cloudamqp` = AMQP 0-9-1, `artemis` / `azureServiceBus` = AMQP 1.0. The deployed mcpbff gets AMQP_<NAME>_* environment variables per provider: HOST, PORT, VHOST and USE_TLS as committed env lines on every slot, USERNAME, PASSWORD and CONNECTION_STRING as CI/CD variables of the mcpbff repo; no business service carries any. Mirrors the bucketProvidersSettings / notificationProvidersSettings shape — a named array; multiple entries can share the same provider brand (e.g. two RabbitMQ clusters).
ProjectSettings.__enterpriseIntegrationsSettings.doc: Settings for enterprise-platform integrations (Salesforce, SAP S/4HANA + ECC, Microsoft Dynamics 365, HubSpot; NetSuite, ServiceNow, Workday and Zoho are accepted as anticipated brands whose connector has not shipped yet). Each entry is a named integration bound to one platform; the mcpbff service discovers the entries from the blueprint and owns ALL connectivity — regular services never open a connection to the platform, they run business logic around the enterprise object and reach the platform through the mcpbff bridge over signed M2M. Unlike a plain class/method integration, an OpenAPPL compiler understands each platform's metadata + organization, so enterprise integrations go beyond method calls to match DataObjects and (later) bi-directional sync. The generator emits ENTERPRISE_<NAME>_* environment variables per integration so the mcpbff bridge can construct the platform client at runtime. Mirrors the amqpProvidersSettings shape — a named array; the connectors are TypeScript-only (mcpbff), never ported to the 6 non-Node targets.
ProjectSettings.__videoProvidersSettings.doc: Settings for video-conference / live-broadcast providers used by the service `videoRooms[]` chapter (docs/ADR-video-conference-pattern-family.md). Each entry is a named media backend referenced by `VideoRoom.roomBasics.providerName`; service code resolves it at runtime through VIDEO_<NAME>_* environment variables. Brands: `native` (platform-provisioned LiveKit — no credentials, the NativeBucket precedent), `livekit`, `jitsi`, `daily`, `agora`, and the broadcast-only `awsIvs` / `mux` / `cloudflareStream`. Mirrors the bucketProvidersSettings shape — a named array.
ProjectSettings.__mailAccountsSettings.doc: Settings for project-level mail accounts — real mailboxes the project can listen to, check, read, and send from (docs/ADR-mail-account-family.md). Each entry is a named account bound to one platform (imapSmtp, gmail, microsoftGraph) with a password or xoauth2 credential set. When autoListen is on, the mcpbff bridge host watches the mailbox and publishes every new message as a normalized envelope to the account's Kafka listenTopic (default new-email-arrived) — regular services stay pure Kafka and never open a mailbox connection (the amqpProvidersSettings mirror precedent). Mail actions (check/read/send-on-behalf) reference an account by name. The generator emits MAIL_ACCOUNT_<NAME>_* environment variables per account so the bridge and actions can construct the client at runtime. Mirrors the notificationProvidersSettings shape — a named array; multiple accounts can share the same platform.
ProjectSettings.__clamAvSettings.doc: Settings for the ClamAV virus scanner that checks bucket uploads when bucket.virusScan is true. When disabled, the scanner uses the platform ClamAV REST service at the default ClamAV host (`clamav.mindbricks.com`). Configure this section to point at a private ClamAV (another REST endpoint, or a self-hosted clamd with protocol clamd) or to adjust the timeout. The platform endpoint is plain HTTP, so file bytes travel in clear text to that host.
ProjectSettings.__pipelineTemplates.doc: A list of ejs templates that renders custom CI-CD files for your services. Each file will be created in the root of your microservices after rendered using the templates with service configuration. Use these templates if you will take out your project to ypur own deployment environment and you want the compiler to generate your deploy pipeline files.
ProjectSettings.__servicePlan.doc: The microservice-definition plan carried into the blueprint FOR REFERENCE: the services the project intends to create. Written at design time (the designer agent is the usual author, but a hand-authored blueprint may set it too); absent on imported projects and on most hand-authored projects, and an absent plan changes nothing. The plan is NOT binding and NOT an inventory: a planned service that never gets built is not a defect, a service that exists but is not in the plan is not a finding, and the plan may be deleted once the last planned service exists. It has exactly one effect — a design-time reference into a service that does not exist yet is reported as a WARNING when the plan names that service, and stays an ERROR when it does not, which is the first time a forward reference is distinguishable from a typo. It never exempts anything at build or codegen time.
ProjectSettings.__socialLoginProvidersSettings.doc: Settings for social login providers: the OAuth client each brand (google, apple, facebook, microsoft, linkedin, github, gitlab) signs users in with, one entry per brand. An entry in the list is active; a brand with no entry has no social login. This is the canonical location of social login credentials. The older `authentication.socialLogins` block is still read: an enabled legacy brand counts as an entry named after the brand, a provider entry wins over a legacy entry of the same brand (validation WARNING SOCIAL_LOGIN_PROVIDER_SHADOWS_LEGACY), and the moveSocialLoginsToProviders tool moves the legacy entries here on request. The auth service reads each entry through fixed env variables (GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID / GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET, FACEBOOK_APP_ID / FACEBOOK_APP_SECRET, MICROSOFT_CLIENT_ID / MICROSOFT_CLIENT_SECRET / MICROSOFT_TENANT, LINKEDIN_*, GITHUB_*, GITLAB_*, APPLE_CLIENT_ID / APPLE_TEAM_ID / APPLE_KEY_ID / APPLE_PRIVATE_KEY); secrets are masked in API responses and delivered as CI/CD variables, never committed. Per-environment clients come from the environment values of the entry (family socialLogin), not from a second entry. Missing credentials never block a build or the boot: the login route of the brand answers a typed 503 errMsg_OAuthProviderNotConfigured_<brand> until they are set.
ProjectSettings.__elasticLogsSettings.doc: Registry of ElasticLog declarations (docs/ADR-elastic-log-pattern.md). Each entry is an owner-defined, ES-only append log (name, mapping fields, retention/ILM) — NOT a DataObject. The mcpbff service owns each log's ES index lifecycle (mapping + ILM + rolling write alias); every other service writes/reads the log DIRECTLY against Elasticsearch via generated writeToESLog_<name> / queryESLog_<name> helpers (no interservice hop). Mirrors the bucketProvidersSettings shape — a named array.
ProjectSettings.__mcpbffSettings.doc: Settings of the mcpbff system service. `chatSurfaces[]` exposes the mcpbff NATIVE full-API assistant (a user chats every project API as themselves) over messaging apps: each entry names a channel provider (`provider`, a `notificationProvidersSettings.notificationProviders[]` entry of kind `whatsapp` or `telegram`) exactly like an aiAgent chat surface does, and carries the per-surface binding (identity strategy, an optional Telegram webhook path). The surface type comes from the provider kind; the credentials are the provider's. A provider backs at most ONE conversational consumer: an aiAgent surface or an mcpbff exposure, never both (two of them would both answer every message of the number).

__BasicProjectSettings.doc: Defines the basic settings of your OpenAPPL project, including its identity, descriptive metadata, environment variables, and current lifecycle stage. These values are essential for naming, documentation, and runtime configuration.

BasicProjectSettings.__name.doc: The short name of the project. This is a required field and is often a single word. It is used as a prefix for naming project assets and resources.
BasicProjectSettings.__fullname.doc: The full, descriptive name of the project. This will appear in dashboards, documentation, and UIs.
BasicProjectSettings.__description.doc: A long-form description of the project. This text is used in documentation materials and for internal references.
BasicProjectSettings.__avatar.doc: A URL to the project's avatar icon. This image is shown in UI panels and documentation headers.
BasicProjectSettings.__frontendDocument.doc: A text based information to inform the frontend developer or frontend AI agent about the general UX behaviour of the application based on user stories and use cases. The format may be either text or markdown(recommended). Write the document as an AI prompt and describe application gneric UX behaviours. Any service or data object specific information should be given as a brief key sentence, since they will be detailed in their own objects. Note that this document will be given to the AI agent or human developer combined with all technical details that is generated from the project design,so this document should only focus on application-global behavioral UX business logic.
BasicProjectSettings.__hasAuthentication.doc: Determines if the project uses an authentication system (for users, administrators, etc.). Enabling this typically activates an auth microservice and related security features. Detailed settings are in the main authentication module.
BasicProjectSettings.__ignoreDeploymentSpecificFiles.doc: Use this in your custom deployment not to generate auto-deployemnt specific files so you can integrate your own files to your repository. AI Agents should keep this false.
BasicProjectSettings.__explicitMode.doc: Project-wide pattern mode — always `true` in this framework (the only mode). Every BusinessApi declares its full request shape via `requestParameters` and its full dataClause map via `dataClauseItems`; the framework auto-injects values from `sessionSettings` and `staticJoin` when those blocks are present on the property. Legacy implicit constructs (autoParams, DataProperty `source`) are accepted ONLY at blueprint-migration time and converted to explicit before validation/build.
BasicProjectSettings.__customVariables.doc: Key-value pairs defining custom environment variables for the project. These variables are available in runtime and can be accessed in service logic and functions. A variable whose name has a secret-shaped segment (TOKEN, SECRET, KEY, PASSWORD, ...) is a deploy secret unless its entry says secret: false: its value stays out of the committed env files and is pushed as a CI/CD variable.
BasicProjectSettings.__description.sample: Babil Online Book Store is a project to sell books online. It is a basic sample project with a BFF service and several microservices for learning purposes.
BasicProjectSettings.__frontendUrl.doc: Per-environment base URLs for the frontend application. Used to derive callback URLs (e.g. social login redirect). Defaults: dev=http://localhost:5173, test=`https://{codename}.<test-domain>`, stage=`https://{codename}-stage.<app-domain>`, prod=`https://{codename}.<app-domain>`, where the domains are set by the hosting platform. Override when using a custom domain.
BasicProjectSettings.name: String

__NotificationProvidersSettings.doc: Container for notification provider configurations (email, SMS, push, Telegram, WhatsApp). Each entry is a named provider that can be referenced by EventNotification.providerName, sendMailAction.provider, sendSmsAction.provider, sendPushNotificationAction.provider, and sendWhatsAppAction.provider. The generator emits NOTIFICATION_PROVIDER_<NAME>_* environment variables per provider so service code can construct an SDK client at runtime without revisiting the project config. Mail has a BUILT-IN fallback: if a selected email provider's credentials are incomplete at runtime, the framework sinks the message into a mock SMTP endpoint rather than failing, so mail flows are exercisable in preview without a real mailbox. The sink is framework-owned — it is never declared in this list — so declare your real provider (or none) and add no placeholder entry. A message to a RESERVED non-deliverable recipient (an email domain under .invalid, .test, .example or .localhost, example.com / example.net / example.org, or a phone number in the fiction ranges +1 NXX 555-0100..0199 and +44 7700 900000..900999) is always stored in the channel's built-in sink and never handed to a real provider, on every deployment including production, so demo data cannot get a provider account flagged for bounces.

NotificationProvidersSettings.__notificationProviders.doc: List of configured notification providers. Add one entry per messaging account you want available. Multiple entries can share the same provider type (e.g. two Twilio accounts, or one Twilio for SMS and one for WhatsApp).

__NotificationProvider.doc:
A named notification provider configuration. The `name` is the lookup key used by EventNotification.providerName / send*Action.provider and the env-var prefix (e.g. `mainSmtp` → `NOTIFICATION_PROVIDER_MAINSMTP_*`). The `kind` selects the channel; the `provider` enum selects the backend SDK. `kind` and `provider` are orthogonal — the same SDK (e.g. Twilio) can serve multiple kinds via separate entries. The `configuration` is a free-form key/value list whose required keys depend on the chosen `provider`; the UI and the agent ontology doc enforce the per-provider shape.

Expected configuration keys per provider:
- smtp (email): emailFrom, emailHost, emailPort, emailUser, emailPass, isSecure
- sendgrid (email): emailFrom, sendGridApiKey
- resend (email): emailFrom, resendApiKey
- amazonsns (sms, push): awsAccessKeyId, awsSecretAccessKey, awsRegion; push also takes platformApplicationArn (optional). kind=sms publishes direct to a PhoneNumber. kind=push publishes SNS mobile push: a recipient that is an SNS platform-endpoint ARN is published to directly, a raw FCM/APNs device token (what the DeviceToken registry stores) is first registered against platformApplicationArn with CreatePlatformEndpoint. Declare one entry per channel (kind='multi' is refused). NOT email: the AmazonSNS email adapter was removed; email over AWS is amazonses (Amazon SES).
- twilio (sms): twilioAccountSid, twilioAuthToken, twilioSender
- twilio (whatsapp): twilioAccountSid, twilioAuthToken, whatsappFrom (e.g. 'whatsapp:+14155238886'). twilioAuthToken also verifies the delivery-status callbacks of the notification service, which are requested only when SERVICE_URL is set.
- vonage (sms): vonageApiKey, vonageApiSecret, vonageSender
- netgsm (sms): netgsmUsername, netgsmPassword, netgsmSender
- firebase (push): firebaseProjectId, firebaseClientEmail, firebasePrivateKey
- onesignal (push): oneSignalAppId, oneSignalApiKey
- telegram (telegram): telegramBotToken, telegramApiBase (optional, default https://api.telegram.org), telegramWebhookSecret (optional; the secret token Telegram presents on the webhook of an aiAgent surface or an mcpbff exposure bound to this provider - without it that webhook refuses every update). A telegram provider is also the CHANNEL PROVIDER of chat surfaces: an agent surface or mcpbff exposure that names it replies with its telegramBotToken
- whatsapp (whatsapp, Meta Cloud API): whatsappAccessToken, whatsappPhoneNumberId, whatsappApiVersion (optional, default v20.0), whatsappApiBase (optional, default https://graph.facebook.com), whatsappAppSecret and whatsappVerifyToken (they authenticate this provider's ONE inbound door on the notification service, POST/GET /v1/whatsapp-webhooks/meta/<name>, where Meta sends every webhook of the number: inbound customer messages for the agents and bots bound to this provider by name, delivery statuses for the delivery log, other field changes - without them the door refuses every call). An aiAgent chat surface or an mcpbff exposure names this provider in `provider` and carries no credential of its own: its replies post with this provider's whatsappAccessToken, whatsappPhoneNumberId and whatsappApiVersion (chat bots are retired)

Secret keys (emailPass, sendGridApiKey, resendApiKey, awsAccessKeyId, awsSecretAccessKey, twilioAuthToken, vonageApiSecret, netgsmPassword, firebasePrivateKey, oneSignalApiKey, telegramBotToken, telegramWebhookSecret, whatsappAccessToken, whatsappAppSecret, whatsappVerifyToken) are masked in API responses and emitted to NOTIFICATION_PROVIDER_<NAME>_<KEY> env vars at codegen time.

MAIL NEVER SILENTLY FAILS FOR WANT OF A CREDENTIAL. The framework carries a BUILT-IN mock SMTP mail sink, and it is not a provider you declare, seed or maintain — there is no entry for it in this list and there is nothing to point at it. If the email provider a send selected has incomplete credentials at runtime (a required key unset in that deployment's environment), the framework routes that message to the sink instead of failing in the SMTP dialogue: the sink accepts the session and captures the message so email verification, password reset and any other mail flow can be exercised end to end without a real mailbox and without leaking mail to real addresses. A loud WARN names the bypassed provider and the missing variable NAMES; in production the boot report raises the same finding as an ERROR.

THE SINK REPORTS SUCCESS ONLY WHERE ITS HOST EXISTS. The sink is a real mock-SMTP endpoint the deployment must provide (infra requirement `mail-sink`: port 465, cleartext session, accepts any credentials or none, stores what it accepts readably) - it is NOT an in-process log-and-drop. Where an environment has not provisioned that host, every send to the sink FAILS with a named connection error and is retried; the error names the missing requirement, so do not read it as an outage of the provider you declared. On the deployed preview and stage environments the sink is dialled on port 587 in cleartext with the project codename as the SMTP user and a password the sink ignores (`ignored`) - the sink keeps each project's messages apart by that user; the build compiles this coordinate into the service environment (MAILSINK_PORT / MAILSINK_USER / MAILSINK_PASS), so there is nothing to configure. A service whose SendSmsAction sends to the built-in SMS sink because it names no `provider` in a project that declares no sms provider carries the same coordinate, since the SMS sink stores each SMS through it. `GET /v1/mail/mock-status` answers 'is mail sinking here, and why' in one call, and tells the two sink-engagement classes apart: `incomplete-credentials` (an email provider is declared but short of a key) versus `no-channel-match` (no declared provider serves email at all).

WHAT THIS MEANS WHEN YOU DESIGN. Declare the real provider you intend to use, with whatever credentials you have, or declare none at all — both work. There is NO placeholder to add and NO placeholder to remove before going to production: as soon as a provider's configuration is complete the fallback stops engaging for it, automatically, with no blueprint change. Do not invent a placeholder mail provider of your own, and do not treat the sink as a delivery mechanism — mail that reaches it was NOT delivered to its recipients.

ALWAYS DECLARE `kind`. It has a default (`email`), so an entry written without one validates clean at every level and then serves the wrong channel: the runtime resolver finds no provider for the send's channel and the message drains into the same mail sink an incomplete credential drains into - a missing channel TYPE and a missing CREDENTIAL become one silent behaviour. A defaulted kind is reported as the warning NOTIFICATION_PROVIDER_KIND_DEFAULTED, and the organization-level provider store refuses to store an item without one.

SMS FALLS BACK TO THE BUILT-IN SMS SINK OUTSIDE PRODUCTION. A real sms provider, when its credentials are set, is used on every deployment. When a `kind: sms` provider's credentials are NOT set, the send goes to the built-in SMS sink on the dev, preview and stage deployments: the sink stores each SMS in the mail sink above as one mail addressed to `sms-<digits of the number>@sms-sink.invalid`, subject `SMS to <number>`, so a tester reads sunk SMS in the same inbox as sunk mail and no second service is needed. Production has NO SMS sink: an sms provider with incomplete credentials fails the send there and the boot report names it. The SMS sink is not a provider you declare: declare the real sms provider you intend to use (with or without credentials). A `multi` entry is not routed to it when an event notification sends through it; a SendSmsAction that names a `multi` entry sends as sms and is routed like an sms provider.

A PROJECT WITH NO SMS PROVIDER SENDS EVERY SMS TO THE SMS SINK. Under the same rule as mail with no mail provider, a project that declares no sms-capable provider gets a framework-synthesised last-resort entry at build time, so mobile verification, mobile 2FA, reset-by-mobile, sms event notifications and a SendSmsAction without a provider all send to the SMS sink - on EVERY deployment, production included. Declaring a real sms provider takes precedence at once. Project validation raises ONE non-blocking warning, SMS_FLOWS_GO_TO_SINK, listing the SMS flows found, until an sms provider is declared (VERIFICATION_FLOW_MISSING_PROVIDER no longer fires for sms); the `smsSink` block of the mock-status answer reads `no-channel-match`. `GET /v1/mail/mock-status` reports it in its `smsSink` block.

WHATSAPP, TELEGRAM AND PUSH FOLLOW THE SMS SINK TABLE. A declared `kind: whatsapp`, `telegram` or `push` provider whose credentials are NOT set sends to that channel's built-in sink on the dev, preview and stage deployments and fails the send on production. A project that declares no provider of the channel (`multi` counts as declared) gets a framework-synthesised last-resort entry at build time (`__whatsappsink__`, `__telegramsink__`, `__pushsink__`), so an event notification of that jobType builds and sends to the sink on EVERY deployment, production included. Each sunk message is stored in the mail sink as one mail to `whatsapp-<digits>@whatsapp-sink.invalid`, `telegram-<chat id>@telegram-sink.invalid` or `push-<first 16 hex of sha256(device token)>@push-sink.invalid`. Project validation raises one non-blocking warning per channel (WHATSAPP_FLOWS_GO_TO_SINK, TELEGRAM_FLOWS_GO_TO_SINK, PUSH_FLOWS_GO_TO_SINK) listing those event notifications; `GET /v1/mail/mock-status` reports the sinks in `channelSinks` and lists a sunk provider with fallback `whatsappSink` / `telegramSink` / `pushSink`. The java and golang runtimes fail those sends loudly until their sinks are ported.

A PROJECT WITH NO EMAIL PROVIDER IS WARNED TOO. Every mail of a project that declares no email-capable provider goes to the mail sink on every deployment, production included, so project validation raises ONE non-blocking warning, MAIL_FLOWS_GO_TO_SINK, listing the mail flows found (email verification, reset by email, email 2FA, email2FARequiredForLogin, email event notifications), until an email provider is declared.

NotificationProvider.__name.doc: Unique provider identifier within the project. Used as the lookup key from EventNotification.providerName / send*Action.provider and the env-var prefix. Must be a valid codeName.
NotificationProvider.name: String
NotificationProvider.__kind.doc: The notification channel this entry serves. 'email' / 'sms' / 'push' are the traditional channels. 'telegram' / 'whatsapp' are chat platforms. 'multi' is for providers that span multiple channels (e.g. Twilio for SMS + WhatsApp).
NotificationProvider.__provider.doc: The backend provider implementation. Selects which keys are expected in `configuration` and which client module the codegen wires up. The (kind, provider) pair drives the per-channel client variant — e.g. (sms, twilio) emits a plain Twilio SMS client, while (whatsapp, twilio) emits the WhatsApp-channel variant.
NotificationProvider.__configuration.doc: Free-form key/value list of provider-specific credentials and settings. The required keys depend on `provider` — see the NotificationProvider doc string for the per-provider key list. The UI enforces the right form fields per provider; agents emit only keys that match. Sensitive keys (passwords, tokens, secrets) are masked in API responses and emitted to environment variables at codegen time.
NotificationProvider.__chatHandling.doc: OPTIONAL - deterministic chat handlers on this CHANNEL PROVIDER (kind `whatsapp` with provider `whatsapp`, or kind `telegram`; any other kind is refused with CHAT_HANDLER_PROVIDER_KIND_UNSUPPORTED). An ordered list of handlers answers inbound messages of the number or bot by calling a business API and replying from a template, with no AI agent in between: the FIRST handler that matches claims the message, BEFORE an agent surface or mcpbff exposure bound to the same provider sees it; a message no handler claims reaches that conversational consumer exactly as before. The notification service runs every handler (it hosts the WhatsApp door, the Telegram door of a provider no agent binds, and the handler topic `<codename>-chat-handler-inbound`); an agent host only claims a Telegram update and forwards it. Push prompts with choices (approve / reject) are declared here too and are answered by `promptReply` handlers. Leave it null and the provider behaves exactly as before. Generated for nodejs and rust for now (CHAT_HANDLER_LANGUAGE_NOT_SUPPORTED otherwise).

__ChatHandlingSettings.doc: Deterministic chat handlers and push prompts of one channel provider (`notificationProviders[].chatHandling`), matched in declared order before any AI agent bound to the provider. Each handler maps a command, a message type, a pattern or a prompt reply to an optional business API call and a reply template; the sender is resolved to a user through the same chat identity seam the agent surfaces use (a linked account, or the phone on WhatsApp with `identityStrategy: phone`). A sender with no linked account is refused unless the handler sets `allowAnonymous`. On a provider with no agent or mcpbff exposure (handler-only) the handler runtime also answers the account link commands (Telegram `/start <code>`, WhatsApp `link <code>`), an unknown `/command` with the help reply, and leaves other unmatched messages unanswered; on a provider with a conversational consumer those reach the consumer.

ChatHandlingSettings.__identityStrategy.doc: How a sender is resolved to an application user before a handler runs: 'link' (default; an account linked with a link code only) or 'phone' (WhatsApp only: the channel-asserted phone is matched against an existing user and the link is written on first use). 'phone' on a Telegram provider is refused (CHAT_HANDLER_IDENTITY_STRATEGY_INVALID): Telegram does not assert a phone.
ChatHandlingSettings.__helpText.doc: The help reply's first lines, sent for an unknown `/command` and a bare `/start` on a handler-only provider. The reply continues with one line per command handler (`/command - description`). Null = the command lines only.
ChatHandlingSettings.__handlers.doc: The handlers, in MATCH ORDER: the first handler whose match fits an inbound message claims it, and a claimed message runs exactly one handler, at most once. Names are unique per provider (CHAT_HANDLER_NAME_DUPLICATE) and so are commands (CHAT_HANDLER_COMMAND_DUPLICATE).
ChatHandlingSettings.__prompts.doc: Push prompts of this provider: an EventNotification delivered by this provider whose message carries choices (WhatsApp reply buttons, a list, or the quick-reply buttons of an approved template; Telegram inline keyboard buttons). A tapped choice is answered by the `promptReply` handler that names the prompt (and the choice). Null = no prompts.

__ChatHandler.doc: One deterministic chat handler: a match, an optional business API call and a reply template. The `match` selects inbound messages, the `action` calls one business API with parameters filled from the message, and the `response` is rendered from the message and the API answer. No action = a static reply. The handler runs for a linked user with that user's session; `allowAnonymous: true` also runs it for a sender with no linked account, with no credential at all, so its API must be login-free. On Telegram the reply goes to the chat the message came from: a handler triggered in a group posts its reply, built from the sender's data, into that group.

ChatHandler.__name.doc: Unique handler name within the provider; it names the handler in the logs. Must be a valid codeName.
ChatHandler.name: String
ChatHandler.__description.doc: Shown after the command in the help reply (`/command - description`). Null = the command alone.
ChatHandler.__match.doc: Which inbound messages this handler claims: a `/command`, a message type (a location, an image, ...), a pattern over the text, or the reply to a push prompt.
ChatHandler.__action.doc: The business API the handler calls. Null = a static reply (the response text alone, no call).
ChatHandler.__response.doc: The reply sent to the sender: a text, a list rendered from the API answer, and the text sent when the call fails. At least one of `text` and `list` (CHAT_HANDLER_RESPONSE_EMPTY).
ChatHandler.__allowAnonymous.doc: When true the handler also runs for a sender with no linked account; the API is then called with NO credential (no bearer, no machine token), so `action.api` must declare `authOptions.loginRequired: false` (CHAT_HANDLER_ANONYMOUS_LOGIN_REQUIRED otherwise). Default false: an unlinked sender gets one reply asking to link the account, and no call is made. A blocked account is refused even here.

__ChatHandlerMatch.doc: What a chat handler claims. `kind` selects which one of the other fields is read: `command` (the word after `/`), `messageType`, `pattern` (a regular expression over the text) or `prompt` and `choice` (a reply to a push prompt of the same provider).

ChatHandlerMatch.__kind.doc: The matcher: 'command' (a text starting with `/<command>`), 'messageType' (a location, image, document, audio, video or contact message), 'pattern' (a regular expression over the text) or 'promptReply' (a tapped choice of a push prompt).
ChatHandlerMatch.__command.doc: kind 'command': the command word without the slash, 1-32 characters of `a-z`, `0-9` and `_`, matched case-insensitively (`/Status` matches `status`). The text after it is the `args` of the templates. `start` and `link` are reserved for account linking (CHAT_HANDLER_COMMAND_RESERVED).
ChatHandlerMatch.__messageType.doc: kind 'messageType': the message type this handler claims.
ChatHandlerMatch.__pattern.doc: kind 'pattern': a regular expression tested case-insensitively against the first 512 characters of the text; its capture groups are `match.<n>` and `match.<name>` in the templates. At most 200 characters; a backreference, a repeated group that contains a quantifier or an alternation, and a repeated lookaround are refused (CHAT_HANDLER_PATTERN_UNSAFE), because the text is attacker-controlled. At runtime a pattern runs under a 50 ms budget: a run past it does not match, and a handler whose pattern times out 3 times within 60 seconds has the pattern switched off for 5 minutes (one `ChatHandlerPatternDisabled` warn line), then tried again.
ChatHandlerMatch.__prompt.doc: kind 'promptReply': the name of a prompt of this provider (`chatHandling.prompts[].name`).
ChatHandlerMatch.__choice.doc: kind 'promptReply': the choice id this handler answers. Null = every choice of the prompt.

__ChatHandlerMatchKind.doc.#: The matcher of a chat handler.
__ChatHandlerMatchKind.doc.messageType: A message of one type: location, image, document, audio, video or contact.
__ChatHandlerMatchKind.doc.pattern: A text that matches a regular expression.
__ChatHandlerMatchKind.doc.promptReply: A tapped choice of a push prompt of the same provider.

__ChatHandlerMessageType.doc.#: An inbound chat message type a handler can claim.

__ChatHandlerAction.doc: The one business API call of a chat handler, over the API's REST route. The call carries the resolved user's session (a token minted for the linked user), or no credential at all for an anonymous sender of an `allowAnonymous` handler. A failed call is answered with `response.errorText` and never retried.

ChatHandlerAction.__service.doc: The service that declares `api`. Null = the one service that declares an API of that name; required when two services do (CHAT_HANDLER_API_AMBIGUOUS) and for an API of a system service (auth, notification, ...).
ChatHandlerAction.__api.doc: The business API to call. It must have a REST controller (CHAT_HANDLER_API_NO_REST otherwise). If the API's `authOptions.requiredCallerKind` (under `basics`) is `machineWithoutUserIdentity`, no chat sender can call it (`CHAT_HANDLER_API_CALLER_KIND` error, and generation fails); `machine` is a warning of the same code, because a linked sender's call passes that gate (the notification service's machine token rides beside the user's session).
ChatHandlerAction.__parameters.doc: The API parameters filled from the message, by parameter name; each value is a template (`{{args.0}}`, `{{location.latitude}}`, ...). Every route segment of the API (`:id`) must be filled (CHAT_HANDLER_PATH_PARAM_UNMAPPED). Null = no parameters.

__ChatHandlerParameter.doc: One name and template value pair of a chat handler: an API parameter of `action.parameters`, or a data key a push prompt records (`prompts[].data`).

ChatHandlerParameter.__name.doc: The API parameter name (action) or the data key (prompt data, read back as `prompt.data.<key>`). The names `__proto__`, `constructor` and `prototype` cannot be carried by the runtime and are refused (CHAT_HANDLER_NAME_RESERVED): rename such a parameter or data key.
ChatHandlerParameter.name: String
ChatHandlerParameter.__value.doc: A template: literal text with `{{path}}` placeholders over a closed set of roots (`text`, `args`, `match`, `location`, `media`, `contact`, `sender`, `user`, `channel`, `provider`, `prompt`; prompt data reads `event`). A value that is exactly one placeholder keeps the JSON type of its source (a latitude stays a number). An unknown root is refused (CHAT_HANDLER_PLACEHOLDER_UNKNOWN); an unknown path at runtime renders empty.

__ChatHandlerResponse.doc: The reply of a chat handler, plain text cut at 4096 characters: `text`, then one line per row of `list`, or `list.emptyText` when the list is empty. `errorText` replaces both when the API call fails.

ChatHandlerResponse.__text.doc: The reply text, a template over the message roots plus `result.<path>` (the API's JSON answer). Null = the list alone.
ChatHandlerResponse.__list.doc: A list rendered from an array in the API answer. Null = no list.
ChatHandlerResponse.__errorText.doc: Sent when the API call fails, a template that may read `error.message` and `error.code`. Null = a generic failure reply.

__ChatHandlerResponseList.doc: A reply list built from an array in a chat handler's API answer: one line per row, rendered from the `item` template.

ChatHandlerResponseList.__source.doc: The dotted path of the array in the API answer (for example `pharmacies` or `data.items`).
ChatHandlerResponseList.__item.doc: One line per row, a template that reads `item.<path>` (the row) and `index` (its 1-based position) besides the message roots.
ChatHandlerResponseList.__maxItems.doc: At most this many rows are listed (1 to 50). Default 10.
ChatHandlerResponseList.__emptyText.doc: Sent instead of the rows when the array is empty or absent. Null = nothing after the text.

__ChatPrompt.doc: A push prompt of a channel provider: an EventNotification delivered by this provider whose rendered text becomes a message with choices. A tapped choice is answered by the `promptReply` handler that names this prompt, within `ttlHours`, once, and only by the chat that received the prompt (and, when the notification resolved a user, only by that user).

ChatPrompt.__name.doc: Unique prompt name within the provider, named by `match.prompt` of a `promptReply` handler. Must be a valid codeName.
ChatPrompt.name: String
ChatPrompt.__notification.doc: The EventNotification (`notificationService.eventNotifications[].eventNotificationBasics.name`) whose message this prompt sends. Its jobType must be this provider's channel and it must be delivered by THIS provider, named explicitly or as the channel default (CHAT_HANDLER_PROMPT_NOTIFICATION_UNBOUND). On WhatsApp a notification that sends an approved template needs as many quick-reply buttons in that template as there are choices.
ChatPrompt.__choices.doc: The choices, 1 to 10 with unique ids (CHAT_HANDLER_PROMPT_CHOICES_INVALID). WhatsApp shows 1-3 as reply buttons and 4-10 as a list.
ChatPrompt.__ttlHours.doc: How long a choice can be tapped, in hours, 1 to 168 (CHAT_HANDLER_PROMPT_TTL_INVALID). Default 24. A tap after expiry, a second tap, or a tap from another chat is refused with a reply and no API call.
ChatPrompt.__data.doc: Data recorded with the prompt and read back by the reply handler as `prompt.data.<key>`; each value is a template over `event.<key>` (the notification's event record, for example `{{event.orderId}}`). Null = no data.

__ChatPromptChoice.doc: One choice of a push prompt: the id a `promptReply` handler matches and the title shown on the button or list row.

ChatPromptChoice.__id.doc: The choice id, 1-24 characters of `a-z`, `0-9` and `_`, unique within the prompt; it rides the button payload. The ids `__proto__`, `constructor` and `prototype` cannot be carried by the runtime and are refused (CHAT_HANDLER_NAME_RESERVED).
ChatPromptChoice.__title.doc: The button or list row title, 1 to 20 characters.
ChatPromptChoice.title: String

__AiProvidersSettings.doc: Container for AI provider configurations — LLM, image, audio, and video backends used by AI agents (`agentHub.aiAgents`), `AiCallAction` business-API actions, and the mcpbff chat surface. Each entry is a named provider that can be referenced by AIAgent.modelSettings.providerName / AiCallAction.providerName / chat agent config. The generator emits AI_PROVIDER_<NAME>_* environment variables per provider so service code can construct an SDK client at runtime without revisiting the project config. Replaces the legacy `aiSettings` (fixed openAI + Anthropic key pair) with the same shape used by bucketProvidersSettings and notificationProvidersSettings — multiple entries can share the same provider type (e.g. two OpenAI accounts on different orgs, or one OpenAI for chat and one for embeddings).

AiProvidersSettings.__aiProviders.doc: List of configured AI providers. Add one entry per AI account / backend you want available. Multiple entries can share the same provider type (e.g. two OpenAI keys on different orgs).
AiProvidersSettings.__modelPrices.doc: Optional model price overrides for the AI agent cost governor. The agent runtime prices every provider call from a versioned, dated built-in table in USD per 1M tokens (input, output, prompt-cache read and prompt-cache write, with the date each row was read and its source) covering the current Anthropic Claude models, the current OpenAI and Google Gemini models, and xAI and DeepSeek. A model id is matched exactly first, then by the longest family prefix (the key followed by '-', '@', ':' or '_'); a model that matches nothing is priced by the '*' fallback (3 USD input / 15 USD output per 1M tokens) and its cost is marked estimated. Costs are approximate: list prices, without batch, priority, regional or contract discounts. Each entry here is merged OVER the built-in table in every generated service that hosts agents; the AGENT_MODEL_PRICES environment variable (JSON map of model key -> { inputPerMTok, outputPerMTok, cacheReadPerMTok, cacheWritePerMTok }) is merged last and wins. Use it for a model the built-in table does not know (self-hosted, fine-tuned, a new release) or whose contract price differs.

__AiModelPrice.doc: One model price override for the AI agent cost governor: a model key and its USD prices per 1M input, output, prompt-cache read and prompt-cache write tokens. Matched against the agent's model id case-insensitively: an exact key first, then the longest key that is a family prefix of the id (e.g. 'gpt-4o-mini' matches 'gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18'), across the built-in table, these entries and AGENT_MODEL_PRICES; an override key that is neither still matches as a substring of the id, after every exact and prefix match.

AiModelPrice.__model.doc: Model id or family prefix this price applies to, e.g. 'gpt-4o-mini', 'llama-3.3-70b', 'my-finetune'. Matched case-insensitively against the agent's resolved model id (modelSettings.model or the provider's defaultModel): an exact match first, then the longest family prefix, then a substring.
AiModelPrice.__inputPerMTok.doc: Price in USD per 1,000,000 input (prompt) tokens. 0 for a free/self-hosted model.
AiModelPrice.__outputPerMTok.doc: Price in USD per 1,000,000 output (completion) tokens. 0 for a free/self-hosted model.
AiModelPrice.__cacheReadPerMTok.doc: Optional price in USD per 1,000,000 prompt-cache read (cache hit) tokens. Leave empty to bill cache reads at inputPerMTok.
AiModelPrice.__cacheWritePerMTok.doc: Optional price in USD per 1,000,000 prompt-cache write tokens (the default 5-minute cache). Leave empty to bill cache writes at inputPerMTok.

__AiProvider.doc:
A named AI provider configuration. The `name` is the lookup key used by AIAgent.modelSettings.providerName / AiCallAction.providerName / mcpbff chat-agent config, and the env-var prefix (e.g. `summarizer` → `AI_PROVIDER_SUMMARIZER_*`). The `provider` enum selects the backend SDK / adapter shipped under `_common/nodejs/src/common/ai-providers/`. The `configuration` is a free-form key/value list whose required keys depend on the chosen `provider`; the UI and the agent ontology doc enforce the per-provider shape.

Expected configuration keys per provider:
- openai: apiKey, organization (optional), defaultModel (optional, e.g. 'gpt-4o-mini')
- anthropic: apiKey, defaultModel (optional, e.g. 'claude-sonnet-4-5'), baseUrl (optional, the API root of a proxy or gateway; the adapter posts to <baseUrl>/v1/messages)
- xai: apiKey, defaultModel (optional, e.g. 'grok-4')
- deepseek: apiKey, defaultModel (optional)
- moonshot: apiKey, defaultModel (optional)
- fal: apiKey, defaultModel (optional, e.g. 'fal-ai/flux/dev')
- elevenlabs: apiKey, voice (optional default voice id), defaultModel (optional, e.g. 'eleven_multilingual_v2')
- runway: apiKey, defaultModel (optional)
- google: projectId + location, plus serviceAccountJson for an inline service account (omit it to authenticate with GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS / Application Default Credentials), defaultModel (optional, e.g. 'gemini-2.0-flash'). apiKey is NOT supported by the Vertex adapter and is rejected by validation (AI_PROVIDER_UNSUPPORTED_CONFIG)
- azure-openai: apiKey, baseUrl, deployment, apiVersion (optional, default '2024-10-21')
- bedrock: awsAccessKeyId, awsSecretAccessKey, awsRegion, defaultModel (optional, e.g. 'anthropic.claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022-v2:0')
- ollama: baseUrl (e.g. 'http://localhost:11434'), defaultModel (optional) — keyless
- custom: apiKey (optional), baseUrl, apiFormat ('openai'|'anthropic'|'raw'), extraHeaders (optional JSON string)

Secret keys (apiKey, awsAccessKeyId, awsSecretAccessKey, serviceAccountJson) are masked in API responses and emitted to AI_PROVIDER_<NAME>_<KEY> env vars at codegen time. The apiKey listed for a brand is the application owner's (saas) key: when `credentialScopes` makes a tenant or user level `required` the entry may leave it out, because each tenant or user stores their own key through the auth service (nodejs services; see AiProviderCredentialScopes).
- mock: seed (optional, defaults to `mindbricks`). Keyless offline text completions, declared explicitly, never a credential fallback. Node.js and Rust; other deployment languages refuse the brand until ported. [[mock-ai reply=<text or JSON>]] steers test responses only with explicit matching dev/preview/staging deployment signals; production and unknown signals refuse directives.

AiProvider.__name.doc: Unique provider identifier within the project. Used as the lookup key from AIAgent.modelSettings.providerName / AiCallAction.providerName / mcpbff chat config and as the env-var prefix. Must be a valid codeName.
AiProvider.name: String
AiProvider.__provider.doc: The backend provider implementation. Selects which keys are expected in `configuration` and which adapter the codegen wires up. The mock brand is explicitly declared keyless offline text completion on Node.js and Rust, never an implicit fallback; see the mock AI provider guide.
AiProvider.__configuration.doc: Free-form key/value list of provider-specific credentials and settings. The required keys depend on `provider` — see the AiProvider doc string for the per-provider key list. The UI enforces the right form fields per provider; agents emit only keys that match. Sensitive keys (apiKey, awsSecretAccessKey, serviceAccountJson) are masked in API responses and emitted to environment variables at codegen time.
AiProvider.__credentialScopes.doc: Optional. Lets a tenant or a user bring their own key (BYOK) for this provider entry instead of, or as well as, the application owner's key in `configuration`. Leave it empty, or set every scope to `off`, and the entry behaves exactly as before: one key, the application owner's. The levels are saas (the owner's key in `configuration`, deployed as a secret), tenant (multi-tenant projects only), resource (a row of a data object that carries a membership configuration, such as a workspace, a team or a company: its owner and its admins set one key every member uses; see `credentialScopes.resource`) and user. At call time the key is taken from the user, then the resource, then the tenant, then the saas level, skipping any level that is `off` or has no stored key. A scoped credential carries only the secret key plus the brand's organisation or project field (openai: apiKey, organization, project; the other supported brands: apiKey); `baseUrl`, the model and every other option stay this entry's, so a user can never point calls at another host. Supported brands: openai, anthropic, xai, deepseek, moonshot, elevenlabs, runway, fal, custom. google, azure-openai, bedrock, ollama and mock cannot enable a scope. Keys are saved through the auth service (`/my-provider-credentials`, `/tenant-provider-credentials`), checked with a cheap live call before they are stored, and kept encrypted; no API, log or error ever returns them.

__AiProviderCredentialScopes.doc: Which credential levels below the application owner (saas) may supply the key for one AI provider entry, and who pays for calls made with those keys. Every scope is `off` by default, which keeps the entry exactly as it was. `optional` lets the tenant or user save a key that is used when present, with fallback to the next level. `required` means the level must have a key: a call without one fails with HTTP 428 and the code `AI_PROVIDER_CREDENTIAL_REQUIRED` (the problem body's `errorCode`, the mcpbff chat's `code`; the message names the provider and the scope) and the saas key is never used, so a frontend can ask the user to add their key. When a lower scope is `required` the saas key in `configuration` becomes optional and a BYOK-only project needs none. Validation: `tenant` must stay `off` in a single-tenant project (the chain there is saas then user); a scope cannot be enabled on a brand that does not support scoped keys; and on a brand without a cheap live check (fal, custom) a warning says saved keys will be stored as `unverified`. Covered callers (nodejs services only; the other languages do not read this setting yet): AI agents and each of their fallback providers, agentHub agents, AiCallAction, the mcpbff chat and AI completion, and the AgentHarness model gateway. Video-layer and content-layer AI calls always use the saas key. Kafka and cron runs have no user, so they resolve tenant then saas. Stored keys are sealed under the deploy secret `PROVIDER_CREDENTIAL_KEY`, which auth, the AI-calling services and the mcpbff must receive in every slot. The `resource` block adds a fourth level between the user and the tenant: a key owned by one row of a membership-bearing data object (a workspace), managed by the row's creator and the member roles named in `managers`, and used by the members named in `users`. The full order is user, then resource, then tenant, then saas; set `user` to `off` when the workspace key must win over a personal one. Like the other levels it is `off` by default, and an entry without it is unchanged.

AiProviderCredentialScopes.__tenant.doc: Tenant level: `off` (default), `optional` or `required`. A tenant owner or tenant admin saves the tenant's key with `PUT /tenant-provider-credentials/:providerName` on the auth service; saas admins and super admins may manage any tenant with `?tenantId=`, and each such action on another tenant is audited. Only valid in a multi-tenant project: anything other than `off` in a single-tenant project is a validation error.
AiProviderCredentialScopes.__user.doc: User level: `off` (default), `optional` or `required`. Each user saves their own key with `PUT /my-provider-credentials/:providerName` on the auth service and reads the status (has a key, last 4 characters, valid / invalid / unverified, last verified and last used times) with `GET /my-provider-credentials`. A user key wins over the tenant and saas keys. Calls with no user (Kafka or cron runs) skip this level, even when it is `required`.
AiProviderCredentialScopes.__costPolicy.doc: Who pays for calls made on a tenant, resource or user key. `ownerPays` (default): usage on a user key is charged to that user's own budget only; usage on a tenant key is charged to the user and to the tenant's own-key budget, which no ceiling reads; usage on a resource key is charged to the user and to that row's own budget, which only the row's `resource.budget.dailyCostCeilingUsd` reads. None of them is charged to the tenant, agent or project (saas) budgets, and the daily cost ceiling does not apply to them; the per-user daily token budget still does. Usage is still recorded so each owner can see their own spend. `saasPays`: every call counts toward the saas budgets as it does today.
AiProviderCredentialScopes.__resource.doc: Optional. The resource level: a key owned by ONE ROW of a data object that carries a membership configuration (a workspace, a team, a company, a project), set by that row's creator or its admins and used by its members. Use it when users group themselves into several such rows without the project being multi-tenant, or inside one tenant, and each row must run on its own provider key; a user may belong to several rows, each with its own key. Leave it empty, or set `mode` to `off`, and nothing changes. The block names the data object, how the row id is read from the call (`idFrom`), and which member roles may set the key (`managers`) and use it (`users`); the row's creator always may do both. Before a resource key is ever used, the caller's membership in the named row is verified by the service that owns the data object, so a row id read from the call is never trusted on its own: a caller who is not a member gets the same answer as when the row has no key. The level adds no session field, no role and no permission of its own: a member is whoever the data object's membership configuration already says is one. Both single-tenant and multi-tenant projects take it. It cannot be combined with an AgentHarness that runs on the owner's subscription (`modelSettings.auth: userSubscription`). The owning service serves the routes that set, read and delete a row's key (managers set and delete it; plain members see only whether a key is stored and its status), and agents, `AiCallAction`, agentHub, AgentHarness `providerKey` sessions and the MCP-BFF chat resolve it at call time in the order user, resource, tenant, saas. Under `costPolicy: ownerPays` usage on a row's key is charged to the caller and to that row's own budget, never to the application owner's, and `budget.dailyCostCeilingUsd` caps the row's daily spend.

__AiProviderResourceCredentialScope.doc: The resource level of one AI provider entry's scoped credentials: which data object's rows may own a key, how the row is found from a call, and which member roles manage and use the key.
