ColdSinkBinding.__objectPrefix.doc: [s3Parquet] Key prefix under which Parquet objects are written (e.g. `vehicle-pings/`). Combined with the provider's configured prefix.

__AnalyticsBinding.doc: [P4 DONE] Binds an EventStream's analytics store + declares rollups. References a `bigLoadProvidersSettings` clickhouse store BY NAME (engine MUST be clickhouse) and lists the windowed aggregations. Codegen emits a raw MergeTree table + a materialized-view→AggregatingMergeTree per rollup, maintained incrementally on insert.

AnalyticsBinding.__provider.doc: Name of the bigLoadProvidersSettings store (engine clickhouse) the analytics rollups are written to.
AnalyticsBinding.__table.doc: The ClickHouse table the raw analytics inserts land in. Defaults to the stream name + `_analytics`.
AnalyticsBinding.__rollups.doc: Windowed aggregation definitions (AnalyticsRollup[]) materialized over the stream (density, supply/demand, KPIs).

__AnalyticsRollup.doc: [P4 DONE] One windowed aggregation materialized over an EventStream into the ClickHouse analytics store as a materialized-view→AggregatingMergeTree. `window` lowers to a CH time-bucket fn; `aggregations` support count() and avg|sum|min|max(<numericField>); `groupBy` fields become extra key columns.

AnalyticsRollup.__name.doc: Rollup identifier (the materialized view / target table suffix). Must be a valid codeName.
AnalyticsRollup.name: String
AnalyticsRollup.__window.doc: The time window for the aggregation, e.g. `1m`, `5m`, `1h`. Kept as String in v1.
AnalyticsRollup.__groupBy.doc: Names of the eventSchema fields the aggregation groups by (e.g. geoCell, region). A judged column (a classify cleaning rule's `targetColumn`, or its `<targetColumn>DecidedBy`) may be named too; any other name fails validation (ANALYTICS_ROLLUP_GROUPBY_UNKNOWN).
AnalyticsRollup.__aggregations.doc: The aggregation expressions (e.g. `count()`, `avg(speed)`). Kept as Strings in v1.

__RetentionPolicy.doc: [P4 DONE] An EventStream's retention/rollup/archival cadence. Drives a generated retention cron that prunes cold rows older than coldRetentionDays (the hot-store TTL on HotStoreBinding ages the hot tier natively). archiveToParquet is the P5 trigger.

RetentionPolicy.__hotTtlSeconds.doc: Hot-store retention in seconds (mirrors HotStoreBinding.ttlSeconds; the cron enforces it for engines without native TTL).
RetentionPolicy.__coldRetentionDays.doc: Cold-sink retention in days. 0/absent = retain indefinitely.
RetentionPolicy.__rollupCron.doc: Cron expression for the rollup/archival cadence, e.g. `*/15 * * * *`. Reuses the existing cron-controller runtime.
RetentionPolicy.__archiveToParquet.doc: When true, the retention cron triggers the cold-archival-to-Parquet path (Phase 5).

__EventStreamReadSurface.doc: A generated read API over an EventStream's stores. Each surface is a query archetype selected via `type` and exposed as an api-layer route under `/<stream>/<name>`. Phase 3 wires the hot-store surfaces: `latestN` (the last-N records for a partition, ordered by the clustering column) and `currentState` (the single most-recent record for a partition).

EventStreamReadSurface.__name.doc: Read-surface identifier — the generated route suffix (`/<stream>/<name>`) and the asset-name-path. Must be a valid codeName.
EventStreamReadSurface.name: String
EventStreamReadSurface.__type.doc: The read archetype: `latestN` (last-N records for one partition from the hot store, ordered by the clustering column DESC — the default), `currentState` (the single most-recent record for a partition), `historySince` (records since a timestamp — cold/hot, P4), `analyticsRollup` (a rollup query against the analytics store, P4), `replaySince` (replay records since a timestamp, P4). Kept as String in v1; Phase 3 emits latestN + currentState.
EventStreamReadSurface.__partitionParam.doc: The route/query parameter that supplies the partition value (e.g. `vehicleId`). Defaults to streamBasics.partitionKey.
EventStreamReadSurface.__rollup.doc: [analyticsRollup] Name of the analytics.rollups[] this surface reads. Defaults to the first declared rollup when absent. Ignored by non-analyticsRollup surfaces.
EventStreamReadSurface.__defaultLimit.doc: [latestN] Default number of records returned when the request omits a limit. Defaults to 50.
EventStreamReadSurface.__maxLimit.doc: [latestN] Hard cap on the returned record count (guards a hot-store scan). Defaults to 1000.
EventStreamReadSurface.__loginRequired.doc: When true (default), the read route requires a valid login token.
EventStreamReadSurface.__judgement.doc: [latestN] Optional judged page (DecisionPageJudgement): a decision provider reranks or filters the records this surface would answer, in one provider request per page. Absent = the unjudged page, exactly as a surface without it answers. The judged surface clamps the request limit to the judgement's page cap, judges only rows the caller would have received unjudged, and answers a `judgement` attribution next to the items. Nodejs only for now: another service language refuses the block (DECISION_PAGE_LANGUAGE_UNSUPPORTED), and only a `latestN` surface takes it (DECISION_PAGE_SURFACE_UNSUPPORTED).

__DecisionPageJudgement.doc: Reranks or filters one bounded page of a read surface with a decision provider, in one provider request per page. Each item reaches the provider only as its declared state projection (`stateFields`), addressed by its stable id (`idField`), and the judged page is always a subset (filter) or a reordering (rerank) of the page the surface would have answered unjudged: a judgement can never add an item. A `filter` asks one noul per item and keeps the items whose probability reaches `confidenceThreshold`; a `rerank` asks one score per item against the ordered `criteria` and sorts by it, ties keeping the original order. The failure rule: a filter fails closed (the request fails, or answers the empty page under `matchNothing`) and never answers the unfiltered page; a rerank may keep the original order (`keepOrder`, its default). A page is never split into several requests, never retried and never truncated: a page over `pageCap` (framework hard maximum 256 items) or over the provider's token budget is not judged and takes the failure rule. The response carries a `judgement` attribution (mode, provider, model, judged, degraded) so a degraded page is never served as judged. Never an authorization surface (DECISION_ON_AUTHZ_SURFACE). Bound today to an `EventStreamReadSurface` of type `latestN`, nodejs only.

DecisionPageJudgement.__mode.doc: Required. `filter` narrows the page to the items the statement in `instructions` holds for (one noul per item); `rerank` orders the page by a score against the ordered `criteria` (one score per item). The two modes never mix on one block.
DecisionPageJudgement.__providerName.doc: Name of the `projectSettings.decisionProvidersSettings.decisionProviders[]` entry that judges the page. A dangling name fails validation (DECISION_PROVIDER_NOT_FOUND). The provider must advertise noul questions for a filter and score questions for a rerank (DECISION_QUESTION_TYPE_UNSUPPORTED).
DecisionPageJudgement.__model.doc: The PINNED model version, overriding the provider entry's own; a floating tag is refused (DECISION_MODEL_NOT_PINNED). Null = inherit the provider entry's pin, which must then exist.
DecisionPageJudgement.__instructions.doc: What is judged about ONE item, in plain language. For a filter it is the statement that holds for an item that STAYS on the page; for a rerank it is what the score measures. The framework addresses each item by its id around this text, so never refer to an item by its position.
DecisionPageJudgement.__criteria.doc: [rerank] The ordered score levels, lowest first: each entry's `name` is a level and its `value` describes it, and entry ORDER is the scale. 2 to 10 levels (DECISION_PAGE_CRITERIA_INVALID). Not allowed on a filter (DECISION_PAGE_FIELD_NOT_FOR_MODE).
DecisionPageJudgement.__stateFields.doc: Required, non-empty. The explicit per-item state projection: the eventSchema fields of an item that reach the provider, and nothing else. The name `id` is reserved for the item address (DECISION_PAGE_STATE_FIELD_RESERVED). A filter may not project an identity stamp field (the ingestion `actorField`, `sessionField` or `tenantField`): it would decide visibility by who wrote the row (DECISION_ON_AUTHZ_SURFACE).
DecisionPageJudgement.__idField.doc: Required. The eventSchema field whose value is the stable id of an item: it addresses the item in the request and in the answers. Pick a field that is unique per row (the clustering key or the ingestion idempotency key); any other field is warned about (DECISION_PAGE_ID_FIELD_NOT_UNIQUE), and a page with two items of one id is not judged.
DecisionPageJudgement.__confidenceThreshold.doc: [filter] Probability at or above which an item stays. Default 0.8. Must sit outside the provider's `probabilityDriftBand` of 0.5 (DECISION_THRESHOLD_IN_DRIFT_BAND); an item within half the band of the threshold is dropped as near-threshold. Not allowed on a rerank (DECISION_PAGE_FIELD_NOT_FOR_MODE).
DecisionPageJudgement.__pageCap.doc: Most items one judged page carries. Default = the surface's `defaultLimit`; framework hard maximum 256 (DECISION_PAGE_CAP_EXCEEDS_HARD_MAX), and never above the surface's `maxLimit`. The surface clamps the request limit to the cap, and the cap times the static size of one item must fit one request of the provider's context (DECISION_PAGE_CAP_OVER_TOKEN_BUDGET).
DecisionPageJudgement.__onProviderError.doc: What happens when the page cannot be judged (a provider failure, a malformed answer, a page over the cap or the token budget). filter: `failClosed` (the default: the request fails with 503) or `matchNothing` (an empty page marked degraded); a filter never fails open (DECISION_NARROWING_FILTER_FAILS_OPEN). rerank: `keepOrder` (the default: the original order, marked not judged) or `failClosed`.

__DecisionPageMode.doc: How a DecisionPageJudgement judges a page. `rerank` orders the page by one score per item against ordered levels; `filter` keeps the items a noul statement holds for.
__DecisionPageFailureMode.doc: What a DecisionPageJudgement does when a page cannot be judged. `failClosed` fails the request; `matchNothing` (filter only) answers an empty page marked degraded; `keepOrder` (rerank only) answers the original order marked not judged. A filter never answers the unjudged page.
__JobStream.doc: An async-job-orchestration pattern (docs/ADR-async-job-orchestration-patterns.md). A `JobStream` is a durable, reconnectable, observable async BUSINESS job that GENERALIZES `ComputeJob`: it reuses ComputeJob's durable event-outbox + reconnectable SSE-tail machinery, but the 'work' is a **BusinessApi invocation** (not a native compute kernel). deliveryMode is `push` (a worker drains a Kafka work topic and calls the target API; the target needs no change). From ONE declaration codegen emits: an enqueue edge (produce → job topic + create the job record + return jobId), a Kafka-consumer WORKER controller on the target BusinessApi bound to that topic, a durable per-job event outbox, and a reconnectable SSE observation edge keyed by jobId — AND it SUPPRESSES the target BusinessApi's public REST route (binding-as-JobStream-target ⇒ internal by default; `targetApi.keepPublicRoute` re-exposes it). Clients enter through the enqueue and SSE observation edges. Server-side code in the same service can call `enqueueJobStream(name, input, { session, requestId })` from the generated job-stream-layer barrel; it runs the same enqueue gate against the supplied session and creates the same durable job row and work message as the REST enqueue route. Suppression is REST-ONLY: a target that ALSO declares a gRPC, SSE or kafka controller keeps that transport mounted with its own auth posture, so 'reachable only via the worker' holds when REST is the api's sole transport. Lifecycle: queued→started→[relayed progress]→ended (the terminal `ended` carries a result reference/link). Relay rule = the target's nature: an SSE/progress target relays its progress into the outbox; a solid REST target emits only started+ended. The sibling `WaitingRoom` (pull/admission-control) is a separate pattern in the same ADR.

JobStream.__streamBasics.doc: The job stream's scalar identity + axes (JobStreamBasics): name/codeName/description, the Kafka job (work) topic, the optional partition key for worker consumer-group parallelism, and the enqueue input schema (the fields the enqueue edge accepts, mapped onto the target API input). Grouped into a section because a chapter is a container of sections, not loose scalar columns (the ComputeJob.jobBasics idiom).
JobStream.__targetApi.doc: Binds the processing BusinessApi this stream drives (JobStreamTargetBinding): the target's `api` name (a businessLogic[] BusinessApi in THIS service) + the `action`, the input/result field mappings, and `keepPublicRoute`. The binding implies: emit a kafka WORKER controller on the job topic AND do NOT emit the target's public REST route (internal by default). REQUIRED — a JobStream with no target has nothing to run.
JobStream.__observation.doc: The reconnectable SSE + durable-outbox observation config (JobStreamObservation): the SSE channel/event name, retention of the per-job outbox (so a reconnect replays everything-since-cursor by jobId), and `relayTargetApiProgress` (relay the target's own SSE/progress events into the outbox when the target emits them; otherwise only started+ended are observed). Null = sensible defaults (reconnectable outbox on, relay off).
JobStream.__jobState.doc: The durable job record (JobStreamState): the status lifecycle (queued→started→[progress]→ended), the store (DB by default), and the field on the `ended` event that carries the result reference/link the frontend navigates to. Null = a DB-backed job record with the default lifecycle.
JobStream.__access.doc: Who may enqueue a job, and who may observe or snapshot one (JobStreamAccess). The enqueue edge stands in for the target BusinessApi's public route (which binding as a JobStream target suppresses), so by default it INHERITS that api's own `authOptions`; observation and snapshot are bound to the principal + tenant that created the job. Null = that fail-closed default, with no stream-wide privileged observer.

__JobStreamBasics.doc: Defines a job stream's identity, work topic, partition key and enqueue input schema. The job stream's scalar identity + axes (section): name/codeName/description, the Kafka job (work) topic, the optional `partitionKey` for worker consumer-group parallelism, and the enqueue `inputSchema` (the fields the enqueue edge accepts, mapped onto the target API input).

JobStreamBasics.__name.doc: Unique job-stream identifier within the service. Drives the enqueue route base (`/jobstreams/<name>`), the SSE observation route, the default job (work) topic name, the worker consumer-group, and the asset-name-path. Must be a valid codeName. For services resolved to Java, authored Kafka listener names and group IDs are limited to 249 Unicode code points; longer values are refused at design time before Spring listener startup. This Java-specific bound does not refuse other service languages or unresolved contexts.
JobStreamBasics.name: String
JobStreamBasics.__codeName.doc: Optional machine code name override. Defaults to `name` when absent.
JobStreamBasics.__description.doc: Optional human-readable description of what business job this stream runs.
JobStreamBasics.__jobTopic.doc: The Kafka topic the enqueue edge produces onto and the worker controller consumes (the work queue). When absent, codegen derives `<projectCodename>-<service>-<name>-jobs` (the standard event-topic shape).
JobStreamBasics.__partitionKey.doc: Optional name of an inputSchema field used as the Kafka partition key for worker consumer-group parallelism (so all messages for one entity process in order on one worker). When absent, jobs are round-robined across the consumer group.
JobStreamBasics.__inputSchema.doc: The input fields the enqueue edge accepts (JobStreamInputField[]). The enqueue handler validates the body against these and maps them onto the target BusinessApi input (per targetApi.inputMapping). Keep this the job's request payload — large inputs belong in a bucket, referenced by key.

__JobStreamInputField.doc: One field of a JobStream's enqueue input schema: `name`, `type` and `required`. The enqueue handler validates the request body against these fields and maps them onto the target BusinessApi input (per `targetApi.inputMapping`). Keep the payload small — large inputs belong in a bucket, referenced by key.

JobStreamInputField.__name.doc: The input field name as it appears in the enqueue body and is mapped onto the target API input.
JobStreamInputField.name: String
JobStreamInputField.__type.doc: The field DataType. Defaults to String.
JobStreamInputField.__required.doc: When true, the enqueue handler rejects a body missing this field (400).

__JobStreamTargetBinding.doc: Binds a job stream to a processing BusinessApi in the same service. Binds the processing BusinessApi a JobStream drives (section): the target `api` name (a businessLogic[] BusinessApi in THIS service) + `action`, the enqueue `inputMapping` MScript, `resultLinkField`, and `keepPublicRoute`. The binding emits a Kafka WORKER controller on the job topic and suppresses the target's public REST route unless `keepPublicRoute` is set.

JobStreamTargetBinding.__api.doc: Name of the processing BusinessApi this stream drives — a `businessLogic[].basics.apiOptions.name` declared in THIS service. Binding it as a JobStream target makes codegen emit a kafka WORKER controller on the job topic and SUPPRESS the target's public REST route. REQUIRED. The worker runs the target with the session the enqueue gate forwarded and no session manager, so a target that declares `authOptions.permissionCheck` is refused (403) on every run and the job is marked failed; validation warns (PERMISSION_CHECK_ON_CALLERLESS_DOOR). Gate a JobStream target with `checkRoles` / `absoluteRoles` / `ownershipCheck`.
JobStreamTargetBinding.__action.doc: Optional name of the specific action/operation on the target BusinessApi the worker invokes, when the API exposes more than one. Defaults to the API's primary action.
JobStreamTargetBinding.__keepPublicRoute.doc: Override the default suppression: when true, the target BusinessApi ALSO keeps its public REST route (in addition to the kafka worker controller). Default false — binding as a JobStream target drops the api's public REST route, so the stream's worker is normally its only caller. Suppression is REST-ONLY: a target that ALSO declares a gRPC, SSE or kafka controller keeps that transport mounted with its own auth posture, so 'internal-only' holds only when REST is the api's sole transport.
JobStreamTargetBinding.__inputMapping.doc: Optional MScript mapping the enqueue payload (the inputSchema fields) onto the target BusinessApi input. When absent, codegen maps inputSchema fields onto same-named API inputs.
JobStreamTargetBinding.__resultLinkField.doc: Optional name of the field on the target API result that holds the result reference/link carried in the terminal `ended` event (e.g. `reportUrl`). When absent, jobState.resultLinkField is used (and the whole result is attached if neither is set).

__JobStreamObservation.doc: Configures reconnectable SSE observation and durable event replay for a job stream. The reconnectable observation config of a JobStream (section): the SSE `channelName` clients tail, `reconnectable` + `retainEventsSeconds` (the durable per-job outbox a reconnect replays everything-since-cursor from, by jobId), and `relayTargetApiProgress` (relay the target API's own progress events into the outbox; otherwise only started+ended are observed).

JobStreamObservation.__channelName.doc: The SSE channel / event name the observation edge emits lifecycle frames on. Defaults to the stream name.
JobStreamObservation.__reconnectable.doc: When true (default), the per-job event outbox is retained so a refreshed SSE observation by jobId REPLAYS everything-since-cursor (queue phase OR api phase) before live-tailing — the key to closing the tab and coming back. When false, only a live tail is offered (no replay).
JobStreamObservation.__relayTargetApiProgress.doc: When true, the worker RELAYS the target BusinessApi's own SSE/progress events into the job outbox (use when the target is itself progress-emitting). When false (default), only `started` and `ended` are emitted (the target is a solid REST API).
JobStreamObservation.__retainEventsSeconds.doc: How long (seconds) the durable per-job outbox events are retained for replay-on-reconnect after the job ends. Defaults to a safe window when absent.

__JobStreamState.doc: Configures a job stream's durable status record and result link. The durable job record config of a JobStream (section): the `store` backing the status lifecycle (queued→started→[progress]→ended; DB by default) and `resultLinkField` — the field on the `ended` event that carries the result reference/link the frontend navigates to.

JobStreamState.__store.doc: Where the durable job record lives: `db` (default — a durable, queryable job-state row, mirroring the sys_computeEvent outbox precedent) or `redis` (fast, ephemeral). Kept as String in v1.
JobStreamState.__resultLinkField.doc: Default name of the field carried in the terminal `ended` event that holds the result reference/link the frontend navigates to (e.g. `reportUrl`). Overridden per-binding by targetApi.resultLinkField. When neither is set, the whole target result is attached to `ended`.

__JobStreamAccess.doc: The authorization config of a JobStream (section). A JobStream emits three raw routes — enqueue, durable SSE observation and snapshot — and suppresses the target BusinessApi's public route, so these routes are the only way to run the target and the only way to read what it produced. Without this section they authorized nothing and a job id acted as a bearer capability over the job's input, result and error. `enqueueAccess` decides who may create a job (inheriting the target api's own `authOptions` by default); every job is then bound to the creating principal + tenant, and observation/snapshot require that binding unless `observerRoles`/`observerPermission` grant a stream-wide privileged read.

JobStreamAccess.__enqueueAccess.doc: Who may enqueue a job on this stream. `inherit` (default) applies the target BusinessApi's own `authOptions` in full — `loginRequired`, `M2MAllowed`, `absoluteRoles` (a bypass grant), `checkRoles` (the role requirement) and `requiredCallerKind` (the caller-kind refusal: an api declaring `machine` refuses every human caller here too, and no absoluteRole bypasses it) — reaching the same verdict ApiManager.checkBasicAuth plus checkRequiredCallerKind would have reached on the public route the JobStream binding suppressed; this is what makes a `loginRequired: true`, role-gated or machine-only target actually enforce that. `session` forces an authenticated caller regardless of the target's declaration. `public` allows anonymous enqueue; such jobs are bound to no principal and are therefore observable by anyone holding the job id, so use it only for work that carries no private input or result, and declaring it against a target that itself requires a login or a role is refused at design time rather than silently downgrading that api. `session` and `public` are both statements about HUMAN callers, so declaring either against a target that declares `requiredCallerKind` is refused at design time as a contradiction rather than a relaxation. Lane status: the inherited `requiredCallerKind` refusal on this edge is enforced in nodejs, python, dotnet, java and rust; the golang enqueue gate does not carry the caller-kind field yet. Kept as String in v1.
JobStreamAccess.__observerRoles.doc: Roles that may observe or snapshot ANY job on this stream, not only their own. EMPTY by default — privileged access is never implicit, so an unconfigured stream lets nobody read another principal's job, administrators included. Grant it to support-console or operations roles that genuinely need cross-principal visibility. The machine role `system` belongs here when a peer service must poll jobs it did not create.
JobStreamAccess.__observerPermission.doc: A PBAC permission granting the same stream-wide observation right as `observerRoles`, resolved through the project's permission manager so a narrower role can be authorized by grant rather than by name. Null (default) = no permission path; the role list is then the only privileged route in.
JobStreamAccess.__grandfatherLegacyJobs.doc: Serve job rows written BEFORE the owner binding existed (their owner column is NULL). FALSE by default: the framework cannot know which principal submitted a legacy job, so serving one would preserve exactly the bearer-capability exposure the binding removes — legacy rows are therefore unreadable over HTTP and age out with the stream's retention window. Set true only for a bounded migration window, and only on a stream whose jobs carry nothing private.

__WaitingRoomFairnessPolicy.doc.#: The fairness policy a WaitingRoom uses to order who gets admitted next out of the front room. Drives the Redis sorted-set score the metered promoter pops by.
__WaitingRoomFairnessPolicy.doc.fifo: Strict first-in-first-out by arrival time (the default). The Redis sorted-set score is the arrival timestamp; the promoter admits the lowest score (earliest arrival) first. Predictable and explainable to end users ("you are number N in line").
__WaitingRoomFairnessPolicy.doc.randomizedDraw: Randomized admission draw among the front room's waiters (a lottery). The promoter picks a random member of the eligible front-room set rather than the earliest, which defeats bots/scripts that race to be first at the on-sale instant. Position is reported as an approximate band rather than an exact integer.

__WaitingRoom.doc: A PULL-mode admission-control queue pattern (docs/ADR-async-job-orchestration-patterns.md, the WaitingRoom section) — the Taylor-Swift-ticketing turnstile. A `WaitingRoom` meters a thundering herd through N gated Redis `rooms` so a bound **public** BusinessApi is never stampeded: clients join the room (a Redis sorted-set keyed by arrival/fairness), see a live `position` over the room's OWN realtime channel, and a metered cron-promoter advances front-of-room → next room → final admission at each room's `admissionRatePerSecond`. When admitted the room mints a one-shot, time-boxed `QueToken` (Redis-backed, single-use, queue-scoped) and the CLIENT calls the target BusinessApi DIRECTLY with it. CONTRAST `JobStream` (push): a WaitingRoom does NOT hide or proxy the target — the target BusinessApi keeps its public REST/SSE/WS route and merely GAINS the `QueToken` gate (`authOptions.queueTokenRequired: <waitingRoomName>`), an additional M2M-parity check beyond login. From ONE declaration codegen emits: a join edge (ZADD into room 0 + return a waiter handle), the metered promoter, the position realtime channel, the admission token-mint, and the Redis one-shot `QueToken` verify the gated target consumes. The position channel is SEPARATE from the target API's own event channel.

WaitingRoom.__roomBasics.doc: The waiting room's scalar identity + global policy (WaitingRoomBasics): name/codeName/description, the fairness policy (fifo default | randomizedDraw to defeat bots), and the abandonment TTL (a waiter who stops heart-beating / idles past it is dropped from its Redis room so it stops holding a slot). Grouped into a section because a chapter is a container of sections, not loose scalar columns (the ComputeJob.jobBasics idiom).
WaitingRoom.__rooms.doc: The staged admission gates (WaitingRoomStages): an ordered list of N rooms (`stages`), each with an `admissionRatePerSecond` (the CEILING the adaptive metered promoter drains that room's front at), an optional `minAdmissionRatePerSecond` floor, and an optional `capacity`. The promoter advances front-of-room 0 → room 1 → … → final admission, each hop rate-limited by the destination room's rate — and it is CLOSED-LOOP: under DB saturation an internal PI controller backs each room's effective rate off toward its floor, recovering to the ceiling as the database recovers (`WAITINGROOM_ADAPTIVE_DISABLED=true` reverts to a static ceiling drain). REQUIRED — a WaitingRoom with no room has no gate to meter.
WaitingRoom.__token.doc: The admission token config (QueTokenSettings): the one-shot, time-boxed `ttlSeconds` and Redis-backed single-use semantics of the `QueToken` minted when a waiter reaches final admission. The token is queue-scoped (only valid for THIS room's bound target) and, when `singleUse` is true (the default), consumed on first use by the target's `QueToken` gate. Null = a single-use token with the default TTL.
WaitingRoom.__targetApi.doc: Binds the PUBLIC BusinessApi this room fronts (WaitingRoomTargetBinding): the target's `api` name (a businessLogic[] BusinessApi in THIS service) + the `action`. UNLIKE JobStream, the binding does NOT suppress the target — the target KEEPS its public route and GAINS the `QueToken` gate (the client calls it directly with the minted token). REQUIRED — a WaitingRoom with no target has nothing to admit clients to.
WaitingRoom.__positionChannel.doc: The room's OWN realtime/SSE position channel config (WaitingRoomPositionChannel): the channel/event name clients subscribe to for live position (ZRANK) + admission ("you're in, here is your token") updates. This is SEPARATE from the target BusinessApi's own event channel — it carries queue lifecycle only. Null = a sensible-default SSE position channel named after the room.

__WaitingRoomBasics.doc: Defines a waiting room's identity, fairness policy and abandonment timeout. The waiting room's scalar identity + global policy (section): name/codeName/description, the `fairnessPolicy` (`fifo` default | `randomizedDraw` to defeat bots) and `abandonmentTtlSeconds` (a waiter who stops heart-beating past it is dropped from its Redis room so it stops holding a slot).

WaitingRoomBasics.__name.doc: Unique waiting-room identifier within the service and the asset-name-path. Unless `codeName` is set, it is also the room key: the join route base (`/waitingrooms/<key>`), the position channel route, the Redis room key prefix (`waitingroom:<key>:room:<n>`), the QueToken key namespace and the `authOptions.queueTokenRequired` value a gated target references (which may name the room by either). Must be a valid codeName.
WaitingRoomBasics.name: String
WaitingRoomBasics.__codeName.doc: Optional machine code name override. When set, it is the room key that the routes, the Redis keys and the QueToken namespace use. Defaults to `name` when absent.
WaitingRoomBasics.__description.doc: Optional human-readable description of what high-demand event this room meters.
WaitingRoomBasics.__fairnessPolicy.doc: How the metered promoter orders who gets admitted next out of the front room: `fifo` (default — strict arrival order, exact position) or `randomizedDraw` (a lottery among the front room to defeat bots; approximate position). Drives the Redis sorted-set score the promoter pops by.
WaitingRoomBasics.__abandonmentTtlSeconds.doc: Abandonment / idle TTL in seconds: a waiter whose heartbeat stops (tab closed) or who idles past this window is dropped from its Redis room (its sorted-set member expires) so it stops holding a slot and the line keeps moving. The join/heartbeat edge refreshes it. Defaults to a safe short window when absent.

__WaitingRoomStages.doc: The staged admission gates of a WaitingRoom (section): the ordered `stages` list — room 0 (the entry room a join lands in) through the final room (final admission mints the QueToken). The adaptive promoter advances front-of-each-room into the next room, capped by the next room's `admissionRatePerSecond` ceiling (backing off toward each stage's `minAdmissionRatePerSecond` floor under DB saturation).

WaitingRoomStages.__stages.doc: The ordered list of staged admission gates (WaitingRoomStage[]) — room 0 (the entry room a join lands in) through the final room (final admission mints the token). The metered promoter advances front-of-each-room into the next room capped by the NEXT room's admissionRatePerSecond. At least one room is required.

__WaitingRoomStage.doc: Defines one Redis admission stage with a rate ceiling, optional rate floor and capacity. One staged admission gate (a Redis room): `name`, the `admissionRatePerSecond` CEILING the adaptive metered promoter drains this room's front at, an optional `minAdmissionRatePerSecond` floor for the closed-loop back-off, and an optional `capacity`.

WaitingRoomStage.__name.doc: Optional human-readable name for this room/stage (e.g. `lobby`, `preCheckout`). Defaults to `room<index>` by position. Used in position channel frames and the Redis key suffix.
WaitingRoomStage.name: String
WaitingRoomStage.__admissionRatePerSecond.doc: The CEILING on waiters per second the metered promoter advances INTO this room from the previous room's front (the final room's rate = the effective admission rate into the target API). This is the throttle that converts a thundering herd into a safe trickle. The promoter is CLOSED-LOOP: while the service's database is healthy it drains at exactly this rate, and under sustained DB saturation an internal PI controller (setpoint and gains are platform internals, never authored) lowers the effective rate toward the stage's floor (`minAdmissionRatePerSecond`), climbing back to the ceiling as the database recovers. Ops kill-switch: `WAITINGROOM_ADAPTIVE_DISABLED=true` (or a service with no relational DB signal) reverts to a static drain at exactly this rate. REQUIRED per room.
WaitingRoomStage.__minAdmissionRatePerSecond.doc: Optional FLOOR on waiters per second for the adaptive promoter: under sustained database saturation the closed-loop controller never lowers the effective drain rate below this (admission slows, never stops). When absent the floor defaults to max(1, 10% of `admissionRatePerSecond`). Values above the ceiling are clamped to it. Irrelevant while adaptive admission is off (`WAITINGROOM_ADAPTIVE_DISABLED=true`) or the service has no relational DB saturation signal — the promoter then drains statically at the ceiling.
WaitingRoomStage.__capacity.doc: Optional maximum number of waiters allowed to occupy this room at once (a ceiling on the in-flight set). When the room is full the promoter stalls upstream advancement until it drains. When absent the room is unbounded (rate-limited only).

__QueTokenSettings.doc: The admission token config of a WaitingRoom (section): the one-shot, time-boxed `ttlSeconds` and Redis-backed `singleUse` semantics of the QueToken minted when a waiter reaches final admission. The token is queue-scoped (only valid for this room's bound target) and consumed on first use by the target's QueToken gate.

QueTokenSettings.__ttlSeconds.doc: The time-box (seconds) of the one-shot QueToken minted on final admission: the admitted client must call the bound target BusinessApi within this window or the token expires (the Redis key TTLs out) and the client must re-queue. Keep it short enough to deter token resale/sharing, long enough for a real checkout. Defaults to a sensible short window when absent.
QueTokenSettings.__singleUse.doc: When true (default), the token is consumed on first use — the target's QueToken gate atomically deletes the Redis key on a successful check, so a replay is rejected (true one-shot). When false, the token is reusable until its TTL expires (a session pass rather than a one-shot ticket).

__WaitingRoomTargetBinding.doc: Binds the PUBLIC BusinessApi a WaitingRoom fronts (section): the target `api` name (a businessLogic[] BusinessApi in THIS service) + `action`. Unlike JobStream, the binding does NOT suppress the target — it keeps its public route and gains the QueToken gate.

WaitingRoomTargetBinding.__api.doc: Name of the PUBLIC BusinessApi this room fronts — a `businessLogic[].basics.apiOptions.name` declared in THIS service. UNLIKE a JobStream target, this API is NOT suppressed: it keeps its public REST/SSE/WS route and GAINS the QueToken gate (the codegen pass sets/honours `authOptions.queueTokenRequired: <waitingRoomName>` on it so it requires a valid admission token). The client calls it DIRECTLY with the minted token. REQUIRED.
WaitingRoomTargetBinding.__action.doc: Optional name of the specific action/operation on the target BusinessApi the admission token authorizes, when the API exposes more than one. Defaults to the API's primary action.

__WaitingRoomPositionChannel.doc: The room's own realtime/SSE position channel (section): the `channelName` clients subscribe to for live position (ZRANK) and admission updates, the `transport`, and `emitPositionEverySeconds`. Separate from the target BusinessApi's own event channel — it carries queue lifecycle only.

WaitingRoomPositionChannel.__channelName.doc: The SSE/realtime channel + event name clients subscribe to for live position (ZRANK in the front room) and admission frames (the `admitted` event carries the minted QueToken). Defaults to the room name. This channel is SEPARATE from the target BusinessApi's own event channel — it carries queue lifecycle only (joined → position → admitted → expired/abandoned).
WaitingRoomPositionChannel.__transport.doc: The realtime transport for the position channel: `sse` (default — a reconnectable Server-Sent-Events stream keyed by the waiter handle) or `websocket`. Kept as String in v1.
WaitingRoomPositionChannel.__emitPositionEverySeconds.doc: How often (seconds) the room pushes a refreshed position frame to a waiting client (a throttle so a deep queue doesn't spam every promoter tick). Defaults to a small interval when absent.

__LoadShield.doc: The service's single in-process priority load shedder (docs/ADR-loadshield-priority-load-shedding.md) — an always-on guard for the WHOLE service against UNPLANNED overload, modeled on Uber's Cinnamon. Declared at most ONCE per service as `service.loadShield` (a singular optional chapter — the shoppingCartConfig idiom, NOT an array: the shield guards ONE shared resource, the service's DB pool + event loop, so two shields would fight over the same budget). At runtime a bounded priority queue sits IN FRONT of route dispatch: every request gets an effective priority from its declared/derived tier (0 = never shed … 5 = first to shed) plus a per-caller cohort (stable within a time-rotation period — the cohort salt time-rotates with a per-caller staggered phase, ADR §13, so the shed-first lottery is redrawn across load events instead of being drawn once forever), a CoDel-style queue-wait bound (`targetQueueLatencyMs`) detects congestion, and shed requests get an immediate DB-free HTTP 429 + Retry-After with errorCode LOAD_SHED. The blueprint surface is deliberately minimal (D6, the zero-config property): tier assignments + the setpoint + enabled/exemptions ONLY — PID gains, cohort count, queue capacity and every other controller internal are platform code constants, never blueprint. CONTRAST `waitingRooms[]` (an opt-in, client-visible PULL queue a designer places in front of ONE known-stampede API for a PLANNED spike): the two compose — the room meters the herd upstream, the shield still protects the service if admitted-rate + background traffic saturates the DB. `eventStream` ingest keeps its OWN declared shedding and is structurally exempt. The nodejs runtime makes the chapter REAL: an active shield emits `src/load-shield-layer/` (static route-table config + middleware + adaptive controller) and mounts it after the session parse and ahead of every business route — a shed is answered before ANY DB work and before the waitingRoom QueToken gate consumes a one-shot token. ADAPTIVE MODE (ADR D7): on a service with a relational pool the shield closes the loop over the shared DB-saturation signal — a PID controller walks a rejection threshold down the 384-point tier×cohort priority scale (worst priorities shed first, IMMEDIATELY on arrival, cohort-granular so partial tiers shed before whole tiers; floor at the tier-1 band start — tier 0 is structurally unsheddable) and an AIMD auto-tuner moves the concurrency cap between internal bounds as the database's measured capacity changes. All controller gains, bounds and cadences are INTERNAL platform constants — never blueprint, never a design tool. Without a relational DB signal the shield automatically degrades to the static behavior. Runtime ops knobs (env, not blueprint): `LOADSHIELD_DISABLED=true` bypasses the shield entirely; `LOADSHIELD_ADAPTIVE_DISABLED=true` keeps the shield on but pins the static degraded stance; `LOADSHIELD_COHORT_ROTATION_SECONDS` overrides the cohort-salt rotation period (default 3600, 0 = fixed pre-rotation mapping). Services that do not declare the chapter (or declare it with `enabled:false`) still generate byte-identical output.

LoadShield.__shieldBasics.doc: The shield's scalar identity + the ONLY tunable (LoadShieldBasics): name/codeName/description, `enabled` (default true) and the CoDel-style `targetQueueLatencyMs` setpoint. Grouped into a section because a chapter is a container of sections, not loose scalar columns (the ComputeJob.jobBasics / WaitingRoom.roomBasics idiom).
LoadShield.__tiers.doc: Per-API/action shed-priority assignments (LoadShieldTiers): `assignments[]` of `{api, action?, tier}` with integer tier 0-5 (0 = never shed, 5 = first to shed). Empty/absent = every route gets its derived default tier (health 0, auth 1, writes 2, single reads 3, lists/reports 4; tier 5 is never auto-assigned — 'shed me first' is always an explicit designer statement). An explicit assignment always wins over the derived default.
LoadShield.__exemptions.doc: APIs that bypass the shield entirely (LoadShieldExemptions) — for the rare route that must never queue nor shed and cannot be expressed as tier 0. Null/absent = no exemptions.

__LoadShieldBasics.doc: Defines a load shield's identity, enabled flag and target queue latency. The load shield's scalar identity + global policy (section): name/codeName/description, the `enabled` on/off flag (default true) and the ONLY tunable — the CoDel-style `targetQueueLatencyMs` queue-wait setpoint. Everything else about the shedder (PID gains, cohort count and rotation, queue capacity, CoDel interval, Retry-After clamps, the concurrency cap) is an internal platform constant, deliberately NOT blueprint surface (ADR D6 — the Cinnamon zero-config property).

LoadShieldBasics.__name.doc: Unique load-shield identifier within the service (there is at most one shield per service, so this names the shield in validation messages, generated comments and observability output). Must be a valid codeName.
LoadShieldBasics.name: String
LoadShieldBasics.__codeName.doc: Optional machine code name override. Defaults to `name` when absent.
LoadShieldBasics.__description.doc: Optional human-readable description of what this shield protects and why its tier policy looks the way it does.
LoadShieldBasics.__enabled.doc: Whether the shield is active (default true). When false the chapter stays declared (the tier policy remains reviewable) but the generated service dispatches exactly as an unshielded service. Distinct from the LOADSHIELD_DISABLED env kill-switch, which is an ops knob, not blueprint surface.
LoadShieldBasics.__targetQueueLatencyMs.doc: The CoDel-style queue-wait setpoint in milliseconds — the maximum time a request should sit in the shield's priority queue before the shield considers itself congested and starts shedding from the low-priority end. The ONLY latency tunable a designer may set (a latency-tolerance intent, not a controller gain). Defaults to an internal platform constant (~5ms) when absent — leave it absent unless you have a measured reason.

__LoadShieldTiers.doc: The shield's per-API/action shed-priority policy (section): the `assignments` list of `LoadShieldTierAssignment` entries. Lives ON the shield so the whole priority policy is reviewable in one place — the ARCHITECT'S OVERRIDE VIEW. An API may ALSO state its own importance locally (`basics.apiOptions.loadShedTier` on a BusinessApi, `edgeControllerOptions.loadShedTier` on an edge controller — the eventStream `loadSheddingPriority` idiom). PRECEDENCE, most specific wins: central action-narrowed assignment > central api-level assignment > per-API `loadShedTier` > derived default by action nature (ADR D2). Empty/absent assignments = per-API values and derived defaults apply; a service WITHOUT a shield ignores every tier surface entirely.

LoadShieldTiers.__assignments.doc: The explicit tier assignments (LoadShieldTierAssignment[]). Each entry pins one API — or one action of one API — to an integer tier 0-5. Routes with no entry fall back to the API's own `loadShedTier` (apiOptions / edgeControllerOptions) when declared, then to the derived default tier (health 0, auth 1, core-object writes 2, single reads 3, lists/search/reports 4). A central assignment always wins over both (action-narrowed beats api-level); the same api+action pair may only be assigned once.

__LoadShieldTierAssignment.doc: One explicit shed-priority assignment: `{name?, api, action?, tier}`. `name` is the assignment's asset identity (derived from `api`/`action` when absent); `api` references a `businessLogic[]` BusinessApi (by `basics.apiOptions.name`) or an edge controller (by `edgeControllerOptions.functionName`) declared in THIS service; `action` optionally narrows the assignment to one action/operation of that API; `tier` is an integer 0-5 (0 = never shed — bypasses the queue entirely; 5 = first to shed under congestion). Under saturation the runtime sheds tier 5 first, then 4, and so on — tier 0 is structurally unsheddable.

LoadShieldTierAssignment.__name.doc: Optional asset identity for this assignment (the array-asset convention — WaitingRoomStage idiom). Defaults transparently on load/validation to `<api>` for an api-level entry and `<api>_<action>` for an action-narrowed one; a colliding derived name gets the lowest free numeric suffix (`<base>1`, `<base>2`, …). This name is what item-addressed blueprint writes/reads use: `services/<svc>/loadShield/tiers/assignments/<name>`. Must be unique (case-insensitive) within `assignments[]`.
LoadShieldTierAssignment.name: String
LoadShieldTierAssignment.__api.doc: Name of the API this assignment tiers — a `businessLogic[].basics.apiOptions.name` BusinessApi or an `edgeControllers[].edgeControllerOptions.functionName` edge controller declared in THIS service. A dangling name fails validation (LOADSHIELD_TARGET_UNKNOWN). REQUIRED.
LoadShieldTierAssignment.__action.doc: Optional name of the specific action/operation on the target API this assignment narrows to, when the API exposes more than one. Absent = the assignment covers the whole API.
LoadShieldTierAssignment.__tier.doc: The shed-priority tier: an integer 0-5. 0 = never shed (platform/health-critical — bypasses the shield queue entirely), 1 = auth-critical, 2 = core writes (committed user intent), 3 = single reads, 4 = lists/search/reports (the queries that amplify DB load), 5 = explicitly expendable (bulk/batch/analytics — never auto-assigned, always a designer statement). Values outside 0-5 fail validation (LOADSHIELD_TIER_INVALID). REQUIRED.

__LoadShieldExemptions.doc: Names APIs that bypass the load shield entirely. The shield's escape hatch (section): `apis[]` names routes that bypass the shield ENTIRELY — never queued, never shed, not even counted against a tier — for the rare route that cannot be expressed as tier 0 (e.g. a third-party webhook whose caller retries destructively). Prefer an explicit tier over an exemption: an exempted route gives the adaptive controller nothing to work with. Each name must resolve to a declared BusinessApi or edge controller (LOADSHIELD_TARGET_UNKNOWN otherwise).

LoadShieldExemptions.__apis.doc: Names of the APIs that bypass the shield entirely — each a `businessLogic[].basics.apiOptions.name` BusinessApi or an `edgeControllers[].edgeControllerOptions.functionName` edge controller declared in THIS service.

__CronJob.doc: A scheduled job of the service: a cron expression that calls one service library function directly (no Business API, no cron controller). The function is `library.functions[].moduleName` and is called as `await LIB.<libFunction>(ctx)` in the service process, with the usual library access (`LIB`, `API`, the db-layer, `common`). `ctx` is `{ jobName, runId, scheduledAt, lastSuccessAt, trigger, runMode, eraId, forced, signal }`: `trigger` is `schedule`, `startup` or `manual`, `signal` is an AbortSignal that fires at the timeout. MULTI-REPLICA: every tick is claimed by inserting a row into `sys_cronJobRun` with a unique (jobName, tickKey); only the replica whose insert wins runs the tick, the others skip it silently. Every run row records status (`running`, `succeeded`, `failed`, `timed_out`), start, end, duration, trigger, replica and the error (credential-masked, at most 2000 characters). A function that throws records `failed` and never crashes the service. RUN MODES: `always` runs every tick; `onceEver` stops for good after the first successful run (stored in the database, so it holds across replicas, restarts and redeploys; a failed run does not count); `oncePerStart` succeeds once per start era (a new build, or a restart of every replica, opens a new era; one replica restarting while others stay alive does not). The data-migration recipe is: write the library function (idempotent), add an `onceEver` job, verify the data, then remove the job and drop the old table in the next version. This is a pragmatic tool for urgent work, NOT a schema-migration system: it is not transactional across tables and it does not version or roll back anything, so back up first. Admins read the jobs and runs and trigger a run at `GET /cron-jobs`, `GET /cron-jobs/:name/runs` and `POST /cron-jobs/:name/run`. Shape: `{ jobBasics: { name, description, enabled, libFunction, timeoutSeconds }, scheduleSettings: { cronExpression, timezone, runMode, runOnStartup } }`.

CronJob.__jobBasics.doc: What the job is and what it calls (CronJobBasics): its name, description, enabled flag, library function and timeout.
CronJob.__scheduleSettings.doc: When and how often the job runs (CronJobScheduleSettings): the cron expression, its time zone, the run mode and the startup run.

__CronJobBasics.doc: The identity section of a CronJob (`jobBasics`): name, description, enabled flag, the `library.functions` module it calls and the timeout of one run. The name keys the run rows and the admin routes.

CronJobBasics.__name.doc: Unique job name within the service (camelCase code name). It keys the run rows in `sys_cronJobRun`, the log lines and the admin routes (`/cron-jobs/<name>`). Renaming a job starts a fresh run history, so a renamed `onceEver` job runs again.
CronJobBasics.name: String
CronJobBasics.__description.doc: What the job does and why it exists (for an urgent one-off job: which version may remove it).
CronJobBasics.__enabled.doc: When false the job is not scheduled and does not run on startup; its run history stays readable and an admin can still trigger it manually with `POST /cron-jobs/<name>/run`. Default true.
CronJobBasics.__libFunction.doc: The `moduleName` of a function in this service's `library.functions` (not `edgeFunctions`). It is called with one argument, the run context. It may be async; the run succeeds when it returns (or its promise resolves) and fails when it throws (or rejects). A name that is not in the library is an error (CRON_JOB_LIB_FUNCTION_NOT_FOUND).
CronJobBasics.__timeoutSeconds.doc: Wall-clock limit of one run, in seconds (1 to 86400). Default 3600. At the limit the run is recorded `timed_out` and the context's `signal` is aborted; JavaScript cannot stop a function that ignores the signal, so a long job should check `ctx.signal.aborted` between batches. A once-mode job does not start a new run while an earlier run is still inside its timeout window.

__CronJobScheduleSettings.doc: The schedule section of a CronJob (`scheduleSettings`): cron expression, time zone, run mode and the startup run. `runMode` is `always`, `onceEver` or `oncePerStart`.

CronJobScheduleSettings.__cronExpression.doc: When the job fires. The same dialect rules as a Business API cron controller apply: 5 fields (minute-first), 6 fields (seconds-first), a 7-field Quartz expression (its year field is dropped, CRON_EXPRESSION_YEAR_DROPPED) or an alias such as `@hourly` / `@daily` (`@reboot` is refused: use `runOnStartup`). On nodejs the Quartz `L` (last day) token is refused because node-cron cannot schedule it. Sub-minute (seconds) schedules write one run row per tick and are warned about (CRON_JOB_SUBMINUTE, CRON_JOB_ONCE_SUBMINUTE).
CronJobScheduleSettings.__timezone.doc: IANA time zone the cron expression is evaluated in, e.g. `Europe/Istanbul`. Default `UTC`. An unknown zone is an error (CRON_JOB_TIMEZONE_INVALID).
CronJobScheduleSettings.__runMode.doc: `always` (default) runs on every tick. `onceEver` runs until one run succeeds, then never again on any replica, across restarts and redeploys (a failed or timed-out run does not count, so the next tick retries). `oncePerStart` runs until one run succeeds in the current start era of the service, then waits for the next era; a new era begins with a new build, a new deployment revision of the same build (a rollout such as `kubectl rollout restart`, read from CRON_ERA_REVISION or POD_TEMPLATE_HASH), or when every replica has stopped, while one replica restarting next to a live replica of its revision stays in the era. A once job never runs twice at the same time: every trigger claims one once key. An admin with an absolute role can bypass the once rule with `force`.
CronJobScheduleSettings.__runOnStartup.doc: Also run the job once when the service starts, in addition to its schedule: once per start era across all replicas, about 36 seconds after boot when the replica has decided its era (one replica restarting while others of its revision stay alive does not run it again). Respects `runMode` and `enabled`. Default false.

__ServiceFiles.doc: The service's design-time static files (`service.serviceFiles`): a chapter holding one `manifest` section that lists every file the service carries. The bytes are not in the blueprint: the manifest names each file by path and pins it by size and sha256, and the build fetches the bytes from the platform bucket (a missing or mismatched file fails the build and names every bad path). Upload, list, read and delete files with the `uploadServiceFile`, `listServiceFiles`, `getServiceFile` and `deleteServiceFile` tools rather than editing entries by hand: only the upload tool computes the hash, enforces the limits and refuses a file that carries a secret.

ServiceFiles.__manifest.doc: The file list (ServiceFileManifest): one `files` entry per file the service carries.

__ServiceFileManifest.doc: The manifest of the service's files (section): the `files` list of `ServiceFile` entries. A path is unique within the service, compared case-insensitively and across both visibilities, so a macOS or Windows checkout never folds two files onto one.

ServiceFileManifest.__files.doc: The service's files (ServiceFile[]). Each entry is `{path, visibility, contentType, size, sha256}`; the path is the identity. Written by `uploadServiceFile` and removed by `deleteServiceFile` (which keeps the stored bytes, because older blueprint versions still reference them).

__ServiceFile.doc: One design-time service file: `{path, visibility, contentType, size, sha256}`. The path is the identity (there is no name). A public file is served at `/service-files/<path>`; a private file is readable only through `LIB.serviceFiles.*`. Every response of the public route carries `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` and a sandbox Content-Security-Policy: HTML and SVG render inline but inert, JavaScript and XML are always sent as an attachment. Unknown and private paths answer the same 404.

ServiceFile.__path.doc: Relative POSIX path of the file, also its URL tail and its place under `service-files/<visibility>/` in the repo, e.g. `legal/terms-v3.md`. Segments use letters, digits, `.`, `_` and `-`, joined by `/`; no leading `/`, no `.` or `..` segment, at most 200 characters and 10 levels (SERVICE_FILE_INVALID_PATH). Unique within the service, case-insensitively (SERVICE_FILE_DUPLICATE_PATH). REQUIRED.
ServiceFile.__visibility.doc: `public` serves the file at `GET <serviceBaseUrl>/service-files/<path>` (nodejs services); `private` (the default) only puts it in the repo, where custom code and MScript read it through `LIB.serviceFiles.*`. A private file that no `LIB.serviceFiles.*('<path>')` call names is reported (SERVICE_FILE_PRIVATE_UNREAD, warning). Private is not secret: anyone who can read the repo can read the file.
ServiceFile.__contentType.doc: MIME type of the file, `type/subtype` with optional parameters (e.g. `text/markdown; charset=utf-8`), sent as the Content-Type of the public route (SERVICE_FILE_INVALID_CONTENT_TYPE). REQUIRED.
ServiceFile.__size.doc: Size of the file in bytes: an integer of at least 0 and at most 10 MB, 10485760 (SERVICE_FILE_INVALID_SIZE, SERVICE_FILE_TOO_LARGE). The sum over every service of the project is at most 100 MB, 104857600 (SERVICE_FILES_PROJECT_QUOTA_EXCEEDED). Set by the upload tool, verified again at build. REQUIRED.
ServiceFile.__sha256.doc: sha256 of the bytes, 64 lowercase hex characters (SERVICE_FILE_INVALID_SHA256). Computed by the upload tool; the build refuses bytes whose hash differs. REQUIRED.

__EtlPipelineBinding.doc: [P5b, defined-but-deferred] The Spark-offloaded data-cleaning/ETL stage of an EventStream. HARD RULE: the transform runs on an EXTERNAL Spark cluster (or equivalent), NEVER inside the generated service — running heavy ETL on the high-throughput ingest path would defeat the big-load strategy. The service is the CONTROL PLANE (submit/trigger/schedule/monitor/cancel the Spark job); the Spark cluster is the DATA PLANE. The designer declares cleanup in a built-in form (declarativeRules, the default) OR supplies a custom Spark script (customScript escape hatch); codegen LOWERS it into the Spark job. Schema-only in Phase 3 — the thin orchestration client lands in Phase 5b.

EtlPipelineBinding.__provider.doc: Name of the bigLoadProvidersSettings store whose engine is `spark` (a compute/ETL provider, added in Phase 5b). The orchestration client submits to its master/Livy/Spark-Connect endpoint.
EtlPipelineBinding.__sourceTier.doc: The source tier the transform reads. v1 supports only `coldSink`, and only when the stream's `coldSink` is bound to an `s3Parquet` store: the Spark job reads the archived Parquet objects under the cold sink's `objectPrefix`. Empty means `coldSink`. `rawTopic` and `hotStore` are not implemented and are refused at validation (`EVENTSTREAM_CLEANING_SOURCE_TIER_UNSUPPORTED`); a stream with a cleaningPipeline and no `s3Parquet` cold sink is refused too (`EVENTSTREAM_CLEANING_SOURCE_NOT_S3PARQUET`, or the coldSink binding's own `EVENTSTREAM_PROVIDER_*` / `EVENTSTREAM_COLDSINK_ENGINE_INVALID` error when its provider is missing, undeclared or on an engine that cannot be a cold sink). Kept as String in v1.
EtlPipelineBinding.__sinkTier.doc: The sink tier the cleaned output is written to: `curatedStore` (empty = this default), `coldSink`, or `parquetLake`. v1 records the value but does not branch on it: the cleaned output is always curated Parquet on S3, written to the `curatedStore` store when one is named and declared (under `sinkObjectPrefix`, else `<streamName>Curated/`), otherwise to the stream's `s3Parquet` cold store (under `sinkObjectPrefix`, else the cold sink's `objectPrefix` with its trailing slash dropped plus `Curated/`: `ping/` gives `pingCurated/`). A pipeline with classify rules may not name `hotStore` here (`DECISION_ON_INGEST_PATH`). Kept as String in v1.
EtlPipelineBinding.__mode.doc: How the cleanup is authored (mirrors ComputeJob.implementationMode): `declarativeRules` (default) = an ordered list of built-in cleanup rules codegen COMPILES into the Spark transform (the designer never sees Spark); `customScript` = an advanced designer supplies a Spark script codegen embeds. Kept as String in v1.
EtlPipelineBinding.__rules.doc: [mode=declarativeRules] The ordered cleanup rules (CleaningRule[]) — validate / dedup / normalize / filter / cast / rename — codegen lowers into the Spark transform. Schema-only in Phase 3 (the exact rule schema is finalized in Phase 5b).
EtlPipelineBinding.__customScript.doc: [mode=customScript] The advanced Spark script / embedded transform codegen embeds into the Spark job. Schema-only in Phase 3.
EtlPipelineBinding.__schedule.doc: The trigger: a cron expression (batch cadence) OR `streamContinuous` (a long-running structured-streaming job). Kept as String in v1.
EtlPipelineBinding.__curatedStore.doc: [Phase 5b] Optional name of a bigLoadProvidersSettings s3Parquet store the CURATED (cleaned) output is written to when sinkTier=curatedStore. Defaults to writing a `Curated/` path on the cold s3Parquet store, next to the cold sink's `objectPrefix` (its trailing slash dropped: `ping/` gives `pingCurated/`).
EtlPipelineBinding.__sinkObjectPrefix.doc: [Phase 5b] Optional S3 object prefix the curated cleaned Parquet output is written under (e.g. `vehiclePingCurated/`). Defaults to `<streamName>Curated/` on a declared `curatedStore`, else to the cold sink's `objectPrefix` with its trailing slash dropped plus `Curated/` (`ping/` gives `pingCurated/`).

__CleaningRule.doc: [P5b, defined-but-deferred] One built-in cleanup rule lowered into the Spark ETL transform (see the family's design record, §4.1). Applied IN SPARK, never in the service. Schema-only in Phase 3.

CleaningRule.__name.doc: Rule identifier. Must be a valid codeName.
CleaningRule.name: String
CleaningRule.__op.doc: The cleanup operation: `validate` | `dedup` | `normalize` | `filter` | `cast` | `rename` | `classify`. Kept as String in v1. `classify` judges `field` with a decision provider and needs the `classify` block.
CleaningRule.__field.doc: The eventSchema field the rule operates on (for cast/rename/normalize/validate on a single column).
CleaningRule.__expression.doc: An MScript-backed predicate (validate/filter) or expression (normalize/cast/rename) over the event schema, which codegen compiles into a Spark SQL / DataFrame op.
CleaningRule.__classify.doc: [op=classify] The judged-column declaration (CleaningClassifySettings): the target column, the decision provider and pinned model, the question, the threshold and the source kind. Null for every other op.

__CleaningClassifySettings.doc: A classify cleaning rule: judges the rule's `field` with a decision provider and writes a judged column plus `<targetColumn>Confidence` and `<targetColumn>DecidedBy` (the pinned model). It runs only in the Spark cleaning stage, never on the ingest path (DECISION_ON_INGEST_PATH). An `enumerable` source (the default) is lowered to a Spark broadcast join: the stage collects the DISTINCT values of the column, the service classifies that set once through the shared decision cache, and the value -> label map is broadcast and joined, so the number of decisions depends on the distinct values and never on the row count. A `freeText` source is checked against a design-time budget and is not generated yet (CLEANING_CLASSIFY_FREE_TEXT_NOT_IMPLEMENTED). When the stream has an analytics binding the judged columns land in its raw ClickHouse table too, so an AnalyticsRollup may group by `targetColumn`.

CleaningClassifySettings.__targetColumn.doc: The judged column this rule produces. It must not collide with an eventSchema field, another judged column or a companion; the rule also produces `<targetColumn>Confidence` (Double) and `<targetColumn>DecidedBy` (the model version).
CleaningClassifySettings.__sourceKind.doc: How the judged `field` is lowered: `enumerable` (default) classifies its distinct values once and broadcast-joins the labels; `freeText` would batch rows per partition and is budget-checked at design time but not generated yet.
CleaningClassifySettings.__providerName.doc: Name of the `projectSettings.decisionProvidersSettings.decisionProviders[]` entry that judges the values. A dangling name fails validation (DECISION_PROVIDER_NOT_FOUND).
CleaningClassifySettings.__model.doc: The PINNED model version sent by this classify rule, overriding the provider entry's pin. Null inherits the entry. The selected model separates cached labels, and `<targetColumn>DecidedBy` records the model that answered. Floating tags are refused (DECISION_MODEL_NOT_PINNED).
CleaningClassifySettings.__question.doc: The ONE typed question asked about each value (a DecisionQuestion): `noul` stores the decision as a boolean, `choice` stores the option key and needs an escape option. `score` is refused (CLEANING_CLASSIFY_SCORE_UNSUPPORTED): a fractional level is not a stable label to group by.
CleaningClassifySettings.question: DecisionQuestion
CleaningClassifySettings.__confidenceThreshold.doc: Confidence at or above which an answer is stored as the label; below it the label stays null and only the confidence and model are recorded. Must sit outside the provider's drift band of 0.5 (DECISION_THRESHOLD_IN_DRIFT_BAND).
CleaningClassifySettings.__maxDistinctValues.doc: [enumerable] Ceiling on the distinct values one run classifies. Default 1000, framework ceiling 5000; a run whose source column has more fails closed with CLASSIFY_CARDINALITY_EXCEEDED before any decision is asked.
CleaningClassifySettings.__declaredRecordsPerWindow.doc: [freeText] The record volume one cleaning window must judge. With `windowMinutes`, `maxRecordChars` and `requestsPerMinute` it drives the design-time budget check (CLEANING_CLASSIFY_BUDGET_EXCEEDED).
CleaningClassifySettings.__windowMinutes.doc: [freeText] The minutes one cleaning window may spend judging `declaredRecordsPerWindow` records.
CleaningClassifySettings.__maxRecordChars.doc: [freeText] The longest judged text, in characters; it sizes how many records fit one request (the batch is token-derived, at ~3.5 characters per token). Default 1000.
CleaningClassifySettings.__requestsPerMinute.doc: [freeText] The provider request rate the budget assumes. Default 30, a conservative declared figure: no rate wall was measured, so set it from throughput measured on your own account.

__ElasticLogsSettings.doc: Registry container for the project's ElasticLog declarations (docs/ADR-elastic-log-pattern.md). Mirrors the bucketProvidersSettings shape: a single named array under projectSettings. Each ElasticLog is an ES-only, append-only, ILM-retained log — the mcpbff owns its index lifecycle and every service writes/reads it directly via generated helpers.

ElasticLogsSettings.__elasticLogs.doc: List of declared ElasticLogs. Add one entry per ES-only append log (audit trail, send record, telemetry) you want available project-wide.

__ElasticLog.doc: A single ES-only append log declaration. Sibling of DataObject but with NO relational baggage (no SQL/Mongo model, no soft-delete, no relations). Declares its own mapping fields, a self-owned timestamp field, and a retention window. The mcpbff creates + maintains the ES index (mapping + ILM + rolling write alias); services write with writeToESLog_<name>(obj) and read with queryESLog_<name>(body) directly against ES.

ElasticLog.__name.doc: Unique log identifier within the project. Used as the ES index/alias base (`<codename>_<name>`), the lookup key from writeToElasticLogAction.logName, and the generated helper suffix (writeToESLog_<name>). Must be a valid codeName.
ElasticLog.name: String
ElasticLog.__description.doc: An optional human-readable description of what this log records and why.
ElasticLog.__ownerService.doc: Optional name of the service that owns the admin read surface for this log. The mcpbff always owns the index lifecycle (mapping/ILM); ownerService only scopes where the low-volume admin search route is generated. When null, every service that writes the log can also read it directly.
ElasticLog.__timestampField.doc: Name of the self-owned timestamp field stamped on every appended log line (the ILM / time-range query anchor). Defaults to `@timestamp`.
ElasticLog.__retentionDays.doc: Retention window in days. The mcpbff registers an ES ILM policy that deletes indices older than this. 0 or negative disables retention (operators manage it externally).
ElasticLog.__fields.doc: The mapping fields of this log. Each field becomes an Elasticsearch mapping property; `filterable` fields are emitted as keyword/exact-match searchable.

__ElasticLogField.doc: One mapping field of an ElasticLog — becomes an Elasticsearch mapping property of the given type.

ElasticLogField.__name.doc: The field name as it appears in the ES mapping and in the logged object.
ElasticLogField.name: String
ElasticLogField.__type.doc: The Elasticsearch field type. 'keyword' = exact-match string; 'text' = full-text analyzed; 'long'/'double' = numeric; 'boolean'; 'date'; 'object' = free-form JSON (mapped as ES `flattened`: every leaf is indexed as an exact-match keyword whatever JSON type it carries, so mixed value shapes under one key can never poison the index; a leaf that needs numeric range/aggregation support belongs in its own typed field); 'ip' = IP address; 'geo_point' = lat/lon.
ElasticLogField.__filterable.doc: When true, this field is intended to be used in admin search filters (exact-match / range). Informational hint surfaced to the generated read route + mcpbff mapping; analyzed `text` fields are searchable regardless.

__ElasticLogFieldType.doc.#: The Elasticsearch mapping type of an `ElasticLogField` — how the field is indexed and queried in the ES index.
__ElasticLogFieldType.doc.keyword: Exact-match string — not analyzed; for identifiers, statuses and tag-like values, filtering and aggregations.
__ElasticLogFieldType.doc.text: Full-text analyzed string — tokenized for search; not suited to exact filtering or aggregations.

__McpbffSettings.doc: Settings of the mcpbff system service (the project's native full-API assistant host). `chatSurfaces[]` lists the messaging surfaces the assistant is reachable over: one entry per channel provider, the same ChatSurfaceSettings shape an aiAgent uses. A Telegram exposure is a webhook of the mcpbff (`/chat/<provider>/webhook` unless `webhookPath` overrides it) verified with the provider's `telegramWebhookSecret`; a WhatsApp exposure consumes the provider's inbound messages from the dispatcher topic `<codename>-whatsapp-inbound-message` (one consumer group per exposure). Replies use the provider's credentials only.

McpbffSettings.__chatSurfaces.doc: The messaging surfaces of the mcpbff full-API assistant. Each entry names a channel provider (kind whatsapp or telegram) and carries its identity strategy and, for Telegram, an optional webhook path. A provider may back at most one conversational consumer project-wide. Each surface may set typingIndicator false to disable read/typing signals; default on sends WhatsApp read plus typing every 20 seconds or Telegram typing every 4 seconds while its turn runs. Provider credentials only; status failures never fail the turn.

__ChatProvidersSettings.doc: RETIRED (patterns 1.60.0) - kept loadable so an older blueprint converts on load. Chat bots no longer exist: agents and the mcpbff bind directly to a channel provider (a WhatsApp or Telegram notification provider) that owns every credential of the channel. See ProjectSettings.chatProvidersSettings for the conversion rules.

ChatProvidersSettings.__chatProviders.doc: RETIRED. The legacy bot list; every entry is converted on load and the list is dropped from the saved blueprint. Add nothing here: bind an aiAgent surface or mcpbffSettings.chatSurfaces[] to a channel provider instead.

__ChatProvider.doc: RETIRED (patterns 1.60.0) - a legacy chat bot, kept loadable for the on-load conversion only. A bot has no channel and holds no credential any more: a WhatsApp bot is converted to the `whatsappProvider` it named, a Telegram bot to the telegram notification provider whose `telegramBotToken` names the same env var as the bot's `botToken` (else to a generated telegram provider named after the bot, whose credentials the operator fills), and every surface or mcpbff exposure that referenced the bot is re-pointed to that provider. `botToken`, `verifyToken`, `appSecret`, `phoneNumberId` and `webhookPath` are dropped by the conversion (a Telegram `webhookPath` of an mcpbff bot moves to the mcpbff surface entry). Validation warns per converted bot (CHAT_BOT_CONVERTED); save the converted blueprint to silence it.

ChatProvider.__name.doc: RETIRED. The legacy bot name; after the conversion the provider name is the binding key.
ChatProvider.name: String
ChatProvider.__surface.doc: RETIRED. The legacy bot channel; the surface type now comes from the bound provider's kind.
ChatProvider.__webhookPath.doc: RETIRED. Moves to the mcpbff surface entry (`mcpbffSettings.chatSurfaces[].webhookPath`) for a converted Telegram bot that was exposed in mcpbff; dropped otherwise.
ChatProvider.__botToken.doc: RETIRED. Dropped by the conversion: the bound provider's `telegramBotToken` / `whatsappAccessToken` is the outbound credential (env NOTIFICATION_PROVIDER_<PROVIDER>_<key>). For a Telegram bot, a telegram provider whose `telegramBotToken` names this env var is matched; otherwise a provider is generated.
ChatProvider.__verifyToken.doc: RETIRED. Dropped by the conversion: the Telegram webhook secret is the bound provider's `telegramWebhookSecret`.
ChatProvider.__appSecret.doc: RETIRED. Dropped by the conversion: the Meta app secret lives only on the WhatsApp provider (`whatsappAppSecret`).
ChatProvider.__phoneNumberId.doc: RETIRED. Dropped by the conversion: the phone number id is the WhatsApp provider's `whatsappPhoneNumberId`.
ChatProvider.__whatsappProvider.doc: RETIRED. The conversion target of a WhatsApp bot: the surfaces that referenced the bot are re-pointed to this provider.
ChatProvider.__exposeInMcpbff.doc: RETIRED. A bot exposed in mcpbff is converted to an `mcpbffSettings.chatSurfaces[]` entry naming the provider.

__WriteToElasticLogAction.doc: BusinessApiAction that appends an object to a declared ElasticLog by name. Compiles to a direct call to the generated writeToESLog_<logName> helper — a local ES write, NOT an interservice call (logs are high-volume).

WriteToElasticLogAction.__logName.doc: The name of the target ElasticLog (must match a projectSettings.elasticLogsSettings.elasticLogs[].name). Resolves to the writeToESLog_<name> helper at codegen time.
WriteToElasticLogAction.__logObject.doc: An MScript expression evaluating to the object to append to the log. Its keys should match the ElasticLog's declared mapping fields; the timestamp field is stamped automatically when absent.

__FetchFromElasticLogAction.doc: BusinessApiAction that queries a declared ElasticLog by name with an Elasticsearch search body and writes the hits to the action context. Compiles to a direct call to the generated queryESLog_<logName> helper. The context property receives a normalized ENVELOPE — `{ items, aggregations, total }` and nothing else: `items` is the matching lines (each hit's `_source`), `aggregations` is the response's aggregation result verbatim (null when the body asks for none), and `total` is the total hit count — so a single line is read as `this.<contextPropertyName>.items[0]?.<field>` and a rollup as `this.<contextPropertyName>.aggregations.<name>.buckets`, never `this.<contextPropertyName>.<field>`, which is undefined by construction (CONTEXT_ENVELOPE_MEMBER_UNDEFINED).

FetchFromElasticLogAction.__logName.doc: The name of the ElasticLog to query (must match a declared projectSettings.elasticLogsSettings.elasticLogs[].name).
FetchFromElasticLogAction.__body.doc: An MScript expression evaluating to an Elasticsearch search-body object (query / sort / from / size in ES's own format, not the abstract MScript query format). Defaults to a match_all over the most recent lines when absent.

__GraphQueryAction.doc: Runs a parameterized graph traversal and writes mapped records to the action context. BusinessApiAction that runs a parameterized graph traversal against a service's Bolt driver pool and writes the mapped records to the action context (docs/ADR-graph-database-layer.md §8a — peer of FetchFromElasticLogAction). Compiles to a direct `runGraphQuery` call (inline Cypher) or the generated `runNamedGraphQueryResult` dispatcher (a declared query). `query` resolves to either a declared service.graphLayer.queries[].name (the `named:<name>` form or a bare name) or an inline Cypher string; `params` is an MScript expression evaluating to the parameter object. The context property receives a normalized ENVELOPE — `{ records, total, ok, status }` and nothing else: `records` / `total` are the mapped rows, and `ok` / `status` say whether the query RAN (`ok: false` with `status` `unavailable` or `error` is an outage, not a zero-row answer, so a permission decision reads `ok` first) — so a single record is read as `this.<contextPropertyName>.records[0]?.<field>`, never `this.<contextPropertyName>.<field>`, which is undefined by construction (CONTEXT_ENVELOPE_MEMBER_UNDEFINED).

GraphQueryAction.__provider.doc: Name of the graphProvider to run against (must match a projectSettings.graphProvidersSettings.graphProviders[].name).
GraphQueryAction.__query.doc: Either a reference to a declared graph query (`named:<graphLayer.queries[].name>` or a bare query name) or an inline Cypher string.
GraphQueryAction.__params.doc: An MScript expression evaluating to the Cypher parameter object (e.g. `{ "js": "{ userId: this.session.userId, tenantId: this._tenantId }" }`). Optional — defaults to no parameters. NOTE the tenant read: there is no generic `this.session.tenantId` - nothing stamps it, so it reads `undefined` on every request. The manager slot `this._tenantId` is the generic spelling that IS real, and `this.session.<tenantName>Id` is the session field itself.

__GraphEdge.doc: A standalone, graph-only relationship hosted on a service (docs/ADR-graph-database-layer.md §4c). Unlike the FK property `graphEdge` (§4a) or the edge-object `projectsAsEdge` (§4b), a GraphEdge has NO relational home — it exists only in the graph (e.g. a computed `SIMILAR_TO` between documents). Its `properties[]` reuse the standard DataProperty shape. Sibling of computeJobs / dbBuckets on the service.

GraphEdge.__relationshipType.doc: The Neo4j relationship type, e.g. `SIMILAR_TO`. Unique within the service; used as the edge's name.
GraphEdge.__provider.doc: Name of the graphProvider this edge lives in (must match a projectSettings.graphProvidersSettings.graphProviders[].name).
GraphEdge.__from.doc: The source node label (a projected node label, e.g. `Document`).
GraphEdge.__to.doc: The target node label (a projected node label, e.g. `Document`).
GraphEdge.__properties.doc: Optional properties carried on the relationship, declared with the standard DataProperty shape.

__GraphCardinality.doc.#: The cardinality of a graph relationship between its endpoint node labels.
__GraphCardinality.doc.OneToOne: Each source node relates to at most one target node and vice versa.
__GraphCardinality.doc.OneToMany: Each source node relates to many target nodes; each target to one source.
__GraphCardinality.doc.ManyToMany: Source and target nodes relate many-to-many.
