FacebookLoginSetting.__useFacebookLogin.doc: A boolean value to enable or disable Facebook OAuth login. When true, users can sign in using their Facebook (or Instagram) accounts.
FacebookLoginSetting.__configuration.doc: The configuration object for Facebook OAuth login. Leave it null if useFacebookLogin is false.
FacebookLoginSetting.__emailVerification.doc: When a sign-in through this provider counts the returned email as verified: 'providerSignal' (default, the provider's own verification signal), 'requireVerification' (never) or 'trusted' (always). The decision marks a new account's email verified and is what lets a sign-in reach an EXISTING account with the same email: an email this setting does not count as verified creates an unverified account (which verifies through the normal email verification flow) and never signs in to an existing account by email; that sign-in is refused with 403 errMsg_SocialLoginEmailNotVerified and the user signs in with the existing method instead. A provider account linked to a user in the auth userSocialAccount object (written at the social registration and at a verified-email sign-in) is matched first and reaches that user whatever this setting decides. 'trusted' is only for a deployment locked to one directory you control (for Microsoft: configuration.tenant set to your own directory ID); see the SocialEmailVerification value docs for the warning.

__FacebookLoginConfig.doc: Configuration details for Facebook OAuth login, including App ID and App Secret. These are obtained from the Meta Developer portal (developers.facebook.com). The Facebook Login product must be added to the app, and 'email' and 'public_profile' permissions are required. Registration is always allowed via social login.

FacebookLoginConfig.__clientId.doc: The Facebook App ID. This should match the identifier registered in your Meta Developer portal application settings.
FacebookLoginConfig.__clientSecret.doc: The Facebook App Secret. This is a confidential key issued by Meta, stored securely in the platform secret store.

__MicrosoftLoginSetting.doc: Configuration for Microsoft Azure AD / Microsoft Entra ID OAuth login. Supports personal Microsoft accounts (Outlook, Hotmail, Xbox), work/school accounts (Azure AD / Microsoft 365), or both — controlled by the tenant setting. Uses OpenID Connect with the Microsoft identity platform v2.0 endpoints.

MicrosoftLoginSetting.__useMicrosoftLogin.doc: A boolean value to enable or disable Microsoft OAuth login. When true, users can sign in using their Microsoft accounts.
MicrosoftLoginSetting.__configuration.doc: The configuration object for Microsoft OAuth login. Leave it null if useMicrosoftLogin is false.
MicrosoftLoginSetting.__emailVerification.doc: When a sign-in through this provider counts the returned email as verified: 'providerSignal' (default, the provider's own verification signal), 'requireVerification' (never) or 'trusted' (always). The decision marks a new account's email verified and is what lets a sign-in reach an EXISTING account with the same email: an email this setting does not count as verified creates an unverified account (which verifies through the normal email verification flow) and never signs in to an existing account by email; that sign-in is refused with 403 errMsg_SocialLoginEmailNotVerified and the user signs in with the existing method instead. A provider account linked to a user in the auth userSocialAccount object (written at the social registration and at a verified-email sign-in) is matched first and reaches that user whatever this setting decides. 'trusted' is only for a deployment locked to one directory you control (for Microsoft: configuration.tenant set to your own directory ID); see the SocialEmailVerification value docs for the warning.

__MicrosoftLoginConfig.doc: Configuration details for Microsoft OAuth login. The clientId and clientSecret are obtained from the Azure Portal (Microsoft Entra ID \> App registrations). The tenant controls which account types are accepted: 'common' allows both personal and work/school accounts, 'organizations' allows only work/school accounts, 'consumers' allows only personal accounts, or a specific Azure AD tenant ID for single-tenant apps. Registration is always allowed via social login.

MicrosoftLoginConfig.__clientId.doc: The Microsoft Application (client) ID. Found in the Azure Portal under App registrations \> Overview.
MicrosoftLoginConfig.__clientSecret.doc: The Microsoft client secret (value, not the secret ID). Created in Azure Portal under App registrations \> Certificates & secrets. Stored securely in the platform secret store.
MicrosoftLoginConfig.__tenant.doc: Controls which Microsoft account types can sign in. Use 'common' (default) for both personal and work/school, 'organizations' for work/school only, 'consumers' for personal only, or a specific Azure AD tenant ID (GUID) for single-tenant apps.

__LinkedinLoginSetting.doc: Configuration for LinkedIn OAuth login. This section defines whether LinkedIn login is enabled, the client ID and secret, and whether users can register using their LinkedIn accounts. LinkedIn uses OpenID Connect with the 'openid', 'profile', and 'email' scopes.

LinkedinLoginSetting.__useLinkedinLogin.doc: A boolean value to enable or disable LinkedIn OAuth login. When true, users can sign in using their LinkedIn accounts.
LinkedinLoginSetting.__configuration.doc: The configuration object for LinkedIn OAuth login. Leave it null if useLinkedinLogin is false.
LinkedinLoginSetting.__emailVerification.doc: When a sign-in through this provider counts the returned email as verified: 'providerSignal' (default, the provider's own verification signal), 'requireVerification' (never) or 'trusted' (always). The decision marks a new account's email verified and is what lets a sign-in reach an EXISTING account with the same email: an email this setting does not count as verified creates an unverified account (which verifies through the normal email verification flow) and never signs in to an existing account by email; that sign-in is refused with 403 errMsg_SocialLoginEmailNotVerified and the user signs in with the existing method instead. A provider account linked to a user in the auth userSocialAccount object (written at the social registration and at a verified-email sign-in) is matched first and reaches that user whatever this setting decides. 'trusted' is only for a deployment locked to one directory you control (for Microsoft: configuration.tenant set to your own directory ID); see the SocialEmailVerification value docs for the warning.

__LinkedinLoginConfig.doc: Configuration details for LinkedIn OAuth login, including client ID and secret. This object is used when LinkedIn login is enabled. LinkedIn uses the 'Sign In with LinkedIn using OpenID Connect' product. Registration is always allowed via social login.

LinkedinLoginConfig.__clientId.doc: The LinkedIn OAuth client ID. This should match the identifier registered in your LinkedIn Developer application.
LinkedinLoginConfig.__clientSecret.doc: The LinkedIn OAuth client secret. This is a confidential key issued by LinkedIn, stored securely in the platform secret store.

__BFFService.doc: Configuration settings for the BFF (Backend-for-Frontend) service in the project. Although optional, a BFF service is highly recommended in microservice architectures to consolidate and simplify data access for frontend clients. Since data is distributed across services, the BFF service acts as a unified interface, retrieving and aggregating data from different sources. An OpenAPPL compiler supports a hybrid CQRS strategy where complex aggregations, defined as DataViews, can be stored and queried efficiently via Elasticsearch. Alternatively, lightweight aggregations can be executed dynamically using dynamic DataViews, which merge data from services at request time without persisting the result. Use Sttaic DataViews for performance-critical or cross-service filtered views, and Dynamic DataViews for dynamic, user-specific aggregations. If no DataViews are defined, the BFF service will not be generated for the project.

BFFService.__serviceSettings.doc: Module-level settings chapter for the BFF service — currently holds the documentation section that MindUI reads when wiring DataView consumers in pages.
BFFService.__dataViews.doc: A list of DataView definitions that describe how data should be aggregated and exposed by the BFF service. A DataView is a REUSABLE QUERY DEFINITION first (main object + projection + aggregates/stats); `viewBasics.isStored: true` adds an Elasticsearch materialisation on top. Both kinds have the same two consumers: a get/list BusinessApi with `apiOptions.dataViewName` (a stored view is read from its index; a dynamic view binds at READ TIME, the api reading its object from the database with its own where clause and the view's joins applied per row) and custom code calling `LIB.dataViews.<name>(filter?, { page, limit }?)`. Code serving a caller passes `{ session }` (or `{ scoped: true }` inside an api request): the read is then pinned to the caller's tenant and active-only, like the consuming api's where clause. Without either option it is a SYSTEM read with no session (no tenant term; soft-deleted rows are left out of a dynamic view unless the filter names `isActive`), for system work only.

__BffServiceSettings.doc: Module-level settings chapter for the BFF service. Holds documentation (UX intent for MindUI) and any future BFF-wide settings.

BffServiceSettings.__documentation.doc: Module-level UX prompt for MindUI's BFF page generation (which DataViews are intended for which page surfaces, density / cardinality expectations, KPI tile vs row data, cross-view drill-downs).

__DataView.doc: A DataView defines an aggregated projection of data for the BFF service in OpenAPPL. It serves as a unified structure that collects and combines information from multiple microservices. DataViews can be configured as either *stored* or *dynamic*. Stored DataViews persist their results in Elasticsearch and are optimal for queries requiring filtering, sorting, or cross-service joins. Dynamic DataViews are assembled at runtime during the request cycle and are suitable for lightweight, user-specific, or real-time scenarios. Both types aim to simplify frontend development by consolidating distributed data into a single, queryable view.

__DataView.useCase.description: Use a DataView to consolidate data from multiple microservices into one queryable projection for the frontend — choose isStored=true (Elasticsearch-backed, filterable/sortable) for cross-service joins, or dynamic for lightweight per-request assembly. This example builds a customer view enriched with their orders and per-customer order stats.

DataView.__viewBasics.doc: Basic metadata and configuration for the DataView, including its name, storage strategy, source object, and selected properties. This section determines the fundamental structure and behavior of the view.
DataView.__aggregates.doc: A list of aggregate definitions that perform data joins from related objects, similar to SQL joins. These are used to enrich the DataView with related datasets, such as joining orders into a customer view.
DataView.__lookups.doc: A list of lightweight lookup definitions used to fetch reference values, typically for UI display purposes (e.g., converting a userType ID into a localized label like 'Administrator'). These join single values from dictionary-like sources.
DataView.__stats.doc: A list of statistical calculations performed within the view to enrich it with precomputed analytics.

__ViewBasics.doc: Configuration for a DataView's identity and structure. It specifies whether the view is stored (in Elasticsearch) or dynamic (evaluated at runtime), the name of the view, the main source object it is built upon, and the list of core properties to retrieve from the main object.

ViewBasics.__name.doc: A unique name for the DataView. Avoid using a name that matches any existing data object to prevent conflicts. Prefer descriptive names like 'UserDetailsView' that clearly indicate the view's purpose. For services resolved to Java, authored Kafka listener names and group IDs are limited to 249 Unicode code points; longer values are refused at design time before Spring listener startup. This Java-specific bound does not refuse other service languages or unresolved contexts.
ViewBasics.__isStored.doc: Whether the view is MATERIALISED in Elasticsearch. `true`: an index is built and kept in sync from the source events, and consumers read the joined document from it (fast, seconds-stale, the right answer when the collected data is more than SQL serves well). `false` (the default): nothing is indexed and the view is computed when read - an api that binds it with `apiOptions.dataViewName` reads its main object from the DATABASE with its own where clause (fresh, so a liveness read like remaining capacity is exact) and the view's aggregates/stats are joined onto each row per request; `LIB.dataViews.<name>()` computes it for custom code; a notification bound to it computes the document when the event arrives. A dynamic view costs its joins on every read, so a read-time list that declares `paginationOptions.unpaged: true` is warned about (DATAVIEW_READ_TIME_UNBOUNDED); every list is paged unless it declares `unpaged`.
ViewBasics.__mainObject.doc: The primary data object or existing view that the DataView is structured around. This object serves as the root of the aggregation.
ViewBasics.__properties.doc: An array of property names from the main object that should be included in the view's result. An empty list (or an omitted one) means every column of the main object is projected: the aggregation writes the whole source document, and a stored view's index declares a mapping for every source column. A hashed or isSecret column is the exception: whether it belongs to the main object or to an aggregate's child, it is never stored in a view document and gets no mapping. List properties only to narrow the view to a subset of them.
ViewBasics.name: String

__ViewAggregate.doc: Defines an aggregate (join) within a DataView that links related objects to the main object, similar to SQL-style joins. Aggregates are resolved at the Elasticsearch layer using replicated microservice data. Each aggregate pulls in one or more records from a child object based on matching keys and optional conditions, then embeds them under the specified property name in the final view output.

ViewAggregate.__name.doc: The property name under which the joined data will be added in the DataView. This is typically a descriptive alias for the child object, like 'userRoles' or 'companyInfo'.
ViewAggregate.__childObject.doc: The name of the data object being joined (child object). This is the source of the aggregated data. Relation-target validation resolves a child DataView through its viewBasics.mainObject, including cycle-safe view-of-view chains, before comparing the parent-key relation target.
ViewAggregate.__parentKey.doc: The key field from the main object used to perform the join. Often this is a foreign key like 'companyId' or 'userId'.
ViewAggregate.__childKey.doc: The key field from the child object that is matched against the parent key. Typically this would be the child's primary identifier or a linking field.
ViewAggregate.__oneToMany.doc: Specifies whether the relationship is one-to-many (true) or one-to-one (false). If true, the result will be an array of records from the child object.
ViewAggregate.__condition.doc: An MScript condition evaluated on the main object to decide whether this aggregation should be executed. The condition runs with the main record bound to `this`, so read record fields as `this.<field>` — e.g. `{ "js": "this.userId != null" }`. A bare field name (`userId != null`) does not resolve in the generated aggregator and fails the bff build.
ViewAggregate.__checkIn.doc: An MScript condition evaluated on each child record to determine whether it should be included in the final aggregation result. The condition runs with the child record bound to `this`, so read record fields as `this.<field>` — e.g. `{ "js": "this.isActive === true" }`. A bare field name does not resolve in the generated aggregator and fails the bff build.
ViewAggregate.__properties.doc: The list of property names to extract from the child object. Only these fields will be included in the aggregated result.
ViewAggregate.name: String

__ViewLookup.doc: Defines a lookup operation in a DataView, typically used to enrich an object with a human-readable label or translated text from a dictionary index. Lookups are similar to aggregates but are optimized for fetching a single value, such as a label, for UI rendering. They are especially useful for localization (e.g., converting 'userType: 0' to 'Administrator') or enriching records with descriptive names from static dictionaries like country, city, or status lists. Multi-language lookups automatically resolve language-specific values based on the user's locale if the view is dynamic; if stored, all language variants are stored with suffixes.

ViewLookup.__name.doc: The name of the lookup field in the DataView output. This is the property that will hold the resolved value, such as 'userRoleName'. For stored DataViews, the generated service stores multilingual variants using suffixes like 'userRoleName_en', 'userRoleName_tr'. When returned to the client, only the relevant language value is exposed.
ViewLookup.__lookupDict.doc: The name of the dictionary index where the lookup value resides. This can be any dictionary-like dataset, such as countries, roles, or labels. For multilingual dictionaries, the runtime automatically appends the language suffix (e.g., '_en', '_tr') to the index name during lookup.
ViewLookup.__multiLang.doc: Whether the lookup dictionary is multilingual. If true, the compiler will automatically manage language-specific fields and suffixes. If false, a single language-independent value is returned.
ViewLookup.__lookupKey.doc: The key field in the main object (or its aggregates) used to match against the dictionary index. This is typically a reference like 'roleId' or 'countryId'. The dictionary index's target key is always assumed to be 'id'.
ViewLookup.__lookupValue.doc: The field in the dictionary index whose value will be returned. For example, 'name' or 'label'. This is what will appear in the DataView as the resolved text.
ViewLookup.name: String

__ViewStat.doc: Defines a statistical aggregation for a DataView. Unlike ViewAggregates that collect related records, ViewStats compute mathematical summaries such as sum, count, average, min, and max over grouped data. These groupings, or 'buckets', are constructed based on parent-child relationships between objects. This is conceptually similar to Elasticsearch's bucket-based aggregations. Each ViewStat joins the main object with a target object (child) using a foreign key relationship and computes one or more aggregates using the defined conditions. It's ideal for summarizing numerical data across associations, such as counting user orders or summing revenue per company.

ViewStat.__name.doc: The name of the statistic in the DataView result. This will appear as a property in the view (e.g., 'totalRevenue', 'userOrderCount').
ViewStat.__childObject.doc: The name of the target object to aggregate data from (e.g., orders, sessions, transactions). Can also be a previously defined view.
ViewStat.__parentKey.doc: The key from the main object that groups the stat results. Acts as the bucket owner (e.g., userId if calculating per user).
ViewStat.__childKey.doc: The foreign key in the target object used to relate it back to the main object. Typically a reference like 'userId' or 'companyId'.
ViewStat.__select.doc: An optional MScript filter applied before bucketing. Use this to narrow the child data (e.g., only 'canceled' orders in the last month). The filter is evaluated per child record with the record bound to `this`, so read record fields as `this.<field>` — e.g. `{ "js": "this.status === 'canceled'" }`. There is no `parent` binding in any DataView script slot — the parent/child correlation is the parentKey/childKey join — and a bare field name or `parent.<field>` read does not resolve and is refused at validation. It is COMPILED into the stat's own Elasticsearch child query, beside the parentKey/childKey term, so it accepts the same expression forms `AggregateItem.filterValue` does and refuses the same ones at validation.
ViewStat.__aggList.doc: The list of AggregateItems to apply on the grouped buckets. Each defines a numeric operation like sum, count, average. If empty, a default count is applied.
ViewStat.name: String

__AggregateItem.doc: Defines a single mathematical operation to apply to a group of records within a ViewStat. Supports standard operations like sum, average, min, max, and count. Each AggregateItem targets a specific field in the child object and may apply additional filters. It is particularly useful when multiple grouped metrics are required from the same set of joined records, such as 'count of failed orders' vs. 'sum of successful order values'.

AggregateItem.__name.doc: The identifier of the computed metric (e.g., 'orderCount', 'totalAmount'). Appears as a key in the result object.
AggregateItem.__aggField.doc: The field of the target object used in the aggregation (e.g., 'amount', 'id'). For count operations, typically use 'id'.
AggregateItem.__dataType.doc: The expected data type of the result (e.g., 'Integer', 'Float'). Often reflects the type of the aggField but may differ (e.g., averaging integers produces floats).
AggregateItem.__filterValue.doc: Optional MScript condition to filter records inside the bucket before applying the operation. Allows multiple filtered aggregations on the same group (e.g., 'totalCanceledAmount', 'totalCompletedAmount'). The condition is evaluated per bucket record with the record bound to `this`, so read record fields as `this.<field>` — e.g. `{ "js": "this.status === 'completed'" }`. There is no `parent` binding in any DataView script slot — the parent/child correlation is the owning stat's parentKey/childKey join — and a bare field name or `parent.<field>` read does not resolve and is refused at validation. It is COMPILED into an Elasticsearch `filter` sub-aggregation around this item's metric, so the expression has to be one Elasticsearch can express: comparisons of `this.<field>` against a literal (`==`, `!=`, `===`, `!==`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`) combined with `&&`, `||` and `!`. A function call, an arithmetic expression, a ternary, or a comparison between two fields is refused at validation rather than dropped, and so is an exact filter on a column Elasticsearch analyzes (a scalar Text) or does not index at all - both of those would compile cleanly and match nothing.
AggregateItem.name: String

__AggTypes.doc.#: Specifies the type of aggregation to perform. Translates to Elasticsearch aggregation types at the BFF aggregate emit boundary — `count` here maps to ES `value_count` in the generated query body. Legacy projects that still store `value_count` are accepted and rewritten to `count` on read (see AggTypeMigration).
__AggTypes.doc.sum: Sum the values of the records.
__AggTypes.doc.avg: Average the values of the records.
__AggTypes.doc.min: Find the minimum value of the records.
__AggTypes.doc.max: Find the maximum value of the records.

__Service.doc: Defines the overall structure and configuration for a microservice within the project. Each service acts as an independent domain that encapsulates its own data model, business logic, and interface behaviors. While services primarily manage and expose domain-specific data, this module extends beyond basic CRUD operations by offering customizable patterns, libraries, authentication, and specialized route handling. Use this module to tailor the internal and external behaviors of your service—whether it's securing endpoints, defining edge routes, managing complex data objects, or integrating advanced logic. The service configuration ensures the resulting microservice is robust, secure, and aligned with the specific application requirements.

Service.__serviceSettings.doc: The general configuration for the service, including its basic metadata and authentication rules. This sets foundational behavior such as login requirements and token usage.
Service.__dataObjects.doc: An array of data object definitions representing the internal data schema of the service. Each object defines its fields, relations, and business logic behavior.
Service.__businessLogic.doc: BusinessApi enables the creation of sophisticated backend operations through declarative configuration. It should be used when a project needs to expose business logic as APIs - whether through REST endpoints, real-time WebSocket connections, event-driven Kafka handlers, or scheduled cron jobs. BusinessApi automatically handles CRUD operations on data objects, parameter extraction from multiple sources (request body, Redis, session), authentication, and complex workflows with validation, transformations, and inter-service calls. Use BusinessApi when you need to create, read, update, or delete data, process events, schedule background tasks, or orchestrate multi-step business operations without writing custom backend code.
Service.__library.doc: The service's function library where custom business logic is written. Includes  edge functions, and shared utilities callable across routes and controllers.
Service.__edgeControllers.doc: A set of custom controller endpoints defined at the edge of the service, each connected to a function from the service library. Edge controllers offer custom REST APIs beyond the auto-generated business APIs.
Service.__shoppingCartConfig.doc: Shopping cart configuration chapter. When enabled, provides Redis-first hyper-scalable cart management with automatic price calculations, promotion engine, and generated cart management APIs. All Cart, CartItem, Campaign, and Coupon DataObjects are auto-generated. Only one shopping cart is allowed per service.
Service.__aiAgents.doc: An array of AI Agent definitions for this service. Each agent is a standalone, reusable entity with its own system prompt, model configuration, tool access, and optional conversation management. Agents can handle one-shot tasks, multi-turn chat, or orchestrate other agents and support multiple modalities (text, image, audio, video, vision); they are exposed as dedicated REST/SSE endpoints. NOTE: this chapter is currently hidden from designers — every new AI agent is designed in AgentHub (agentHub/aiAgents) instead. The chapter is kept on Service for two reasons: (1) backward compatibility with older projects that have legacy agents here, (2) reserved for the planned 'smart API' direction where service-local agents take this service's dbLayer functions (create<X> / get<X>ListByMQuery / update<X>ById / etc.) as tools instead of cross-service HTTP APIs, behaving as a smart-API surface over the local data model. TODO(smart-api): when that direction lands, flip the designer prompts and add a dbLayer-tool branch in nodeJs2/src/agent-layer/templates/agent-tool-registry.ejs. Do NOT delete this chapter or the AIAgent pattern.
Service.__realtimeHubs.doc: An array of RealtimeHub definitions for this service. Each hub provides a bidirectional Socket.IO endpoint with room management, typed messages, presence tracking, and auto-generated message DataObjects. Use hubs for chat, collaborative editing, live dashboards, game lobbies, and any scenario requiring persistent two-way communication between clients.
Service.__videoRooms.doc: An array of VideoRoom definitions for this service (docs/ADR-video-conference-pattern-family.md). Each video room binds an existing DataObject to a video-conference / live-broadcast surface: interactive SFU rooms (oneToOne, groupMeeting, webinar) or massive-scale broadcast rooms (RTMP ingest → HLS/CDN), with a layered join-authorization flow, capability-based room roles, auto-generated session/participant DataObjects, recording to a service bucket, and an optional AI pipeline (speech-to-text transcription, meeting analysis, smart search). The generated service is the control plane only — media flows directly between clients and the provider referenced from projectSettings.videoProvidersSettings.
Service.__contentModels.doc: ContentModel declarations generate content storage, publishing transitions and headless delivery for this service. On nodejs editorial Business APIs are generated by default, with optional child and version APIs; configure permissionSettings for editing and publishing. Existing designer-authored object/operation APIs are retained. Set contentBasics.editorialApis: none to opt out of generated editorial APIs. Models, migrations, Elasticsearch indexes and database-change events come from the synthesized DataObjects. Use listContentModelPresets and addContentModelPreset for an ordinary ContentModel preset, then customize fields, project role names, routing and buckets.
Service.__eventSubscriptions.doc: An array of EventSubscription definitions for this service. Each subscription exposes Kafka topics to clients via WebSocket or SSE with authorization derived from the DataObject's access config. Use for dashboards, live feeds, order tracking, and any scenario where clients need to receive server-side events without a full realtime hub.
Service.__dbBuckets.doc: Database-backed file storage buckets. Each bucket creates a PostgreSQL table with a BYTEA column for storing small files (icons, avatars, secret documents) directly in the database without external storage infrastructure. Upload and download routes are auto-generated at /bucket/{name}/.
Service.__remoteBuckets.doc: Remote (cloud) file storage buckets backed by S3, GCS, Azure Blob, or S3-compatible providers (R2, or any S3-compatible endpoint via the s3Compatible provider type). Each remote bucket creates a metadata data object ({name}RemoteFile) holding storageKey + file info; binary content lives in the configured storage provider, not the database. Upload and download routes are auto-generated at /bucket/{name}/ (not /remotebucket/{name}/, which is mounted nowhere): POST /bucket/{name}/upload for multipart bytes, POST /bucket/{name}/upload-url for a presigned PUT, GET /bucket/{name}/download/:key, DELETE /bucket/{name}/object/:key. Use for large files, images, videos, documents — anywhere external object storage is preferred over BYTEA blobs.
Service.__nativeBuckets.doc: Self-hosted file storage buckets backed by a platform-PROVISIONED SeaweedFS (S3-API-compatible) object store (docs/ADR-native-bucket-pattern.md, docs/ADR-seaweedfs-nativebucket.md). Full object-store semantics (presign, large files, streaming, SSE) with NO cloud account, NO cloud credentials, and NO cloud cost — on-prem / data-sovereignty friendly. Unlike RemoteBucket the designer supplies no provider/credentials: the hosting platform provisions and manages the SeaweedFS store (lifecycle, root creds, default-bucket creation), resolved at runtime from project-scoped NATIVEBUCKET_* env. Each native bucket creates a metadata data object named {name}RemoteFile (the SAME twin suffix RemoteBucket uses) holding storageKey + file info; binary content lives in the managed SeaweedFS store. That twin is materialized at BUILD time, so listBlueprint(dataObjects) does not list it, but it is nevertheless a legal childObject / fetch target at design time. Locally backed by the FARM SeaweedFS S3 gateway (mb-seaweedfs, :19900); in deploy the deployer stands up a per-project SeaweedFS store. Reuses the RemoteBucket S3 adapter under the hood. Upload and download routes are auto-generated at /nativebucket/{name}/.
Service.__computeJobs.doc: Compute workloads hosted by this service (docs/ADR-calculation-layer.md §2/§3). Each `ComputeJob` is a long, business-shaped unit of work (batch-transform, ai-inference, media-processing, …) generated as an async, queued, observable, cancellable, retryable job: a submit Business API enqueues it and returns a jobId, a compute-worker controller drains the queue and runs it on the bounded compute pool, and it produces a result plus bucket-backed artifacts and a completion event. The recommended shape for any non-trivial computation. Only valid on rust/python host services (the calculation languages); a non-compute service (Node/Java/…) submits jobs to a compute service over M2M instead of hosting them (§7).
Service.__eventStreams.doc: High-throughput ingest→hot/cold/analytics pipelines hosted by this service. Each `EventStream` is the headline asset of the big-load pattern family: a single chapter that folds the ingestion write contract, the hot-store binding (write-optimized current-state + last-N + TTL), and the read surfaces as sections — composing the existing kafka/compute/realtime layers rather than forking them (the way `ComputeJob` folds its spec/input/result sections). Its hotStore / coldSink / analytics bindings reference a `projectSettings.bigLoadProvidersSettings` store BY NAME. The generated big-load-layer keeps the write path thin (a fast async batched insert — NEVER heavy per-row work) so the ingest layer absorbs far more than a synchronous CRUD endpoint. coldSink/analytics/retention/cleaningPipeline sections are defined in the schema but wired in later phases (P4+).
Service.__jobStreams.doc: Async job-orchestration streams hosted by this service (docs/ADR-async-job-orchestration-patterns.md). Each `JobStream` is a durable, reconnectable, observable async BUSINESS job that generalizes `ComputeJob`: the 'work' is a target `businessLogic[]` BusinessApi invocation (not a native compute kernel). From one declaration codegen emits an enqueue edge, a kafka WORKER controller on the job topic that drives the target API, a durable per-job event outbox, and a reconnectable SSE observation edge keyed by jobId — and it SUPPRESSES the target BusinessApi's public REST route (internal by default; `targetApi.keepPublicRoute` re-exposes it). deliveryMode is push; the lifecycle is queued→started→[relayed progress]→ended with a terminal result link. The sibling pull/admission-control pattern (`WaitingRoom`) is a separate asset in the same ADR.
Service.__waitingRooms.doc: Pull-mode admission-control queues hosted by this service (docs/ADR-async-job-orchestration-patterns.md, the WaitingRoom section). Each `WaitingRoom` is the Taylor-Swift-ticketing turnstile: it meters a thundering herd through N gated Redis rooms into a bound PUBLIC `businessLogic[]` BusinessApi so the target is never stampeded. From one declaration codegen emits a join edge (ZADD into the entry room), a metered cron-promoter advancing front-of-room → next room → final admission at each room's admissionRatePerSecond, the room's own realtime position channel, and a one-shot time-boxed `QueToken` minted on admission. CONTRAST jobStreams (push, which HIDES the target): a WaitingRoom does NOT proxy or suppress the target — the target keeps its public route and gains the `authOptions.queueTokenRequired` gate, and the client calls it DIRECTLY with the minted token. The sibling push/async-job pattern (`JobStream`) is a separate asset in the same ADR.
Service.__loadShield.doc: The service's single in-process priority load shedder (docs/ADR-loadshield-priority-load-shedding.md) — an optional SINGULAR chapter (at most one per service: the shield guards the whole dispatch plane over one shared DB pool, so two shields would fight over the same concurrency budget). Declares the per-API/action shed-priority tiers (integer 0-5, 0 = never shed, 5 = first to shed; unassigned routes get derived defaults by action nature), the CoDel-style `targetQueueLatencyMs` setpoint, an `enabled` flag, and exemptions. CONTRAST `waitingRooms[]`: a waiting room is an opt-in, client-visible PULL queue in front of ONE known-stampede API for a PLANNED spike; the loadShield is the always-on, invisible-until-triggered guard for the WHOLE service against UNPLANNED overload — they compose. `eventStream` ingest keeps its own declared shedding and is structurally exempt. Null/absent = the service dispatches unshielded, exactly as today. Declaring the chapter emits the nodejs runtime: a bounded priority queue + concurrency cap in front of route dispatch with immediate DB-free 429 LOAD_SHED rejection, plus the ADAPTIVE layer — a PID-driven rejection threshold on the tier×cohort scale and an AIMD auto-tuned concurrency cap, both fed by the shared DB-saturation signal and degrading to the static behavior when no relational signal exists. Controller gains are internal platform constants (never blueprint); `LOADSHIELD_DISABLED` / `LOADSHIELD_ADAPTIVE_DISABLED` are the runtime ops kill-switches, and `LOADSHIELD_COHORT_ROTATION_SECONDS` tunes the time-rotating cohort salt (default 3600, 0 = fixed pre-rotation mapping).
Service.__seedData.doc: Declarative seed-data records upserted into the service's DataObjects at startup (after migrations). Each `SeedData` entry is `{ seedBasics, values }` — `seedBasics` names the target `dataObject`, the `matchBy` idempotency key and the `insertOnly` names, and `values` is the map (property → MScript) for the row to insert-if-absent / refresh-if-present. The generator emits a `seed-data` BootstrapModule that runs once on boot via the db-layer. Replaces hand-written init routines (super-admin / root-tenant / admin-group bootstrap); reusable by any custom service that needs initial system records. A data object may carry MULTIPLE seed rows (e.g. three subscription plans): each entry upserts independently, keyed by its `matchBy` values — just make sure every row of the same object has a matchBy key whose seeded values differ (validation rejects rows that collapse onto the same matchBy identity with SEED_ROW_NOT_DISTINGUISHABLE). Item addressing: each row persists in its own storage slot keyed by its matchBy identity, and the item-addressed `seedData/{<dataObject>}` path resolves the object's FULL ROW SET — the row itself when one row is stored, an array of rows when several are; a row's own `id` addresses one exact row.
Service.__oauthFlows.doc: Declarative OAuth redirect flows hosted by this service. Each `OAuthFlow` exposes its own REST start (redirect to the provider) + callback (token exchange → normalized profile) route, backed by the config-driven common OAuth runtime. On the auth service the callback completes the login (find-or-register + mint session); every flow also publishes its `completeKafkaTopic` completion event so other services can react. Replaces the hand-written social-login router.
Service.__graphLayer.doc: The service's graph-database surface (docs/ADR-graph-database-layer.md §4c/§8/§9) — a single namespaced block so the graph collections don't clutter the Service top level. Holds the service's standalone `GraphEdge`s, declarative `GraphQuery`s, and composite `HierarchicalResourceGraph` resources. Null/absent when the service declares none. (DataObject node projections live on `objectSettings.graphProjection`; graph providers live on `projectSettings.graphProvidersSettings`.)
Service.__serviceFiles.doc: Design-time static files that ride in the generated service repo (an optional singular chapter, `ServiceFiles`). Each file is uploaded once with the `uploadServiceFile` tool, which stores the bytes in the platform bucket and writes one manifest entry `{path, visibility, contentType, size, sha256}` here; the build fetches and verifies the bytes and writes them to `service-files/public/<path>` or `service-files/private/<path>` in the repo. On a nodejs service a public file is served at `GET <serviceBaseUrl>/service-files/<path>`, and every file (public or private) is read from custom code and MScript with the synchronous `LIB.serviceFiles.text(path)` / `.json(path)` / `.bytes(path)` / `.info(path)` / `.has(path)` accessor, for example `AddToContextAction` with value `LIB.serviceFiles.text('legal/terms-v3.md')`. Other languages get the files in the repo but no route or accessor yet. A private file is NOT secret: anyone who can read the service repo, a preview or a runner image can read it, so never put credentials in one; use secrets or custom variables. Limits: 10 MB per file, 100 MB for all service files of the project. Null/absent when the service carries no files.
Service.__cronJobs.doc: Scheduled jobs of this service (`CronJob[]`). Each cron job (`{ jobBasics, scheduleSettings }`) calls one function of the service library (`jobBasics.libFunction`, a `library.functions` module) on a cron schedule, with no Business API in between. The generated runtime claims every tick in the service database (table `sys_cronJobRun`, unique on job name and tick), so exactly one replica runs each tick and no Redis is needed; it records every run (status, timings, a masked and capped error), enforces a timeout, and serves an admin surface (`GET /cron-jobs`, `GET /cron-jobs/:name/runs`, `POST /cron-jobs/:name/run`). `scheduleSettings.runMode` makes a job run on every tick (`always`), succeed only once ever (`onceEver`, the urgent data-migration tool), or succeed once per start era of the service (`oncePerStart`). Use a cron job for scheduled work that is plain code; use a Business API cron controller (`BusinessApi.cronSettings`) when the scheduled work should run through an API's parameters, actions, workflow and events. Emitted by the nodejs runtime only: a service whose language is known to be another one is refused (CRON_JOBS_LANGUAGE_NOT_PORTED). A service without cron jobs emits exactly what it emitted before this pattern existed.

jobBasics.name: moveLegacyOrders
jobBasics.description: One-off: copy rows from legacyOrder into order.

__GraphServiceLayer.doc: The service's graph-database surface, namespaced under `service.graphLayer` so the graph collections don't pollute the Service top level (docs/ADR-graph-database-layer.md §4c/§8/§9). Groups the service's standalone `GraphEdge`s (graph-only relationships, §4c), declarative `GraphQuery`s (curated traversal archetypes, §8b), and composite `HierarchicalResourceGraph` resources (the flagship authorization graph, §9). DataObject node projections live on `objectSettings.graphProjection`; graph providers live on `projectSettings.graphProvidersSettings`.

GraphServiceLayer.__edges.doc: Standalone graph-only relationships hosted by this service (§4c). A `GraphEdge` exists ONLY in the graph — no FK, no join object backs it (contrast the FK property `graphEdge` §4a and the edge-object `projectsAsEdge` §4b).
GraphServiceLayer.__queries.doc: Declarative graph-traversal query archetypes (§8b). Each `GraphQuery` selects a curated archetype via `type` (GraphQueryType) — reachableNodes / effectivePermission / permissionExplain / ancestors / descendants / shortestPath / neighborhood / recommendation / custom — and carries its typed sub-spec under the `spec` wrapper (the ComputeJob idiom). Referenced by name from `GraphQueryAction.query` and `ComputeJob.graphIO.reads.query`.
GraphServiceLayer.__resources.doc: Flagship composite graph patterns (§9). A `HierarchicalResourceGraph` expands into node projections, hierarchy/permission edges, an inheritance policy, and a ready set of queries for the document-management authorization use case.

__ServiceSettings.doc: Defines the foundational settings of the service module, including basic metadata and authentication configurations. These settings must be established before designing the service's data model. They determine the service's identity, behavior within the project, and how it handles authentication. This configuration acts as the entry point for service-level behavior, ensuring consistency and security from the outset of development.

ServiceSettings.__serviceBasics.doc: Defines the basic metadata of the service, including its unique name, description, and optional custom configuration variables. These basics are used throughout code generation, routing, and documentation.
ServiceSettings.__serviceOptions.doc: Defines basic options of the service for authentication, http and data model
ServiceSettings.__serviceAuthentication.doc: Manages service-level authentication settings, allowing each service to enforce its own login rules, support for login endpoints, and object sharing mechanisms via secure tokens.
ServiceSettings.__httpSettings.doc: Defines the HTTP server configuration for the service, including which port it should listen on for incoming requests.
ServiceSettings.__dataModelOptions.doc: The configuration object containing high-level data model options for the service module. These options include metadata or global flags that influence the behavior of the data model or govern shared behaviors across all data objects.
ServiceSettings.__realtimeConfig.doc: Configures the Socket.IO server for realtime hubs and WebSocket event subscriptions. Only relevant when the service has at least one RealtimeHub or WebSocket EventSubscription. Controls the scaling adapter (Redis for multi-instance, memory for dev), heartbeat timings, and per-user connection limits.
ServiceSettings.__grpcClients.doc: A list of FOREIGN (non-OpenAPPL) gRPC servers this service can call from a `GrpcCallAction` (docs/ADR-grpc-interservice-and-grpccall.md, Part B). Each entry declares a named gRPC client: the foreign server's endpoint, its `.proto` contract (supplied INLINE as `protoSource` — the codegen writes it into the caller's gRPC-client assets at `controllers/grpc/proto/<name>.proto`), the `package`/`service` to load from that proto, optional static auth metadata headers, and optional TLS. A `GrpcCallAction` references one of these by `grpcClientName` and a `grpcMethodName`. This is the foreign-server counterpart of the auto-selected interservice gRPC path (Part A): an OpenAPPL target is known to the framework and needs zero config, while a foreign target is declared here once. Calls ride the shared `grpcUnaryCall` engine — same engine the interservice gRPC branch uses.

__GrpcClientConfig.doc: A named, FOREIGN gRPC server this service can call via a `GrpcCallAction` (docs/ADR-grpc-interservice-and-grpccall.md, Part B). Declared under `serviceSettings.grpcClients[]`. The designer supplies the foreign server's `.proto` (primarily as INLINE `protoSource` text; a path/URL is a documented follow-on) plus the `package`/`service` to load from it; codegen writes that proto into the caller's gRPC-client assets (`controllers/grpc/proto/<name>.proto`) and the runtime loads it through the shared `grpcUnaryCall` engine by a `__dirname`-relative path. `endpoint` is a literal `host:port` or a `$ENV:VAR` reference resolved from the environment at runtime. `metadata[]` are STATIC headers (e.g. an API-key / Bearer token the foreign server expects — there is no OpenAPPL M2M trust to a foreign server) and may themselves use `$ENV:` refs. `tls` selects insecure (dev default) vs SSL.

GrpcClientConfig.__name.doc: Unique codeName for this gRPC client within the service. Referenced by `GrpcCallAction.grpcClientName`.
GrpcClientConfig.__endpoint.doc: The foreign gRPC server's address. Either a literal `host:port` (e.g. `payments.internal:50051`) or a `$ENV:VAR` reference (e.g. `$ENV:PAYMENT_GRPC_URL`) resolved from the environment at runtime. Prefer `$ENV:` so the endpoint isn't baked into the generated code.
GrpcClientConfig.__protoSource.doc: The FOREIGN server's `.proto` contract, supplied INLINE as proto text (the primary form). Codegen writes it verbatim to `controllers/grpc/proto/<name>.proto` so the runtime loads it through proto-loader with the same options the gRPC server uses. The proto MUST declare the `package` and `service` named below. (A path/URL source is a documented follow-on.)
GrpcClientConfig.__package.doc: The proto `package` name to load from `protoSource` (e.g. `payment`). Must match the `package` declared in the proto.
GrpcClientConfig.__service.doc: The proto `service` name to load from `protoSource` (e.g. `PaymentService`). Must match a `service` declared in the proto; `GrpcCallAction.grpcMethodName` must be one of its rpc methods.
GrpcClientConfig.__metadata.doc: Optional STATIC metadata headers sent on every call to this foreign server (e.g. an API key or a Bearer token the server expects). Each value may be a literal string or a `$ENV:VAR` reference resolved at runtime. Unlike the interservice gRPC path, there is no OpenAPPL M2M trust to a foreign server — auth is whatever the foreign server requires, declared here.
GrpcClientConfig.__tls.doc: Optional transport security. When omitted or `mode: 'insecure'` (the dev default) the channel uses insecure credentials — matching the interservice gRPC default. `mode: 'ssl'` uses TLS; `caCert` (literal PEM or `$ENV:VAR`) overrides the system trust roots when the server presents a private/self-signed certificate.
GrpcClientConfig.name: String

__GrpcClientMetadataItem.doc: A single STATIC gRPC metadata header sent on every call to a foreign gRPC server (see GrpcClientConfig.metadata). The value is a literal string or a `$ENV:VAR` reference resolved at runtime — NOT MScript (these are static credentials, not per-call dynamic values).

GrpcClientMetadataItem.__name.doc: The metadata header name, preserved VERBATIM (NOT codeName-normalized — header names are dash-case by convention, e.g. `authorization` or `x-api-key`; gRPC lowercases them at runtime).
GrpcClientMetadataItem.__value.doc: The static header value, either a literal (e.g. `Bearer abc123`) or a `$ENV:VAR` reference (e.g. `$ENV:PAYMENT_GRPC_TOKEN`) resolved from the environment at runtime.
GrpcClientMetadataItem.name: String

__GrpcClientTls.doc: Transport security for a foreign gRPC client (see GrpcClientConfig.tls). `insecure` (default) matches the interservice gRPC dev default; `ssl` enables TLS with an optional CA override for private / self-signed server certificates.

GrpcClientTls.__mode.doc: `insecure` (default) uses plaintext credentials — fine for dev / trusted networks. `ssl` enables TLS.
GrpcClientTls.__caCert.doc: Optional CA certificate (literal PEM string or a `$ENV:VAR` reference) used to verify the foreign server's TLS certificate when it is signed by a private / self-signed CA. Only consulted when `mode: 'ssl'`. When omitted, the system trust roots are used.

__ServiceOptions.doc: Defines a configuration class for the basic options of the service for authentication, http and data model

ServiceOptions.__serviceAllowsUserToLogin.doc: Keep this false unless you know what you are doing. If true, the service provides login endpoints for users, allowing it to act as an authentication provider. This option is used if you want to make your own auth/user service instead of the default one created with authentication module configuration.
ServiceOptions.__httpPort.doc: The port number that the service will use to listen for HTTP traffic. Recommended to use ports in the 3000-3099 range for consistency across microservices. The LOCAL dev env does not read this as a position: it derives a stable per-service port from the service name (the same name always gets the same port, and adding, removing or reordering services does not renumber the others), unless an explicit httpPort other than the 3000 default is authored, which is honoured there too. A literal 3000 is treated as unauthored.
ServiceOptions.__routerSuffix.doc: Use this in your custom deployment if you have any suffix in your service url to be removed before evaluated in express router. AI Agents should keep this null.
ServiceOptions.__dataModelName.doc: The name identifier of the data model configuration. For current OpenAPPL versions, use 'main' or 'default'. In future versions with support for multiple data models per service, this name will distinguish them.
ServiceOptions.__dbType.doc: Specifies the type of database engine used for storing the service's data. It must be one of the values in the DbTypes enum: postgresql (fully supported) or mongodb (beta). `mysql` was REMOVED from the vocabulary on 2026-08-01 — it was implemented only by the PHP / Laravel target, whose service codegen lane was retired on 2026-07-31. A service that still declares it is refused at design time (RETIRED_DB_TYPE) rather than silently downgraded to another engine. The engine also fixes the form of the framework's system-asset ids (root tenant, super admin, admin group and its member) at codegen: the canonical UUIDs on postgresql, their 24-hex ObjectId form on mongodb. The service's seeds write that form for the row ids AND for every reference to them, and the generated comparisons (session config, root tenant checks, the PBAC tenant clause, the tenant-move guard) compare that form; nothing decides it at runtime.
ServiceOptions.__ormType.doc: Specifies the Object-Relational Mapping (ORM) library used to interact with the database. This must be one of the OrmTypes enum values. Currently, Sequelize is supported; Mongoose is in beta.
ServiceOptions.__useSoftDelete.doc: Indicates whether records are soft-deleted (i.e., marked inactive using an 'isActive' flag) instead of being physically removed from the database. This setting applies globally unless overridden at the data object level.
ServiceOptions.__wrapMScriptExecution.doc: Controls whether generated MScript expressions are wrapped with runtime error tracing via runMScript(...). Keep this true for safer diagnostics. Set false only after thorough testing if you need maximum runtime performance.
ServiceOptions.__blockedM2MClients.doc: An array of service names that are blocked from accessing this service using machine-to-machine tokens. Services listed here cannot call this service's APIs with machine tokens. However, blocked services can still access public APIs (loginRequired: false) and can trigger event-based functions on behalf of users when using user tokens. This provides fine-grained control over inter-service communication while maintaining flexibility for public endpoints and user-initiated actions. This is the DENY list of the M2M caller gate; it is a SECOND-LEVEL guard that only narrows callers whose M2M token ALREADY verified against the issuing service's JWKS — it is never authentication. When both lists are configured, this one WINS: a caller named here is refused even if `allowedM2MClients` also names it. Names are matched case-folded (they are `codeName` values). Renamed from `machineToMachineBlockList` on 2026-08-01 for symmetry with `allowedM2MClients`; the old spelling is refused at design time.
ServiceOptions.__allowedM2MClients.doc: An array of service names that are allowed to access this service using machine-to-machine tokens. When non-empty, ONLY services listed here may call this service's APIs with an M2M token; every other caller is refused with 403 `M2M_CLIENT_NOT_ALLOWED`. When empty, every caller presenting a valid M2M token is allowed (subject to `blockedM2MClients`). This is the ALLOW list of the M2M caller gate; it is a SECOND-LEVEL guard that only narrows callers whose M2M token ALREADY verified against the issuing service's JWKS — it is never authentication. `blockedM2MClients` wins when a name appears on both. Names are matched case-folded (they are `codeName` values). The gate applies to the M2M path only: a caller that is not on this list still reaches `loginRequired: false` APIs and still works through a user token.
ServiceOptions.__secureEvents.doc: Event ALIASES (NOT raw topic strings) on which the project's Ed25519 signature is required. Use the short alias form designers already write everywhere else — e.g. `userCreated`, `paymentSucceeded`, `order-cancelled`. The runtime maps each alias to its full Kafka topic name (typically `<projectCodename>-<serviceName>-<objectName>-<action>`) via the registered topicAliasResolver (see _common/<lang>/.../topic-alias). On the **publish** side: when this service emits an event whose alias is listed here, the publisher wraps the payload as `{ payload, sig, kid, jwks_url }` before placing on the resolved topic. On the **subscribe** side: when this service consumes an event whose alias is listed here, the subscriber verifies the signature and drops the message on failure. Use across trust boundaries — payment confirmations, audit-trail writes, cross-tenant fan-outs.
ServiceOptions.__publishes.doc: Kafka topics this service publishes from designer code that is NOT a library module, declared so the project's producer census counts them as produced. Prefer declaring on the library function that publishes (`library.functions[].publishes` / `library.edgeFunctions[].publishes`); use this service-level list for a publish the census cannot attribute to a module, e.g. an inline lifecycle-hook script. Same contract as `LibModule.publishes`: the wire name of each topic, codename-prefixed when it sits in a service's framework namespace (`<projectCodename>-<serviceName>-service-<event>`), as authored otherwise; an unprefixed framework-namespace name or a malformed topic is a design-time error. Without a declaration a subscription to such a topic is reported as producerless (`KafkaSubscriptionsWithoutProducer` at boot, `KAFKA_TOPIC_NO_PRODUCER` at design time).
ServiceOptions.__postgresMajorVersion.doc: Optional declared PostgreSQL server major version. Required and at least 15 when a CompositeIndex opts into nullsNotDistinct. It describes the deployment target; it does not upgrade a server. MongoDB does not use this field.

__ServiceBasics.doc: Provides core identifiers and metadata for the service. Includes the service's internal ID, a unique name (used in code, routing, and service naming), a descriptive text for documentation, and any custom variables required for runtime configuration.

ServiceBasics.__id.doc: Unique identifier of the service, automatically managed within the project.
ServiceBasics.__name.doc: Service name used for naming files, folders, endpoints, and routes. Use short, single-word names in camelCase if needed. This field impacts many system-level identifiers.
ServiceBasics.__description.doc: A clear, human-readable explanation of what the service does. This description appears in service-level documentation and interface annotations.
ServiceBasics.__frontendDocument.doc: A text based information to inform the frontend developer or frontend AI agent about the service specific UX behaviour of the service logic based on user stories and use cases. The format may be either text or markdown(recommended). Write the document as an AI prompt and describe service gneric UX behaviours. Any data object specific information should be given as a brief key sentence, since they will be detailed in their own objects. Note that this document will be given to the AI agent or human developer combined with all technical details that is generated from the servic design,so this document should only focus on service-specific behavioral UX business logic.
ServiceBasics.__customVariables.doc: A list of custom key-value pairs that will be available to all scripts and functions within the service. Useful for environment-specific settings or reusable values. A variable whose name has a secret-shaped segment (TOKEN, SECRET, KEY, PASSWORD, ...) is a deploy secret unless its entry says secret: false: its value stays out of the committed env files and is pushed as a CI/CD variable.
ServiceBasics.__packages.doc: A unified, language-agnostic list of third-party package dependencies for this service. Each entry names a package manager (`npm`, `pip`, `maven`, `nuget`, `gomod`, `cargo`), the manager-native package id, and a version. The codegen target for the service's language picks the entries whose `manager` matches that language's ecosystem and injects them into the generated manifest (package.json, pyproject.toml, pom.xml, .csproj, go.mod, Cargo.toml). This is the canonical replacement for the deprecated `nodejsPackages` field.
ServiceBasics.name: String

__PackageManager.doc.#: The package manager / language ecosystem a `Package` dependency belongs to. The codegen target for a service's language injects only the packages whose manager matches that ecosystem.
__PackageManager.doc.npm: Node.js / TypeScript packages from the npm registry (e.g. `axios`, `@scope/pkg`). Injected into package.json.
__PackageManager.doc.pip: Python packages from PyPI (e.g. `requests`). Injected into pyproject.toml dependencies.
__PackageManager.doc.maven: Java/JVM artifacts from Maven Central. The `name` is `groupId:artifactId`. Injected as a <dependency> in pom.xml.
__PackageManager.doc.nuget: C#/.NET packages from NuGet (e.g. `Newtonsoft.Json`). Injected as a <PackageReference> in the .csproj.
__PackageManager.doc.gomod: Go modules (e.g. `github.com/foo/bar`). Injected as a require directive in go.mod.
__PackageManager.doc.cargo: Rust crates from crates.io (e.g. `serde`). Injected under [dependencies] in Cargo.toml.
__PackageManager.doc.composer: PHP packages from Packagist (`vendor/package`, e.g. `guzzlehttp/guzzle`). Injected as a `require` entry in composer.json for Laravel services. ARCHIVED: the php service lane was retired on 2026-07-31, so no selectable service language consumes this ecosystem — entries are carried but never injected.
__PackageManager.doc.vcpkg: Native C/C++ libraries from vcpkg (e.g. `opencv`). Provisioned into the build image and discoverable via CMake `find_package`; referenced from a `NativeKernel` by its `links` name.
__PackageManager.doc.conan: Native C/C++ libraries from Conan (`name/version`, e.g. `fftw/3.3.10`). Provisioned into the build image for `NativeKernel` linking.
__PackageManager.doc.apt: System packages from the Debian/Ubuntu apt repositories (e.g. `libfftw3-dev`). Installed into the build image; used to provide system C/C++ libraries a `NativeKernel` links against.

__Package.doc: A unified, language-agnostic third-party package dependency declaration. A single `Package` shape covers every supported language: the `manager` field selects the ecosystem and the codegen target for the service's language injects only the matching entries into its native manifest. This generalizes the deprecated `NodeJsPackageItem` (npm-only) to all seven supported languages.

__Package.useCase.description: Declare a third-party dependency on a service. The `manager` selects the ecosystem and the matching language codegen injects it into the generated manifest. This example adds the npm `axios` HTTP client (latest) bound to the `axios` alias for use in function/MScript code, plus a cargo crate with a feature flag.

Package.__manager.doc: The package manager / language ecosystem this dependency belongs to. Required. Only packages whose manager matches the service's language are injected into that language's manifest.
Package.__name.doc: The manager-native package identifier. Required. npm: `axios` or `@scope/x`; pip: `requests`; maven: `group:artifact`; nuget: `Newtonsoft.Json`; gomod: `github.com/foo/bar`; cargo: `serde`; composer: `vendor/package`.
Package.__version.doc: The version constraint for the package. Required. Use an asterisk (`*`) to request the latest version.
Package.__importAs.doc: Optional. The binding alias used when the package is imported in generated function/MScript code (generalizes the npm-only `defaultImportConst`). When omitted, no automatic import binding is wired and the package is only added to the manifest.
Package.__options.doc: Optional manager-specific extras as key/value pairs (e.g. cargo `features`). Interpretation is manager-dependent.
Package.name: String

__DbTypes.doc.#: Enumeration of supported database types for service-level data models. RETIRED ENGINE: `mysql` was removed from this vocabulary on 2026-08-01 — its only implementation was the PHP / Laravel target, and the php service codegen lane is frozen and archived. It is no longer selectable, and a project whose service still names it is refused at design time rather than silently downgraded to another engine. Use postgresql (fully supported) or mongodb (beta).
__DbTypes.doc.postgresql: Use PostgreSQL for relational database management. The default across every language target.
__DbTypes.doc.mongodb: Use MongoDB for document-oriented data storage (currently in beta).

__ServiceLanguage.doc.#: Target language a service is generated in. Each service compiles to exactly one language; mixed-language projects are supported by setting this per service. When unset, falls back to the project-level default and finally the framework default (nodejs). RETIRED TARGET: `php` was removed from this vocabulary on 2026-07-31 — the php service codegen lane is frozen and archived. It is no longer selectable, and a project that still names it is refused at design time rather than silently downgraded to another language. The php SDK target (a client library for a service written in ANY language) is unaffected and remains fully available.

__DataObject.doc: A DataObject is the core building block of a service in OpenAPPL. It represents both the data schema (like a table in SQL or a collection in MongoDB) and the business logic that operates around it. Each DataObject includes a set of DataProperties (fields), and it governs how the data is stored, validated, secured, and exposed through automatically generated business APIs. Beyond simple data modeling, DataObjects enable complex logic configurations, such as access control, field-level behaviors, validation, and custom API route behavior. They serve not only as data containers but also as logical units of functionality within the microservice. A DataObject declared `objectSettings.basicSettings.virtual: true` is the one exception to the table: it is a response-only record (a computed decision, a report row) with no table, model or db layer, bound only by get and list apis whose actions build the response.
__DataObject.specNotes: The property names `id`, `isActive`, `createdAt`, `updatedAt`, `recordVersion` and `_type` are reserved, in any letter case and in their snake_case spellings (`is_active`, `created_at`, `updated_at`, `record_version`): the compiler adds these fields to every stored data object, and a blueprint that declares one is refused with `RESERVED_PROPERTY_NAME`.

__DataObject.useCase.description: Use a DataObject to model a domain entity — its persisted schema plus the access control, indexing, and CRUD behavior around it. This example models a project entity scoped per tenant with a slug, status enum, and an owner relation.

basicSettings.name: project
basicSettings.description: A project owned by a user within a tenant, tracking its lifecycle status.

DataObject.__objectSettings.doc: Settings that define general behavior and characteristics of the data object, such as naming, indexing, visibility, and access options.
DataObject.__properties.doc: The list of data properties of the data object. Each property represents a field and encapsulates both the type of the data and behavioral configurations like default values, constraints, visibility, or computed logic. Note: the compiler automatically creates standard fields (`id`, `isActive`, `createdAt`, `updatedAt`), so avoid defining these manually.

__CrudTypes.doc.#: CrudTypes define the fundamental operation mode of a route. Each route is classified by a CRUD type that reflects its intended data operation: create, update, read, or delete.
__CrudTypes.doc.create: Specifies that the route handles creation operations. It inserts a new record into the associated data object. The compiler auto-generates default behavior for create routes, but custom logic can be defined via the route’s createSettings.
__CrudTypes.doc.update: Specifies that the route handles update operations for a single existing record. The primary access criterion is the record's ID. The compiler auto-generates default behavior for update routes, but customizations can be added using updateSettings.
__CrudTypes.doc.get: Specifies that the route retrieves a single record of the data object. The primary access criterion is the record's ID. The compiler provides default logic, but route-specific getSettings can be applied for custom retrieval.
__CrudTypes.doc.list: Specifies that the route retrieves multiple records of the data object. By default, results are filtered by authorization rules. List-level customizations can be configured through listOptions and paginationOptions
__CrudTypes.doc.delete: Specifies that the route handles deletion of a single record. The access criterion is the record's ID. OpenAPPL supports both hard and soft deletes, with behavior controlled through deleteOptions.

__ObjectSettings.doc: Configuration settings that govern the behavior, access control, and optimization strategies of a data object. These settings allow fine-grained control over how the data object behaves in terms of authorization, caching, indexing, payment processing, ledger accounting, and membership relationships. This is the central point to define how the object integrates with infrastructure and security policies in a microservice.

__ObjectSettings.useCase.description: Use ObjectSettings to declare a data object's identity, access control, indexing, and infrastructure opt-ins (caching, payments, ledger, membership) in one place. This example configures a tenant-scoped, privately-accessed order object with Redis entity caching and a unique composite index.

basicSettings.name: order
basicSettings.description: A customer order with line items and a lifecycle status.

ObjectSettings.__basicSettings.doc: Core definitions of the data object such as its name, label, and description. These settings influence how the object appears in documentation and interfaces.
ObjectSettings.__authorization.doc: Rules and permissions that control access to this data object. These object-level rules enhance or override project-level authorization to implement fine-grained security models. Optional — omit (or null) when unused; never [].
ObjectSettings.__redisEntityCacheSettings.doc: Configuration for enabling Redis-based entity-level caching. Useful for frequently accessed, lightweight records that benefit from high-speed lookups and smart cache invalidation. Optional — omit (or null) when unused; never [].
ObjectSettings.__compositeIndexSettings.doc: Defines one or more composite indexes to ensure uniqueness across multiple fields and improve the efficiency of compound queries. This is especially critical for enforcing business constraints or query performance in relational databases. Please note that if you need unique constraints on a single field, you can use the `unique` property of the DataProperty instead.
ObjectSettings.__checkout.doc: Provider-neutral one-time-payment activation for this data object. When enabled, the framework auto-generates the sys_<X>Payment system data object and the start/refresh/callback APIs, routed through the PaymentProvider named in `configuration.providerName`. This is the recommended shape for one-time-payment objects, binding to any configured PaymentProvider. Optional — omit (or null) when unused; never [].
ObjectSettings.__subscription.doc: Provider-neutral subscription activation for this data object. When enabled, the framework treats this object as a recurring-billing entity, generates sys_<X>Subscription and sys_<X>SubscriptionPlan tables, and emits subscribe/cancel/update APIs. Requires the bound PaymentProvider to support subscriptions. Optional — omit (or null) when unused; never [].
ObjectSettings.__marketplace.doc: Provider-neutral marketplace activation for this data object. When enabled, the framework generates sys_<X>ConnectedAccount and sys_<X>Payout tables and wires the KYC / transfer / payout APIs. Requires the bound PaymentProvider to support marketplace. Optional — omit (or null) when unused; never [].
ObjectSettings.__membershipSettings.doc: Settings to enable access control for this object through an external membership relationship. This object represents the protected resource (such as a project), and access to it is managed by another object (such as projectMember) that links users or roles to this resource. Useful in multi-user collaboration domains where permissions are scoped per resource instance. Optional — omit (or null) when unused; never [].
ObjectSettings.__ledgerSettings.doc: Append-only-ledger activation for this data object. When enabled, every ROW of this object owns a ledger of integer value (points, credits, cents, stock units): the framework generates the satellite lot/movement(/reservation) objects and the earn/consume/reserve/commit/release/getBalance/listEntries/adjust API roster, bound to the owner row by a single FK. Requires a relational dbType on the owning service. Optional — omit (or null) when unused; never [].
ObjectSettings.__graphProjection.doc: Opt-in graph-database projection for this DataObject (docs/ADR-graph-database-layer.md §3/§4b). When populated, the object is projected into the named graph provider — either as a NODE (set `labels` + `projectedProperties`, the object-level analogue of the property-level `indexedInElastic` flag) or as an EDGE (set `projectsAsEdge` when the object's rows ARE relationships, e.g. a permissionGrant join/grant table). A projection is node-shaped OR edge-shaped, never both. The graph is a secondary, rebuildable projection over the relational source of truth, synced on write like the ES projection. Leave null/absent when the object is not projected.
ObjectSettings.__invoicing.doc: Provider-neutral accounts-receivable invoicing activation for this data object. When enabled, the framework treats this object as an invoice-bearing entity: the invoice ledger (sys_<X>Invoice and satellites) and the issue/finalize/void/apply-payment surface are generated around it, bound to the InvoiceProvider named in `configuration.providerName` — or to the framework-internal provider when that is null. Invoicing is a SEPARATE axis from checkout: checkout moves money, invoicing produces the billing document; both can be active on the same object with different providers. Optional — omit (or null) when unused; never [].
ObjectSettings.__fiscalization.doc: Regulatory fiscalization activation for this data object. When enabled, the framework treats this object as the source of fiscal documents (e-invoice, e-archive, fiscal reports): the sys_<X>FiscalDocument ledger and the submit/track surface are generated around it, routed through the FiscalProvider named in `configuration.fiscalProviderName` and the jurisdiction's fiscal policy module. Fiscalization is a SEPARATE axis from invoicing: invoicing produces the commercial billing document, fiscalization adapts it to (or reports it into) the government's fiscal infrastructure — and in reporting-style regimes the fiscalized thing may be transaction data with no invoicing block at all, so this block does NOT require `invoicing` on the same object. Optional — omit (or null) when unused; never [].
ObjectSettings.__enterpriseProjection.doc: Opt-in projection of this DataObject onto an EnterpriseObject declared in enterpriseHub. When populated, this object mirrors an external business object on an enterprise platform (SAP, Salesforce, …): `enterpriseModelName` + `enterpriseObjectName` name the asset, `fieldMap` maps this object's properties to the platform's fields, and `syncMode` decides the data-flow direction (readThrough / pullMirror / writeThrough / bidirectional). The mcpbff bridge does the actual platform I/O; this block is the design-time binding. Leave null when the object is purely local. NOTE: defining an EnterpriseObject in enterpriseHub does NOT require a projection — this is the optional step that also stores it locally.
ObjectSettings.__geoSettings.doc: Settings for the generated /geo REST surface of this data object's geo-typed properties (GeoPoint, GeoRoute, GeoArea). The four spatial routes (inCircle, mostClose, inBBox, inPolygon) honor `authorization.dataObjectAccess` — a non-accessPublic object refuses anonymous callers — and this block adds a designer-declared visibility filter applied on top of that gate. Optional — omit (or null) when unused; never [].
ObjectSettings.__objectModeration.doc: Content moderation for this data object's writes. When `enabled`, every create and update of this object by a moderated caller is judged by a calibrated decision provider against the designer's `policy` before it becomes visible, and every submission is recorded in a framework-generated `sys_<X>ModerationReview` object that reviewers work through injected Business APIs. In the default `staged` mode an unapproved write never reaches the real object at all. This is CONTENT moderation, not authorization: the verdict never feeds a permission check. Use this block as THE answer to "this project needs moderation"; a hand-authored moderation service is the exception for edge cases the pattern does not cover. Optional - omit (or null) when unused; never [].
ObjectSettings.__visitTracking.doc: Object visits, the object-level SINK of the visits pattern (docs/ADR-object-visits-pattern.md). When `enabled`, the framework records who consumed a row of this object, how (access / view / read / seen) and when, as the analytics fact table `sys_<Obj>Visit`, and can keep a quiet counter column and per-actor read state. WHICH call is a visit is declared on the BusinessApi (`apiOptions.visitSettings`), never here: an enabled visitSettings on an api whose object declares no enabled visitTracking is a design-time error (VISIT_TRACKING_NOT_DECLARED). Analytics-first: the event history is the product, read state is one by-product of it. A visit is an engagement signal, never an authorization, filtering or billing input. Optional - omit (or null) when unused; never [].
ObjectSettings.__recommendationSettings.doc: Recommendation lists of this object as the ITEM being recommended (docs/ADR-recommendation-engine.md). Each list names a relation (bought together, viewed together, trending, ...) and the evidence that feeds it; the interactions come from sources the patterns publish (discovered automatically, e.g. a catalog-bound shopping cart) or from sources declared here. A generated refresh cron precomputes tenant-scoped neighbor / popularity tables, and the lists are served under this object's own routes, on the item's own service, behind the item's read gate. Filters are deterministic and re-applied at serve time; a recommendation score never feeds authorization or filtering. Optional - omit (or null) when unused; never [].
ObjectSettings.__defaultChoice.doc: A DEFAULT row of this object (pattern DefaultChoice): a default address, a default saved card, a default shipping company. When `isActive`, the framework adds an `isDefault` column with a one-default-per-scope invariant, makes the first row of a scope its default, promotes the newest remaining row when the default is deleted, and injects the set<Object>AsDefault / getDefault<Object> / set<Object>AsDefaultForUser / getDefault<Object>ForUser apis. `inline` (the default) keeps the default on the user's own rows (one per owner, or per `scopeField`); `inline: false` makes it a system default plus a per-user override table `sys_UserDefaultFor<Object>`. `isDefault` is never writable through the object's generic create / update apis. Optional - omit (or null) when unused; never [].

__DefaultChoice.doc: A default row per scope for a data object (`objectSettings.defaultChoice`). Two shapes occur.
