DataProperty.__uploadSettings.doc: Opt-in upload source for a column of a RemoteBucket / NativeBucket `{name}RemoteFile` twin, declared in `remoteBucketSettings.additionalColumns`. Setting `uploadSettings.fromUploadField: true` lets the bucket's through-server upload route (`POST /bucket/{name}/upload`, `POST /nativebucket/{name}/upload` and the in-process writeBucketObject helper) copy the multipart text field of the SAME name as the column into the twin row it writes, after checking the value against the column type. It has no effect on the property of an ordinary data object (PROPERTY_UPLOAD_FIELD_OUTSIDE_BUCKET_TWIN warning). Leave null/absent otherwise.

__PropertyUploadSettings.doc: Where the through-server upload of a RemoteBucket / NativeBucket takes a `{name}RemoteFile` twin column from. Only meaningful on an entry of `remoteBucketSettings.additionalColumns`.

PropertyUploadSettings.__fromUploadField.doc: When true, the upload route reads the multipart text field named exactly like this column and writes its value into the twin row it creates, so a client that knows the value at upload time (a lifecycle status, the id of the record the file belongs to) needs no second update call. Only flagged columns are read from the multipart body; no other body field reaches the row, and the framework-owned base columns can never be flagged (their names are reserved). The value is checked against the column type before anything is stored: ID (a UUID or a 24-hex ObjectId), String (at most 255 characters), Text, Integer, Short, Double, Float, Decimal (a plain decimal number), Boolean (true / false), Date (an ISO 8601 date or date-time) or Enum (one of its enumOptions, exact spelling); a mismatch answers 400 UPLOAD_FIELD_INVALID naming the field, before the object is stored. An absent field leaves the column to its default. Array columns, Object / Geo / Blob types and columns whose value has another source (autoIncrement, sessionSettings, staticJoin, decisionSource) cannot be flagged (REMOTE_BUCKET_UPLOAD_FIELD_UNSUPPORTED); a column named `file` or `fileKey` cannot be flagged either, the route reads those multipart fields itself (REMOTE_BUCKET_UPLOAD_FIELD_NAME_RESERVED). The presigned `/upload-url` path writes no row and carries no fields. Implemented by the nodejs, java, dotnet, rust and python lanes; elsewhere the flag has no effect yet (REMOTE_BUCKET_UPLOAD_FIELD_NOT_IMPLEMENTED warning).

__PropertyDecisionSource.doc: Write-time classification of one DataProperty by a decision provider. The decision is taken once, when the row is written, and stored as a derived column plus three companion columns (`<prop>DecisionConfidence`, `<prop>DecidedBy`, `<prop>DecidedAt`), so reads never consult the model. A stored judgement without its model version cannot be audited or re-derived when the criterion changes, which is why the companions are not optional. Lifecycle: a create decides (unless the caller supplied the value, which pins it as a manual override); an update re-decides only when it writes a `recomputeOn` property (or releases the override by writing `<prop>DecisionOverridden: false`); an update that writes the property itself pins it (`<prop>DecisionOverridden: true`, `<prop>DecidedBy: manual`) and later recompute triggers leave it alone. An answer whose confidence is below `confidenceThreshold` (and a noul whose probability sits inside the provider's drift band of 0.5) is NOT stored as a value: the column stays null while the confidence, model and time are recorded, so a boundary case is never silently classified (ADR rule 8). A provider failure never fails the write: the column and its companions are left unset and the backfill retries the row. The backfill is an in-process sweep of the service (the invoice-status poll precedent) that asks about a token-sized batch of rows (at most `backfillBatchSize`) in ONE request, addressing each row by its id, paced at `backfillRequestsPerMinute`.

PropertyDecisionSource.__providerName.doc: Name of the `projectSettings.decisionProvidersSettings.decisionProviders[]` entry that decides this property. Credentials are read from DECISION_PROVIDER_<NAME>_* at runtime. A dangling name fails validation (DECISION_PROVIDER_NOT_FOUND).
PropertyDecisionSource.__model.doc: The PINNED model version this property's decisions must come from, overriding the provider entry's own pin. A floating tag (`jev-latest`, a bare family name) is refused with DECISION_MODEL_NOT_PINNED. Leave null to inherit the provider entry's pin; one of the two must pin. `<prop>DecidedBy` records the version that actually answered, and the backfill's `stale` mode re-decides rows decided by any other version. The override is applied to create/update decisions and both unset and stale backfill. Questions with different model pins do not share a request.
PropertyDecisionSource.__state.doc: ONE MScript expression producing the state the question is asked about, evaluated against the ROW: `this.<column>` reads the written row's column values (on an update, the full row after the update). The same expression feeds the backfill, so it must not read request or session context. Example: `{ "js": "({ title: this.title, description: this.description })" }`. Keep it to the columns the judgement needs: they are also the default `recomputeOn` set.
PropertyDecisionSource.__question.doc: The ONE typed question whose answer becomes this property's value (a DecisionQuestion; `defaultAnswer` is not used here). noul -> a Boolean column (the probability thresholded at 0.5), choice -> an Enum column whose options include every criteria key (or a String column), score -> a Double / Float / Integer column holding the level position (rounded for Integer). A choice needs an escape option (DECISION_CHOICE_NO_ESCAPE_OPTION); it is also the value a row that fits nothing ends up with, instead of a forced wrong option.
PropertyDecisionSource.__confidenceThreshold.doc: Confidence at or above which an answer is stored as the value. Below it the value column stays null and only the companions (confidence, model, time) are written, so a borderline row is visible as undecided rather than silently classified. Must sit outside the provider's `capabilities.probabilityDriftBand` of the 0.5 boundary (DECISION_THRESHOLD_IN_DRIFT_BAND). Null = store every answer, except that a noul whose probability lies inside the drift band of 0.5 is always withheld (ADR rule 8).
PropertyDecisionSource.__recomputeOn.doc: The properties whose write re-triggers the decision on an update. Presence in the update patch is the trigger (the after-update seam's rule); an update that writes none of them never calls the provider. Null = the row columns the `state` expression reads (`this.<column>`). An overridden value is never recomputed until the override is released.
PropertyDecisionSource.__timeoutMs.doc: Per-request timeout for the write-time decision. A timeout counts as a provider failure: the write still succeeds and the row is left for the backfill. Null uses the decisionSource default of 5000 ms. An isolated call measured 250-400 ms, so a value under ~1000 ms will cut healthy calls.
PropertyDecisionSource.__backfillBatchSize.doc: The most rows asked about in ONE backfill request. Each row becomes one subject of the request's state, addressed by its id, with one question per row naming that id. Measured with explicit item ids: per-item accuracy 1.00 at every size from 1 to 1,150 subjects at ~54 tokens per subject, and a 1,250-subject request was refused whole at the 64k context (`400 max_tokens_exceeded`) - the limit is TOKENS, not accuracy. So this is a cap: the engine sizes every request from its own subjects, filling at most half of the provider's `contextTokenCeiling` by a pessimistic token estimate, so long subjects get smaller batches automatically. A one-row request pays a fixed ~260-token overhead, which is why batching matters. Default 256; at most 1000.
PropertyDecisionSource.__backfillRequestsPerMinute.doc: Pacing of the backfill: at most this many provider requests per minute, one at a time. Set it from MEASURED throughput for your account, not from a published ceiling - the vendor's published request rate was not enforced in measurement, so it is neither a limit you will hit nor a guarantee. A rate-limit or overload answer (429 / 529) ends the pass early; the next pass resumes from the data, because a decided row no longer matches the backfill's predicate.
PropertyDecisionSource.__backfillIntervalSeconds.doc: How often the in-process backfill sweep runs, in seconds. Each pass walks the rows whose `<prop>DecidedAt` is null (never decided, or a write whose decision failed) in keyset order. 0 disables the periodic sweep; the generated `runDecisionSourceBackfill()` can still be called directly (e.g. from a cron Business API) and also offers the `stale` mode.
PropertyDecisionSource.question: DecisionQuestion

__PropertyGraphEdge.doc: Projects an FK-relation property as a graph edge (docs/ADR-graph-database-layer.md §4a). The owning property must declare a relation (`basicSettings.hasRelation: true` + `relationSettings`). `relationshipType` names the Neo4j relationship; `direction` orients it relative to the owning node (e.g. a `folder.parentId -> folder` relation with `relationshipType: CONTAINS` and `direction: inbound` means parent CONTAINS this node — the edge points target → source). On write, the edge is `MERGE`d to the target node alongside the node upsert.

PropertyGraphEdge.__relationshipType.doc: The Neo4j relationship type for the projected edge, e.g. `CONTAINS` or `IN_CATEGORY`.
PropertyGraphEdge.__direction.doc: Orientation of the edge relative to the owning node (GraphDirection): `outbound` (owning node → target), `inbound` (target → owning node), or `undirected`. Defaults to `outbound`.
PropertyGraphEdge.__edgeProperties.doc: Optional properties of the owning row copied onto the relationship (PropRefer[]).

__GraphDirection.doc.#: Orientation of a graph relationship relative to its owning/source node.
__GraphDirection.doc.outbound: The edge points from the owning/source node to the target (source → target).
__GraphDirection.doc.inbound: The edge points from the target to the owning/source node (target → source).
__GraphDirection.doc.undirected: The relationship has no meaningful direction (modeled as undirected for traversal).

__PropertyBasicSettings.doc: Defines the core structure and behavior of a data property. Beyond basic typing, this section governs how the property participates in data integrity, mutability, API exposure, and logic-driven behaviors such as hashing or auto-increment. Use this section to establish the foundational logic and identity of the property within your data object.

PropertyBasicSettings.__name.doc: Unique identifier for the property within the data object. This name is used throughout route definitions, generated code, and logic expressions. Use camelCase formatting, avoid spaces and special characters, and ensure the name is unique within the same data object. Do not name a property `session`: a create / update api binds every column it writes as `this.<name>`, where designer MScript reads `this.session` as the caller's session, so such an api is refused (PARAM_NAMED_SESSION).
PropertyBasicSettings.__type.doc: Defines the property's data type. Use a value from the `DataTypes`. The selected type impacts validation, storage schema, and frontend component inference.
PropertyBasicSettings.__isArray.doc: Indicates if the property stores multiple values (array). Supported by databases like PostgreSQL and MongoDB. Default is `false`.
PropertyBasicSettings.__description.doc: Optional textual description of the property's role in the domain. Useful for documentation and as a semantic hint across logic and UI components.
PropertyBasicSettings.__isRequired.doc: If `true`, the underlying DB column is NOT NULL — the persisted record must hold a non-null value. This is independent of where the value comes from at runtime; the framework will reject the write if no value reaches the column from any of: a `requestParameters` binding consumed by `dataClauseItems`, a `sessionSettings` auto-inject, a `staticJoin` resolution, or a `basicSettings.defaultValue` DB default. Default is `false` — an OMITTED `isRequired` means the column is NULLABLE, and `BusinessApi.validate` reads the same resolution, so a create API is never asked for a value the column does not demand. Say `true` explicitly when the column must be NOT NULL; validation reports `IS_REQUIRED_UNSPECIFIED` while the key is missing so the intent is written down rather than inherited from the default.
PropertyBasicSettings.__allowUpdate.doc:
Controls whether the property can be modified after creation. THREE values:

- `true` (the default) — an update api may write the column as often as it likes.
- `false` — the column is immutable after create. The update codegen filters it out of the write set entirely, so an update `dataClauseItems` entry naming it is a design-time ERROR (`DATA_CLAUSE_ITEM_NOT_EMITTED`) rather than a write that silently never happens.
- `'untilSet'` — WRITE-ONCE. The update path EMITS the clause, guarded `WHERE <column> IS NULL`, so the first write after create wins ATOMICALLY at the database: no read-then-write race, no application-level check. A write aimed at a column that already holds a value answers the typed refusal `WRITE_ONCE_ALREADY_SET` (409) — never a silent no-op. The guard is on every db-layer update helper (by id, by id list, by query - the one every updateCrudAction uses): a bulk or query-scoped write matching a row that already holds the value is refused whole, and each loser of a concurrent first write gets the same 409. A create that lands on an EXISTING row (an `onDuplicate: doUpdate` upsert, a bulk create over an existing id) never overwrites a set write-once column: a replay carrying the SAME value is an idempotent no-op on it, a DIFFERENT value (null included) is refused with the same WRITE_ONCE_ALREADY_SET (409) before anything is written (a bulk create refuses the whole batch), and a column that is still null is filled. Use it for a value that is computable only after the row exists and must then never change again: a capture-time commission snapshot, a settlement reference, an issued document number. Accepted ONLY on a NULLABLE column (`isRequired: false`): the guard is `IS NULL`, so on a NOT NULL column it could never match and every update would be refused (validation reports `WRITE_ONCE_REQUIRES_NULLABLE`).

`'untilSet'` is the remedy the `DATA_CLAUSE_ITEM_NOT_EMITTED` message names for the write-once case; the alternative it replaces — flipping the column to `allowUpdate: true` so one hook can stamp it — leaves captured financial history permanently rewritable by every later update.
PropertyBasicSettings.__requiredInUpdate.doc: If `true`, the property must be present in update operations. Commonly used for fields that must be kept consistent across updates (e.g. version, status).
PropertyBasicSettings.__allowAutoUpdate.doc: If `true`, this property will be automatically included in the update parameters for default routes unless custom logic is applied. Helps streamline generic update routes.
PropertyBasicSettings.__autoIncrement.doc: If `true`, this property will be auto-generated by incrementing the latest existing value. Suitable for numeric IDs or sequences managed internally.
PropertyBasicSettings.__hashed.doc: If `true`, the property is a CREDENTIAL that is one-way hashed before storage. Two things follow, both enforced by codegen: the db-layer bcrypts the value on every create/update (irreversible — the plaintext is unrecoverable, so only a hash-compare can verify it), and the property name is scrubbed from every outgoing response, event and streamed chunk by the api layer. Use it for passwords. Do NOT use it for a value something has to read back verbatim (a digest looked up by exact match, an external token replayed to a third party): bcrypt at write makes that lookup impossible — declare `isSecret` instead, which is the response half without the storage half.
PropertyBasicSettings.__isSecret.doc: If `true`, this property holds a secret value (e.g. an API-key digest, a QR code, a token) that is stored in CLEARTEXT — because something has to read it back verbatim — and must still never leave the service on a payload. The api layer scrubs the property name from every response, event and streamed chunk, exactly as it does for `hashed`, and the emitted OpenAPI response schema and gRPC response message omit it. The difference from `hashed` is the STORAGE half only: `hashed` bcrypts the column on write, `isSecret` leaves it untouched, so a column that is looked up by exact match (auth's `apiKey.keyHash`) can be declared secret without becoming un-lookupable. A value the caller legitimately receives (a freshly minted plaintext key) must be put on the response by the api itself, not read off the record. The ONE opening is per API: a BusinessApi may name this column in `apiOptions.exposeSecrets`, and then THAT api carries it in its own response (a ticket code its owner has to read back); every other api, every event payload and every log keeps the scrub. NOTE: the MCP `***` masking + `__proxyCode` frontend-rendering flow this field once described is NOT implemented in any lane; the realised meaning is the response/event exclusion above. Never name a secret property `accessToken` or `refreshToken` (this applies to `hashed` too): those are the exact keys every login, relogin, social-login and register auto-login answer carries the session token under, the scrub matches by name, so validation refuses the declaration (`SECRET_NAME_SESSION_TOKEN`) - rename it, for example to `providerAccessToken`.
PropertyBasicSettings.__defaultName.doc: If `true`, this property is used as the default display label for records of this data object. When rendering relation dropdowns or record references in the frontend, the value of this property will be shown as the human-readable label. Only one property per data object should be marked as defaultName. If none is set, the frontend will fall back to common field names like 'name', 'title', or the first String property.
PropertyBasicSettings.__hasRelation.doc: If `true`, this property is a foreign-key reference to another data object — populate the `relationSettings` block with the join target. When `false` (the default), the `relationSettings` block is null/absent. The flag lives here on basicSettings rather than nested inside `relationSettings` because it's a property-level decision.
PropertyBasicSettings.__isFilterParameter.doc:
If `true`, the property is exposed as a declared filter parameter on the data object's auto-generated list APIs — on EVERY surface the API exposes (the REST query string or body, an MCP tool call, a gRPC message, a kafka event payload, a cron input, an internal API call), not the REST route alone. The filter name is the property name itself (no separate alias). Filter type/operator follows the property's `type` automatically. An EMPTY value (`?status=`) means no constraint, exactly like omitting the parameter.

The filter is only as good as the column behind it. In explicit mode a column is written ONLY from a create/update api's `requestParameters`, any api's `dataClauseItems`, the property's own `sessionSettings` / `staticJoin` / `defaultValue`, or a framework subsystem binding declared on the object (an invoicing `statusProperty`, say). A filter column in none of those is guaranteed NULL for every row the api creates, so the filter can only ever match rows written from outside the api - a seed, a migration, a direct index write. Validation reports that as the warning `FILTER_COLUMN_NEVER_WRITABLE`: either add the column to a write source, or drop `isFilterParameter`. The check stands down for an object the service declares no create api for at all, since such rows come from somewhere it cannot see.
PropertyBasicSettings.__decimalScale.doc: How many FRACTIONAL DIGITS a `Decimal` column carries - the scale in `Decimal(scale)`. Only meaningful when `basicSettings.type` is `Decimal`; leave it null (the key absent) on every other type, where setting it is a design-time ERROR (`DECIMAL_SCALE_ON_NON_DECIMAL`) rather than a number nothing reads. An omitted scale on a Decimal column resolves to 2, the money default. Legal range 0..6 inclusive (`VALUE_OUT_OF_RANGE`, a fractional one `INVALID_FIELD_TYPE`): 0 for a whole-unit currency (JPY, KRW), 2 for the ordinary case, 3-6 for a rate or a unit price quoted below the currency's smallest unit. The scale is a STATEMENT ABOUT THE COLUMN, not a display hint: the framework rounds every value written to the column to exactly this many digits, half-to-even (banker's rounding, so a long series of .5 cases does not drift upward the way half-up does), at each write boundary - every generated db-layer write helper (create, bulk create, update by id / id list / query, and the upsert of an `onDuplicate: doUpdate` index), which business APIs, create / bulk-create / update CRUD actions, seed data and custom code calling dbLayer all write through; plus a request-parameter transform and the amount handed to a payment or invoice provider. Rounding an already-rounded value changes nothing, so the boundaries agree. Two columns in the same money flow must declare the SAME scale, or a value rounded to 2 on one row and 4 on the next stops reconciling.
PropertyBasicSettings.__maxLength.doc: The maximum number of CHARACTERS a `String` column holds - the n of its `varchar(n)` column. Optional: leave it null (the key absent) and the column keeps the default of 255. Only meaningful when `basicSettings.type` is `String`; on any other type (Text, Enum, ID, ...) setting it is a design-time ERROR (`MAX_LENGTH_ON_NON_STRING`), and it must be a whole number from 1 to 10485760, the PostgreSQL varchar limit (`VALUE_OUT_OF_RANGE`, a fractional one `INVALID_FIELD_TYPE`). The nodejs codegen emits the column as `DataTypes.STRING(n)` - `DataTypes.STRING(255)` when absent, the same varchar(255) column as before - and checks the length BEFORE the write: a value longer than n characters is refused with `422 VALIDATION_ERROR` naming the field (never the value), on the api pipeline and on a hand-written route alike. Characters are counted the way PostgreSQL counts them (Unicode code points, so an emoji is one character), a list is checked per element, and trailing spaces PostgreSQL would trim are not counted. The check reads the STORED value, so a `hashed` column is checked on its 60-character bcrypt digest and a `maxLength` below 60 there is an ERROR (`MAX_LENGTH_BELOW_HASH_DIGEST`). The check also runs on the writes that skip the rest of the model validation: the plain values of a numeric-mutation update (`$inc` and friends) are checked before its single statement. A raw query in custom code bypasses the check and still reaches PostgreSQL, which answers the sanitized `400 BAD_REQUEST`. Raising n on an existing database is a varchar widening the boot reconcile applies on dev/preview; lowering it is a narrowing that is reported and never applied, so longer values already stored are kept. On a MongoDB-backed object only an explicit `maxLength` is enforced (there is no varchar column to default); the generated create, update and upsert writers all check it before the write, with the same 422. Services generated in another language declare it but do not enforce it yet (WARNING `MAX_LENGTH_NOT_ENFORCED`).
PropertyBasicSettings.__enumOptions.doc: Required when `type === 'Enum'`. Ordered list of string values the property can take. Must contain at least 2 options. Leave null/absent for non-enum properties. Enum options are DATA, not code identifiers: the value is stored verbatim in the column and compared verbatim in MScript, and every generator emits it as a string literal (a language identifier, where one is needed at all, is derived by prefixing it with the model + property name). Reserved words (`public`, `default`, `class`, …) are therefore legal option values and are never renamed — write the value you want stored, and use exactly that spelling in MScript.
PropertyBasicSettings.__defaultValue.doc: DB-level LITERAL default for the property's column. Applied at write time when no other source supplies a value (no requestParameter, no sessionSettings auto-inject, no staticJoin, no dataClauseItems entry). Type must match `basicSettings.type` and respect `isArray`, and the value is type-checked at validation. For a SCALAR column (numeric / String / Text / ID / Enum / Boolean) it must be a matching literal — an object, an array, or an MScript-wrapper object (`{ "js": … }`) is rejected with `INVALID_DEFAULT_VALUE` (a string that encodes a number/boolean, e.g. `"0"` on a Double, is coerced to the typed literal with a non-blocking `DEFAULT_VALUE_TYPE_COERCED` warning). For an `Object` column (JSONB / Mongoose Mixed) an object OR array literal is legal data — but an MScript-wrapper object is still rejected there, because it is code, not data. `defaultValue` must NEVER carry code: it is a DB-level literal, applied where MScript cannot run. For a DB-native computed default (current timestamp, …) use the sibling `defaultFn` field and leave `defaultValue` null (if both are set, the literal `defaultValue` wins and `defaultFn` is ignored with a non-blocking warning); for business/computed defaults like `LIB.<fn>()` leave both null and write a per-API `dataClauseItems` MScript entry instead.
PropertyBasicSettings.__defaultFn.doc: A DB-native default FUNCTION for the column, selected from the `DefaultFunction` enum and mapped by each generator to the correct per-engine spelling (e.g. `now` → Sequelize `DataTypes.NOW` / Mongoose `Date.now` / SQL `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`). Use this — not a magic-string `defaultValue` like `now()` — for computed DB defaults. Set it only when `defaultValue` is null: if both are set, the literal `defaultValue` wins and `defaultFn` is ignored (reported as a non-blocking warning). `now` is only valid on a `Date` property; on all other types leave this field null (most properties never set it).
PropertyBasicSettings.name: String

__PropertyIndexSettings.doc: Index configuration for the data property across supported storage and caching layers. This includes Elasticsearch indexing for query performance, relational database indexing for faster selection, and Redis-based optimizations for efficient cache invalidation and retrieval. Use these settings to control how the property contributes to performance, queryability, and caching logic.

PropertyIndexSettings.__indexedInElastic.doc: Determines whether the property is searchable in the Elasticsearch CQRS index. It controls searchability, not storage: the value of every property is stored in the index document either way, and when enabled the property can be used in DataView filters and search queries. A hashed or isSecret property is the exception: it is never written to Elasticsearch at all, whatever this flag says.
PropertyIndexSettings.__fulltextSearch.doc: If set to true, the generated service will create an additional text index in elastic search other than the type based term query. Note that this feature is ignored if indexedInElastic is false. Text type data properties are alread have full text search.
PropertyIndexSettings.__indexedInDb.doc: Specifies whether a native database index should be created for this property to accelerate selection queries. Recommended for frequently filtered or sorted fields.
PropertyIndexSettings.__unique.doc: Indicates whether the property's value must be unique across all records. Enabling this will enforce a uniqueness constraint at the database level.
PropertyIndexSettings.__clusterInRedis.doc:
Makes this property a CLUSTER KEY of the object's query cache — the slice dimension along which cached list answers are invalidated. Supported for query-cache slicing in nodejs and dotnet; this guard still treats java, golang, python and rust as unsupported. This flag slices QUERY answers, not the separate id-based EntityCache. Only meaningful when a list api on this object opts in with `listOptions.queryCache: true`; without one the flag slices nothing and a design-time warning (CLUSTER_IN_REDIS_UNUSED) says so.

With it, a cached answer records the value this property was pinned to by the query (or `all` when the query did not pin it), and a write to a row only flushes the slices that row belongs to — a write in tenant `t1` leaves tenant `t2`'s cached pages intact. Flag the column the object's lists are normally filtered by: a tenant id, an owner id, a parent id. Flagging several multiplies the slices (2^n patterns swept per write), so keep it to the one or two that actually partition the reads.
PropertyIndexSettings.__cacheSelect.doc: Defines whether this property is used as a key in Redis entity cache for batch-select operations. Enables lookup by this value across cached entities.
PropertyIndexSettings.__isSecondaryKey.doc: Marks the property as a secondary identifier, improving query performance on non-primary keys. Useful for access tokens, slugs, or alternative keys.

__PropertyRelation.doc: Defines the foreign-key relationship for this property to another data object. Populate this block when `basicSettings.hasRelation === true`. Leave null/absent otherwise. The activation flag lives on basicSettings (next to `source`) so a single property-level write declares both the source and the relation.

PropertyRelation.__relationName.doc: A single-word, human-readable name that identifies the relationship. This name is used in generated code and documentation to represent joined data via this relation.
PropertyRelation.__relationTargetObject.doc: The name of the data object this property relates to. This defines the target of the foreign key relationship.
PropertyRelation.__relationTargetKey.doc: The property name (usually 'id') in the target object that this property references. This is the destination key for the relation.
PropertyRelation.__onDeleteAction.doc: What happens to THIS row when the referenced (parent) row is deleted. THE ANSWER IS DECIDED BY THE SHAPE OF THE RELATION, NOT BY WHICH OPTION SOUNDS SAFEST — do not reach for setNull because a cascade sounds destructive; on a required FK setNull is not an option at all. Ask two questions in order. (1) Is this row PART OF the parent — a whole/part relationship, meaningless once the parent is gone (an experience of a creator profile, a ticket of an event)? Then `doDelete`. It is no longer a schema default: an omitted onDeleteAction now arrives unset, so state `doDelete` explicitly. (2) Otherwise this row merely POINTS AT the parent and is an independent thing (a venue pointing at whoever created it, a subscription pointing at its plan). Then ask what this row owes the pointer. (a) The pointer may go empty and the row stays meaningful — set basicSettings.isRequired to false FIRST, then `setNull`. (b) The row must keep naming the parent, and the parent must not be deletable while it does — `restrict`, which refuses the parent's deletion. (c) The row must keep naming the parent, but the parent may still be deleted and this row simply survives unchanged — `doNothing`. Rows are soft-deleted, so the kept reference still resolves, to an archived parent; this is how a sold ticket keeps naming its buyer, or an audit row its actor. NOTE: setNull writes NULL into this column, so on a NOT NULL column (isRequired true, which is also the DEFAULT when isRequired is omitted) it is unimplementable and is REJECTED at validation with RELATION_SETNULL_ON_REQUIRED_FK; the lawful answers for a required FK are doDelete, restrict and doNothing.
PropertyRelation.__relationIsRequired.doc: Defines whether the relation is mandatory. If true, the property must always reference a valid record in the related data object.

__RelationOnDeleteAction.doc.#: Defines the available strategies for handling related records when a referenced (parent) object is deleted.
__RelationOnDeleteAction.doc.doDelete: Automatically delete this object if the referenced target object is deleted. This is a cascading delete. The DEFAULT, and the right answer when this row is PART OF the parent — it has no meaning once the parent is gone.
__RelationOnDeleteAction.doc.setNull: Set this property to null when the referenced object is deleted, effectively removing the relation without deleting this object. REQUIRES a nullable column: valid ONLY when basicSettings.isRequired is explicitly false. On a required FK it writes NULL into a NOT NULL column — a guaranteed runtime constraint violation — and validation rejects it (RELATION_SETNULL_ON_REQUIRED_FK).
__RelationOnDeleteAction.doc.restrict: Refuse to delete the referenced (parent) row while any row of this object still references it; the caller must remove or re-point the children first. Use this when this row POINTS AT reference data rather than being part of it — a subscription and its plan, a ledger entry and its payee account, a ticket and its ticket type — and the pointer may not go empty. It is the answer for a NOT NULL foreign key that must neither be nulled (setNull is illegal on it) nor cascade-destroyed (doDelete would take every dependent row with the parent).
__RelationOnDeleteAction.doc.doNothing: Leave this row exactly as it is: the parent may be deleted, this row survives, and the foreign key keeps its value rather than being nulled. Use it for a record that must OUTLIVE the party it names and must still say who that was — a sold ticket naming its buyer, an audit or financial row naming an actor. Rows are soft-deleted, so the reference does not dangle: it still resolves, to an archived parent. This is the only value that keeps a NOT NULL foreign key intact across the parent's deletion — setNull would violate the column, doDelete would destroy the record, and restrict would forbid a deletion the product wants to allow.

__PropertySessionSettings.doc: Defines how this property is populated from the session context when this block is populated. Session-driven properties are commonly used to associate records with the current user automatically. The binding is applied on CREATE: on the main dataObject of a create Business API, and on a child row written by another API's CreateCrudAction or CreateBulkCrudAction, which fills any session-bound column its own mappings do not name. An UPDATE does not refresh the column - map it in the update dataClause to change it. On either create path an authored mapping wins, and a session that carries no value leaves the key ABSENT, so a required column refuses the row rather than being written null. Leave the wrapping object null when no session-binding is configured.

PropertySessionSettings.__sessionParam.doc: Specifies the name of the session field to bind to this property. Defaults to the property name if not explicitly provided. For example, if the session contains `userId`, that can be mapped to this field. The name is CHECKED against the project's session canon at design time (`SESSION_PARAM_UNKNOWN`): the generated data clause reads `this.session['<sessionParam>']` verbatim, so a field the session does not carry writes null into the column on every request -- a 422 `notNull Violation` when the column is required and completely silent when it is not. On a multi-tenant project the tenant id rides the session under the name the project gave its tenant (`workspaceId`, `storeId`, ...), NOT under a generic `tenantId`, which is stamped by nothing; the tenant CODENAME is the one generic spelling that is real (`tenantCodename`). Required for every declaration EXCEPT `ownerProvenance: "payload"`: an event-sourced owner column is written by the create's `dataClauseItems` entry from the trusted event, so it carries no session binding - omit `sessionParam` there (a sessionParam beside `payload` is refused, OWNER_PROVENANCE_PAYLOAD_WITH_SESSION_PARAM). Leaving it blank on any other declaration answers REQUIRED_FIELD_MISSING.
PropertySessionSettings.__isOwnerField.doc: Marks this property as the ownership field for the data object. When true, the property is used to enforce ownership-based access control (e.g., ensuring users can only modify their own records). This should be used when the property semantically identifies the owner of the record, typically a userId. Ownership is session-fed, directly or carried by a trusted internal event - never derived from row data. `ownerProvenance` says which of the two applies; leave it at its default `session` unless the object's create paths are exclusively internal.
PropertySessionSettings.__ownerProvenance.doc: WHERE the owner column's value comes from. `session` (the default, and the original session rule) means the framework stamps the column from the creating caller's own session on every create, and a body-supplied value is never an ownership claim. `payload` means the value is carried by a TRUSTED INTERNAL EVENT instead: the row is created by a kafka consumer or another internal path that has no session of its own, and the owner id it writes was stamped at the ORIGINAL session edge by the producing service and carried through an M2M-verified pipe. Declaring `payload` lets an event-sourced object (an order created from an order-intent event, for example) answer the ownership question that `ownershipCheck` and the payment lifecycle routes ask, instead of silently degrading to a login-only boundary. It is REFUSED on an object that has any caller-facing create path - REST, gRPC or SSE (OWNER_PROVENANCE_PAYLOAD_WITH_REST_CREATE; also gRPC and SSE): where a caller can create the row the session rule stands unchanged. kafka, cron and internal-call creates are the internal producers the declaration is for. It never authorizes deriving the owner from row data. `sessionOrInternalPayload` is the explicit opt-in for an object created BOTH by its owner and by a trusted internal job (a buyer's REST create beside a cron that creates scheduled charges): every caller-facing create (REST, gRPC, SSE) stamps the owner from the session exactly as `session` does (an owner `dataClauseItems` entry stays refused there, OWNER_CLAUSE_SHADOWED_BY_SESSION), and a create whose controllers are ALL trusted internal ones (kafka, cron, internal call) writes its authored owner `dataClauseItems` entry. The column keeps its `sessionParam` (the caller-facing creates need it; only `payload` may omit it, REQUIRED_FIELD_MISSING), stays the object's owner for `ownershipCheck` and the payment start gate, and is generated by the nodejs, python, rust, java and dotnet emitters (another build language refuses it, OWNER_PROVENANCE_SESSION_OR_INTERNAL_LANGUAGE). Optional - omit for the `session` default.

__OwnerProvenance.doc.#: The two sanctioned sources of an owner column's value. Both are session-fed identities; they differ only in whether the session that stamped the value belonged to THIS request or to the request that produced the internal event this row was created from. Neither permits deriving an owner from row data.
__OwnerProvenance.doc.session: The creating caller's own session stamps the column, on every create. The default.
__OwnerProvenance.doc.payload: A trusted internal event carries the owner id, stamped at the original session edge by the producing service. Legal only on an object whose create paths are exclusively internal/kafka.
__OwnerProvenance.doc.sessionOrInternalPayload: Per create path: a caller-facing create (REST, gRPC, SSE) stamps the owner from the creating caller's session, exactly as `session`; a create whose controllers are ALL trusted internal ones (kafka, cron, internal call) writes the owner from its authored owner `dataClauseItems` entry. For an object created both by its owner and by a scheduled or event-driven job. Explicit opt-in; nodejs, python, rust, java and dotnet.

__PropertyStaticJoin.doc: Static join settings define how this property's value is derived from another data object at the time of creation when this block is populated. The join is resolved on every create write path - an API create, a create CRUD action writing a child object, and a seed-data row of the same service - and never on an update (a seeded row is the one exception: the seed refresh re-resolves it on every boot). This approach is useful when a field in the current object depends on a static value from a related object, and that value is not expected to change frequently. Unlike dynamic joins, static joins store the fetched value directly to allow for faster queries and avoid repeated lookups. A common use case is transferring tenant or client identifiers from a parent object into a child record. For example, when creating an email job for a specific user, the system can use the userId to join the User object, fetch its clientId, and statically assign it to the EmailJob object. This makes it easy to query email jobs by clientId without needing to join back to the User table at runtime. Note that static joins are resolved AFTER the API's dataClauseItems are evaluated, so a dataClauseItems expression cannot read the joined value; when a dataClauseItems entry names the joined property itself, its value is written first and the join only fills the column while it is still null. A join keyed on the property it writes (`jointForeignKey` naming this property) can never fire and is refused (STATIC_JOIN_SELF_FOREIGN_KEY). Leave the wrapping object null when no static-join is configured.

PropertyStaticJoin.__jointSource.doc: The name and optionally the service of the source object from which the value will be joined. If the source is in another service, the generated service will automatically use Elasticsearch indexing to perform the join.
PropertyStaticJoin.__jointRead.doc: The name of the property in the source object whose value will be copied into the current property. Defaults to the same name as this property if not specified.
PropertyStaticJoin.__jointSourceKey.doc: The key in the source object used to identify the matching record. This is typically 'id' as the primary identifier of the source object. This field acts as the join source in the static join relationship.
PropertyStaticJoin.__jointForeignKey.doc: The property in the current object used as a reference to the source object (i.e., the foreign key). For example, if joining user.clientId via userId, the foreign key is 'userId'.
PropertyStaticJoin.__defaultValue.doc: An optional fallback MScript value to use when static join cannot find a source record, or when the joined read value resolves to null/undefined.

__SimpleCheck.doc: Defines a lightweight conditional validation. A SimpleCheck runs a script to evaluate a specific business rule and throws an error if the condition fails. Used to enforce custom rules dynamically within access or execution flows.

SimpleCheck.__name.doc: Identifier for the check logic, used for documentation and traceability. It should clearly describe the business rule, e.g., `isDocumentVisible` or `userHasNotRevokedAccess`.
SimpleCheck.__condition.doc: An MScript expression that evaluates to a boolean. If the result is false, the check fails and an error is thrown with the specified message and status.
SimpleCheck.__errorMessage.doc: The message shown to the user or logged when the check fails. It should clearly communicate the reason for denial.
SimpleCheck.__errorStatus.doc: The HTTP status code to be returned when the check fails. This helps convey the nature of the error (e.g., 403 for forbidden access, 404 for missing data, 429 for a rate-limit or quota refusal that clears with time, 503 for a dependency that is down right now). The value set is the ErrorStatus vocabulary; 429 and 503 are retried by callers, so never use them for a permanent refusal.
SimpleCheck.name: String

__ErrorStatus.doc.400: BadRequestError — Returned when request parameters are invalid, malformed, or missing required data.
__ErrorStatus.doc.401: NotAuthenticatedError — Returned when no valid user session is found. Typically indicates a login is required.
__ErrorStatus.doc.403: ForbiddenError — Returned when the user is authenticated but does not have sufficient permissions or rights for the requested operation.
__ErrorStatus.doc.404: NotFoundError — Returned when a required resource or data entry is not found in the system, such as a missing record or object.
__ErrorStatus.doc.409: ConflictError — Returned when the request conflicts with the current state of the resource. The canonical code for 'already exists' / duplicate-key cases (a team is already registered, a stage window for this stage already exists, an active application is already in progress). Prefer 409 over 403 when the issue is uniqueness, not authorization.
__ErrorStatus.doc.422: UnprocessableEntityError — Returned when the request is well-formed and the caller is allowed, but a semantic / business-rule violation prevents processing (e.g., submitting an application before eligibility is confirmed, advancing to a stage that requires prerequisites). Distinct from 400 (request is malformed) and 403 (caller lacks permission).
__ErrorStatus.doc.429: TooManyRequestsError — Returned when the caller is over a rate limit or a usage quota (too many attempts in the window, the plan's monthly quota is used up). The problem body carries errorCode TOO_MANY_REQUESTS. Callers treat 429 as RETRYABLE (back off and try again later), so use it only for a refusal that goes away with time; a refusal that no retry can cure (the plan does not include the feature at all) is 403 or 422.
__ErrorStatus.doc.500: HttpSystemError — Returned for internal server or system-level errors, such as database failures or unexpected exceptions.
__ErrorStatus.doc.503: ServiceUnavailableError — Returned when a dependency this api needs is currently unavailable (a downstream service, provider or maintenance switch is down), so the request cannot be served NOW. The problem body carries errorCode SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE and keeps the authored message (unlike 500, whose body is genericized to INTERNAL_ERROR), so write it for the caller: never put internal detail in it. Callers treat 503 as RETRYABLE, so never use it for a permanent refusal.
__ErrorStatus.doc.#: OpenAPPL error status codes represent standardized HTTP-style error responses used across all controller types. These codes provide consistent semantic feedback for route errors, especially in REST APIs.

__ServiceLibrary.doc: Defines a custom service library for your OpenAPPL service. A ServiceLibrary is a modular container for user-defined code, templates, and assets. It allows developers to inject business-specific logic or reusable components into the service. You can define functions, templates, and assets, as well as edge functions (used by edge controllers to fully control the route lifecycle). These modules can be referenced throughout the service—for example, in validations, permissions, conditions, or hooks. The `hooks[]` partition additionally binds a `functions[]` entry to the service lifecycle itself: a `startup` hook runs on every boot (after db/kafka wiring, before traffic is served; idempotent by contract), a `shutdown` hook runs best-effort on graceful shutdown.

ServiceLibrary.__functions.doc: List of reusable library functions available in the service. These are general-purpose functions used in validations, permissions, and other scripts. Each function is defined as a `LibModule` whose `moduleBody` is multi-language — one body per language key (`js`, `ts`, `python`, `csharp`, `go`, `rust`, `java`, `php`); the generated service emits the body matching its target language. Every language body must follow that language's export contract (documented per key on `LibModuleBody`). For the `js` body this means DIRECTLY assigning the callable — `module.exports = function (...) {...}` (an arrow function or a reference to a function declared in the module also works); named exports (`exports.myFn = ...`, `module.exports = { myFn }`) are rejected because the generated LIB registry `require`s the module and registers its export as the callable.
ServiceLibrary.__nativeKernels.doc: List of native (C++/C) compute kernels exposed to the service as library functions. A `NativeKernel` wraps an existing native library (e.g. CUDA/MKL/OpenCV/a proprietary HPC routine) behind a stable `extern "C"` shim and is compiled and linked into the consuming service via FFI — not bridged. Kernels are referenced from MScript exactly like ordinary library functions (`LIB.computeShippingBatch(...)`). Unlike a `functions` module (which runs from the target-native `moduleBody` key and is never bridged; a missing key emits a failing stub), a kernel is native code linked directly into the consuming binary. Use kernels only when a project must link a specific C/C++ library that has no native equivalent in the service's language; prefer ordinary `functions` authored in the service language otherwise. See `docs/ADR-cpp-kernel-native-lib.md`.
ServiceLibrary.__calculations.doc: List of curated compute primitives (the Tier-1 `Calculation` substrate of docs/ADR-calculation-layer.md §1/§5). Each `Calculation` is a single curated math operation over a crate/package (FFT a buffer, k-means an array, group-by a dataframe), called from MScript like a library function (`LIB.fft(this.signal)`) and answered within the call — synchronously or off-thread — for small/bounded math that belongs in a request. For anything heavy or long-running, declare a `ComputeJob` on the service instead. Only valid on rust/python host services (the calculation languages); a codegen error otherwise.
ServiceLibrary.__edgeFunctions.doc: Functions invoked by edge controllers, enabling fully custom handling of requests. These modules must export an async function that accepts a single request parameter and returns an API response or throws an error. Standard validations will still apply before execution. An edge function is called by an edge controller defined in the service's edgeControllers. An edge controller can be triggered by a REST request, a Kafka message, or a cron scheduler. The request parameter format varies by trigger type: (1) REST: the Express.js request object with body, query, params, and session; (2) Kafka: a message object where the JSON body contains the created, deleted, or updated resource data directly accessible on the request (e.g., request.product), along with session when there is a current user login in the context; (3) Cron: an empty object {}. The session object is attached to REST and Kafka triggers when there is a current user login in the context. Example: `{ 'moduleName': 'helloWorld', 'moduleBody': { 'js': 'module.exports = async (request) => { return { status: 200, message: "Hello from the edge function", date: new Date().toISOString() }; }' } }`
ServiceLibrary.__templates.doc: Templates used within the service to render dynamic content such as emails, documents, or downloads. Typically written in `ejs`, they are evaluated with route data before rendering the final output.
ServiceLibrary.__assets.doc: Static text or image-based files (e.g., credentials, configs, illustrations) used by the business logic. These can be used internally or for generating downloadable content. Each is defined as a `LibModule`.
ServiceLibrary.__public.doc: Public files exposed via a static URL, accessible directly by frontend or client-side apps. Text-formatted assets only: an item's `moduleBody` carries plain TEXT under one of the declared `LibModuleBody` keys (typically `html`, `txt`, `svg`, `ejs`, or `json`) — never base64. `svg` is the only image format carried, so vector assets such as logos live here as SVG text. Binary assets (PNG, JPEG, PDF, fonts) are NOT library items — `LibModuleBody` has no key for them — and will be served by a separate designtime bucket.
ServiceLibrary.__pdfTemplates.doc: PDF templates used by RenderPdfAction. Each is a PdfTemplate (EJS body + page setup + optional header/footer + metadata) rendered to PDF via the service's pdf-layer.
ServiceLibrary.__hooks.doc: Service lifecycle hooks: run a declared library function automatically when the service starts (trigger `startup`) or gracefully stops (trigger `shutdown`). Each hook references a `functions[]` entry of THIS service's library by `moduleName`. RUN-EVERY-BOOT semantics with an IDEMPOTENCY CONTRACT: a startup hook runs on EVERY boot of the service — there is NO persisted run-once marker — so the referenced function MUST be idempotent (safe to repeat on every restart, rolling deploy and crash recovery: use upserts, existence checks or version stamps, never blind inserts). The generated bootstrap awaits startup hooks AFTER the database, migrations, seed data and kafka wiring are up and BEFORE the HTTP listener binds; each hook is try/caught and logged — a hook that throws NEVER blocks the health endpoint and never crashes boot (the service comes up degraded, with the failure in the boot log). A startup hook that exceeds its boot budget (`LIBRARY_STARTUP_HOOK_BUDGET_MS`, default 30000 ms) stops being awaited: boot proceeds and the hook keeps running in the background. Shutdown hooks run best-effort on the graceful-shutdown path (SIGTERM/SIGINT) under `LIBRARY_SHUTDOWN_HOOK_BUDGET_MS` (default 10000 ms); a killed process runs nothing, so never rely on a shutdown hook for correctness. The hook function is invoked with no arguments and may be async; it reaches the db-layer and sibling services exactly like any other library function.

moduleBody.js: module.exports = sortVersions = (versions) => { return versions.sort((a, b) => { const partsA = a.split('.').map(Number); const partsB = b.split('.').map(Number); const maxLength = Math.max(partsA.length, partsB.length); for (let i = 0; i < maxLength; i++) { const numA = partsA[i] || 0; const numB = partsB[i] || 0; if (numA > numB) return 1; if (numA < numB) return -1; } return 0; }); }

ServiceLibrary.__wasmModules.doc: Portable WebAssembly modules exposed to the service as library functions. Unlike a `NativeKernel` (native C/C++ linked via FFI, compute hosts only), a `WasmModule` carries a precompiled, sandboxed, toolchain-free `.wasm` binary whose exported functions become callable library functions.

__LibModule.doc:
Defines a module file in the service library. This object is used for declaring code, templates, or file assets that enhance your business logic. A `LibModule` can be a code function (JavaScript/TypeScript/Python/C#/Go/Rust/Java/PHP), an HTML/EJS template, or a static text/image file.

A module body is **multi-language**: `moduleBody` is a `LibModuleBody` object whose keys carry one body per language/format. The key IS the file extension/language — there is no separate `moduleExtension` field. Code keys (`js`/`ts`/`python`/`csharp`/`go`/`rust`/`java`/`php`) are emitted natively in the generated service's target language; asset/format keys (`html`/`txt`/`svg`/`ejs`/`json`) are language-agnostic and emitted by their format key. When a service compiles to language X and a CODE function has no body for X's key, codegen emits a failing stub (throws/panics with a `TODO(lib)` message) plus a warning — the service still builds. The legacy single-body shape `{ moduleExtension, moduleBody: <string> }` is still accepted and normalized to `{ moduleBody: { <ext>: <string> } }` (default ext `js`).

LibModule.__moduleName.doc: The name of the module. Should be unique within the library. Use lowercase or camelCase (e.g., `updateParent`). This name is used to reference the function or file in route logic.
LibModule.__moduleBody.doc: The content of the module, as a `LibModuleBody` — one body per language/format. The key is the language/extension (e.g. `js`, `ts`, `python`, `csharp`, `go`, `rust`, `java`, `php` for code; `html`, `txt`, `svg`, `ejs`, `json` for assets). At least one key should be set. The generated service picks the body matching its target language (nodejs prefers `ts` then `js`); a missing code body for the target language yields a failing stub + codegen warning. Asset/format modules use the format key directly. The legacy form (a string with a sibling `moduleExtension`) is normalized into this object at load.
LibModule.__publishes.doc: Kafka topics this code module publishes, declared so the project's producer census counts them as produced. Only meaningful on a `library.functions[]` or `library.edgeFunctions[]` module. The census cannot see a publish made from designer code (a `new ServicePublisher(topic, ...)` in the body, whose topic is usually composed at run time), so without a declaration a subscription to that topic reads as producerless: the generated service logs `KafkaSubscriptionsWithoutProducer` at ERROR at boot, and design time reports `KAFKA_TOPIC_NO_PRODUCER` for a consumer in the same project. Name each topic as it goes on the wire. A topic in a service's framework namespace carries the project codename, exactly as the framework's own events do: `<projectCodename>-<serviceName>-service-<event>` (e.g. `acme-commerce-service-issueddocument-requested`). A designer-authored topic (`billing.document.requested`) is written as authored. A framework-namespace name without the codename (`commerce-service-issueddocument-requested`) and a name Kafka refuses are design-time errors that name the fix. A declaration does not publish anything: the body still does, and a declared topic the body never publishes only hides a dead subscription. A lifecycle hook that publishes by calling this function (`LIB.<moduleName>(...)`) is covered by this list; code that is not a library module declares on the service-level `serviceOptions.publishes` instead.

__LibModuleBody.doc: Multi-language body of a `LibModule` — one optional body per language/format key. Code keys (`js`, `ts`, `csharp`, `python`, `rust`, `go`, `php`, `java`) match the MScript compiler set plus js/ts for the nodejs reference; the generated service emits the body matching its target language natively (nodejs prefers `ts` then `js`). Asset/format keys (`html`, `txt`, `svg`, `ejs`, `json`) are language-agnostic — the key is the file extension. All keys are optional `Text`; the key itself names the body's language/extension (there is no separate `moduleExtension`).

LibModuleBody.__js.doc: JavaScript body (nodejs reference; CommonJS `module.exports`). Emitted as `.js`. Export contract: the module's export IS the callable — `module.exports = function <name>(...) {...}`; the generated LIB registry `require`s the file and registers that export under the moduleName with no `.default` interop, so an ES `export default` or named `export` is NOT callable through it.
LibModuleBody.__ts.doc: TypeScript body (nodejs reference, preferred over `js` for nodejs services). Emitted as `.ts`. Export contract: the module's CommonJS export IS the callable - `module.exports = function <name>(...) {...}` or the TypeScript `export = function <name>(...) {...}`, which compiles to the same `module.exports` assignment. The generated LIB registry and the edge adapter bind the bare `require(...)` result with no `.default` interop, so an `export default` or a named `export function <name>` body binds the module namespace instead of the function and the call throws `is not a function`.
LibModuleBody.__csharp.doc: C# body for dotnet services. Emitted as `.cs`. Export contract: a global-namespace `public static class <PascalCase(moduleName)>` exposing `public static object? Invoke(params object?[] args)` — compiled `LIB.<name>(...)` lowers to `<Pascal>.Invoke(...)`.
LibModuleBody.__python.doc: Python body for python services. Emitted as `.py`. Export contract: a top-level `def <moduleName>(...)` — the generated LIB registry imports it by name (`from .functions.<name> import <name>`).
LibModuleBody.__rust.doc: Rust body for rust services. Emitted as `.rs`. Export contract: a `pub fn <snake_case(moduleName)>(...)` with its own natural signature — compiled `LIB.<name>(...)` lowers to `crate::lib_layer::<snake>(...)` with positional value-mode args.
LibModuleBody.__go.doc: Go body for golang services. Emitted as `.go`. Export contract: an exported `func <PascalCase(moduleName)>(...)` — registry.go registers it BY NAME into the commons MScript LIB registry (the generic `func(args ...any) any` ABI dispatches directly; a natural signature dispatches via reflection with JS-style arg semantics).
LibModuleBody.__php.doc: PHP body for php services. Emitted as `.php`. Export contract: a standalone global-namespace file — optional `<?php` prologue + `function <moduleName>(...)` — emitted verbatim under `app/ProjectLib/functions/`; the generated `Lib::<name>` method delegates to the global `\<name>(...)`. ARCHIVED: the php service lane was retired on 2026-07-31 (frozen) and php is no longer a selectable service language, so this key is never emitted by an active target. Kept so existing bodies round-trip unchanged.
LibModuleBody.__java.doc: Java body for java services. Emitted as `.java`. Export contract: a standalone `public final class <PascalCase(moduleName)>` exposing a static `invoke(...)` — emitted verbatim as `lib/<Pascal>.java`; the Lib registry delegates through a reflection adapter (String/Number arg coercion, missing args zero-fill).

__LibModuleBodyKey.doc.#: The set of body keys legal inside a `LibModuleBody` object — code keys matching the MScript compiler set plus language-agnostic asset/format keys. The key itself names the body's language/extension; the generated service emits the body matching its target language natively (nodejs prefers `ts` then `js`). Precedent for `MScriptSourceKey`.
__LibModuleBodyKey.doc.js: JavaScript body (nodejs reference; CommonJS `module.exports`). Emitted as `.js`.
__LibModuleBodyKey.doc.ts: TypeScript body (nodejs reference, preferred over `js` for nodejs services). Emitted as `.ts`.
__LibModuleBodyKey.doc.csharp: C# body for dotnet services. Emitted as `.cs`.
__LibModuleBodyKey.doc.python: Python body for python services. Emitted as `.py`.
__LibModuleBodyKey.doc.rust: Rust body for rust services. Emitted as `.rs`.
__LibModuleBodyKey.doc.go: Go body for golang services. Emitted as `.go`.
__LibModuleBodyKey.doc.php: PHP body for php services. Emitted as `.php`.
__LibModuleBodyKey.doc.java: Java body for java services. Emitted as `.java`.

__ServiceHook.doc: One lifecycle hook of the service library: runs the referenced library function (a `functions[]` entry of the SAME service) automatically when the service starts or gracefully stops. Startup hooks are the designer-facing way to run one-shot boot work — e.g. an idempotent boot data migration that reads records from a peer service and upserts rows locally before first reads serve traffic — without the cron-BusinessApi workaround (which re-runs forever and first fires at the first tick, not at boot). SEMANTICS: run-every-boot. There is NO persisted run-once marker in this iteration, so the referenced function must be IDEMPOTENT — it will run again on every restart, rolling deploy and crash recovery. FAILURE POSTURE: each hook is try/caught and logged by the generated bootstrap; a hook that throws never blocks the health endpoint and never crashes boot (same posture as the boot logger and the boot alter-sync). A startup hook is awaited after db/kafka wiring and before the HTTP listener binds, under a boot budget (`LIBRARY_STARTUP_HOOK_BUDGET_MS`, default 30000 ms) — past the budget, boot proceeds while the hook keeps running in the background.

ServiceHook.__name.doc: Unique name of this hook within the library's `hooks` list. Used in boot logs (`StartupHookCompleted` / `StartupHookFailed` / `ShutdownHookFailed`).
ServiceHook.__trigger.doc: When the hook fires. `startup`: awaited by the generated bootstrap on every boot, after the database, migrations, seed data and kafka wiring are up and before the HTTP listener binds. `shutdown`: best-effort on the graceful-shutdown path (SIGTERM/SIGINT), bounded by `LIBRARY_SHUTDOWN_HOOK_BUDGET_MS`; a killed process runs nothing, so never rely on a shutdown hook for correctness.
ServiceHook.__moduleName.doc: The `moduleName` of a `functions[]` entry of THIS service's library. The generated bootstrap invokes that module's exported function with no arguments (the same callable MScript reaches as `LIB.<moduleName>(...)`); the function may be async and must be idempotent. Design-time validation errors when no library function with this name exists (`HOOK_MODULE_NOT_FOUND`).
ServiceHook.__description.doc: Human-readable explanation of what this hook does.
ServiceHook.name: String

__ServiceHookTrigger.doc: Lifecycle moments a `ServiceHook` can bind to. `startup` runs on every boot after db/kafka wiring and before traffic is served (run-every-boot — the hook function must be idempotent); `shutdown` runs best-effort on graceful shutdown and is never guaranteed (a killed process runs nothing).
__NativeKernel.doc: Defines a native compute kernel exposed to the service as a library function. A NativeKernel wraps an existing native library (CUDA/MKL/OpenCV/a proprietary HPC routine) behind a stable `extern "C"` shim — the only native code an OpenAPPL compiler compiles. The compiler never binds to the C++ library directly and never parses it; it owns only the C-shaped shim contract. The kernel is compiled and linked into the consuming service via FFI (Rust `build.rs`/bindgen, Node napi-rs or koffi, and per-language FFI for the other targets) and is referenced from MScript like any other library function: `LIB.computeShippingBatch(this.weights, this.zone)`. Keep kernels coarse-grained (one large unit of work per call) because every FFI crossing copies the argument buffers. See `docs/ADR-cpp-kernel-native-lib.md`.

NativeKernel.__name.doc: The kernel name. Unique within the service library; referenced from MScript as `LIB.<name>(...)`. Use camelCase (e.g. `computeShippingBatch`).
NativeKernel.__lang.doc: Source language of the kernel shim. `cpp` for an `extern "C"`-wrapped C++ library (the common case), `c` for a plain C library that already exposes a C ABI.
NativeKernel.__params.doc: Ordered list of kernel parameters. Each is a `KernelParam` with a name and a flat value type (scalars, numeric buffers, bytes, or a UTF-8 string). Host objects never cross the boundary — pass minimal serializable inputs.
NativeKernel.__returns.doc: The value type the kernel produces. For buffer return types (e.g. `f64[]`) the default convention is a caller-allocated output buffer sized from the inputs; the generated host wrapper allocates it and decodes the result. C++ exceptions never cross the boundary — the shim returns a status code and the wrapper turns a non-zero status into a Rust `Result`/JS `throw`/Go `error`.
NativeKernel.__includes.doc: Headers of the existing native library that the shim `#include`s (e.g. `existing_shipping.hpp`, `opencv2/core.hpp`).
NativeKernel.__links.doc: Linker names of the existing native library/libraries to link against (e.g. `shipping`, `blas`, `fftw3`). When the library is publicly available, declare its acquisition once on the service via the shared `serviceBasics.packages[]` list using a native manager (`vcpkg`/`conan`/`apt`) — codegen provisions it into the build image — and list its linker name here so the kernel build links it. For a library that is not in any package manager, carry its source via `sources` instead.
NativeKernel.__hostBindings.doc: Which host-language bindings to emit for this kernel. Defaults to the consuming service's language. When both `rust` and `nodejs` are present, the recommended layout makes Rust the sole FFI host and exposes the Rust safe wrapper to Node via napi-rs (one unsafe seam, written once).
NativeKernel.__async.doc: When true (default), the kernel call is dispatched off the request thread — libuv threadpool via napi `AsyncWorker` on Node, `spawn_blocking` on Rust/Tokio — so long compute never blocks the event loop or async runtime. Set false only for short, bounded kernels; codegen emits a blocking call and a warning.
NativeKernel.__shimBody.doc: The body of the generated `extern "C"` shim function — the bridge between the C ABI signature (derived from `params`/`returns`) and the existing library. Has access to the parameters by name, plus `n` (element count for buffer params), `out` (the caller-allocated output buffer), and `err`/`err_len` (the error message buffer). Must wrap calls into the existing library in `try/catch` and return 0 on success or a non-zero status on error. This is the only native code authored per kernel — keep it tiny; the existing library's own source is NOT pasted here, it is acquired via `packages` or `sources`.
NativeKernel.__sources.doc: Fetchable references to the existing library's own source files when it is NOT available via a package manager (a small or proprietary lib). Because designers interact with the platform through the web and the AI agent — never a local filesystem — source files are never inlined; each `KernelSource` points to a platform bucket key (preferred — user/agent uploads the file or tarball; stays inside the trust boundary), an external download URL, or a git remote. Codegen downloads each into the service's `native/` folder at generation time (verifying `sha256` for url/git origins) and compiles it alongside the shim.
NativeKernel.name: String

__KernelSource.doc: A fetchable reference to one source file (or archive) of the existing native library a `NativeKernel` wraps. Designers work through the web and the AI agent, never a local filesystem, so source is never inlined — it is uploaded to the platform bucket (preferred) or hosted at a URL/git remote, and codegen downloads it into the service's `native/` folder at generation time. Use this only for libraries not available via a package manager; otherwise provision the library through the shared `serviceBasics.packages[]` and reference it via `links`/`includes`.

KernelSource.__origin.doc: Where the source is fetched from. `bucket` (preferred) resolves `ref` as a key in the project's platform bucket — the file/tarball the user or AI agent uploaded; it stays inside the platform trust boundary. `url` fetches `ref` over HTTPS. `git` clones the `ref` remote. `inline` carries the content directly in `ref` (only for tiny single-file headers).
KernelSource.__ref.doc: The locator, interpreted per `origin`: a bucket object key, an HTTPS URL, a git remote (optionally `#ref` for a tag/commit), or — when `origin` is `inline` — the literal file content.
KernelSource.__dest.doc: Relative path under the generated service's `native/` folder where the fetched content is written (e.g. `existing_shipping.hpp`, or a directory like `vendor/` when `extract` is true). The kernel's `includes` and `shimBody` reference files by these paths.
KernelSource.__sha256.doc: Hex SHA-256 of the fetched bytes. Required for `url` and `git` origins — codegen verifies it after download and fails generation on mismatch, pinning the supply chain. Optional (but recommended) for `bucket`.
KernelSource.__extract.doc: When true, `ref` points to an archive (`.tar.gz`/`.tgz`/`.zip`) that codegen extracts into `dest`. When false (default), the fetched bytes are written verbatim to `dest`.

__KernelSourceOrigin.doc.#: Where a native kernel's source is fetched from during codegen.
__KernelSourceOrigin.doc.bucket: Preferred — resolves `ref` as a key in the project's platform bucket (the file/tarball the user or AI agent uploaded); stays inside the platform trust boundary.
__KernelSourceOrigin.doc.inline: Carries the content directly in `ref` — only for tiny single-file headers.

__KernelParam.doc: A single parameter of a `NativeKernel`. The value type is flat — a scalar, a numeric buffer, raw bytes, or a UTF-8 string — so it can cross the C ABI without host-object marshaling. For a buffer parameter the generated C signature passes a pointer plus an element count `n`.

KernelParam.__name.doc: Parameter name, used both in the generated C signature and inside `shimBody`. Use camelCase or snake_case (e.g. `weights`, `zone`).
KernelParam.__type.doc: The parameter's value type — a scalar (`f64`/`f32`/`i64`/`i32`/`bool`), a UTF-8 `string`, raw `bytes`, or a numeric buffer (`f64[]`/`f32[]`/`i64[]`/`i32[]`).
KernelParam.name: String

__KernelLang.doc.#: Source language of a native kernel shim.
__KernelLang.doc.cpp: An `extern "C"`-wrapped C++ library — the common case.
__KernelLang.doc.c: A plain C library that already exposes a C ABI.

__KernelValueType.doc.#: A native kernel's flat value type for parameters and returns — scalars, UTF-8 strings, raw bytes, or numeric buffers. For buffer return types the generated host wrapper allocates a caller-allocated output buffer sized from the inputs and decodes the result.

__KernelHostBinding.doc.#: Which host-language bindings to emit for a native kernel. Defaults to the consuming service's language. When both `rust` and `nodejs` are present, the recommended layout makes Rust the sole FFI host and exposes the Rust safe wrapper to Node via napi-rs (one unsafe seam, written once).

__WasmModule.doc: Defines a portable WebAssembly module exposed to the service as library functions. Unlike a `NativeKernel` (native C/C++ compiled + linked via FFI, compute hosts only), a `WasmModule` carries a precompiled, sandboxed, toolchain-free `.wasm` binary whose exported functions become callable from MScript as `LIB.<export>(...)`. Because Wasm is portable and sandboxed, this targets ALL languages with a strong embedded WebAssembly runtime (nodejs via the built-in `WebAssembly` global, go via wazero, rust via wasmtime, python via wasmtime-py, java via chicory, dotnet via wasmtime-dotnet, php via the wasm extension). An OpenAPPL compiler never compiles the module — it owns only the `.wasm` bytes (fetched via `source`) and the declared `exports` contract. Keep exports coarse-grained (one unit of work per call) because every host↔guest crossing marshals the arguments. Host objects never cross the boundary; only Wasm value types (`i32`/`i64`/`f32`/`f64`) plus host-marshalled `string`/`buffer` (UTF-8 / numeric bytes copied through the module's linear memory). See `docs/ADR-wasm-module.md` for the linear-memory marshalling contract every language implements identically.

WasmModule.__name.doc: The module id. Unique within the service library. Use camelCase (e.g. `imageOps`, `mathKit`). Namespaces the module's exports; the exports themselves are referenced from MScript as `LIB.<export>(...)`.
WasmModule.__source.doc: Fetchable reference to the portable `.wasm` binary (or a `.wat` text the toolchain compiles to `.wasm` at codegen time when `wat2wasm` is available). Reuses the `KernelSource` origin/ref/dest/sha256 shape: `bucket` (preferred — the user/AI agent uploads the file, stays inside the trust boundary), `url` (HTTPS, sha256-pinned), `git`, or `inline` (base64 `.wasm` bytes or a tiny `.wat` text carried directly in `ref`). Codegen downloads it into the service's `wasm/` folder at generation time; `dest` names the file under `wasm/` (e.g. `imageOps.wasm`).
WasmModule.__exports.doc: The exported Wasm functions to expose as library functions. Each `WasmExport` declares the export `name` (called from MScript as `LIB.<name>(...)`), its ordered `params` (each a name + Wasm value type), and its `returns` type. Only declared exports are bound; others stay inaccessible.
WasmModule.__wasi.doc: Whether the module needs WASI (WebAssembly System Interface) imports satisfied at instantiation. Default false for pure-compute modules (no syscalls). When true, the host wires a minimal/sandboxed WASI (clock + random + stdio only; no filesystem/network) so a module compiled against `wasi_snapshot_preview1` instantiates. Pure-compute modules should stay `wasi:false` — it keeps the sandbox tighter and instantiation cheaper.
WasmModule.__memoryLimitPages.doc: Optional hard cap on the module's linear-memory growth, in 64KiB Wasm pages. The host enforces it at instantiation (a module that tries to grow beyond is denied). When null, the runtime default applies. Use this to bound a module's memory footprint per call.
WasmModule.__fuelLimit.doc: Optional execution-budget cap (instructions / 'fuel') for a single call, for runtimes that support metered execution (wasmtime). When the budget is exhausted the call traps and the host surfaces an error — a guard against a runaway/infinite-loop guest. When null, execution is unmetered. Runtimes without fuel metering map this to their nearest equivalent or ignore it (and the host warns).
WasmModule.__timeoutMs.doc: Optional wall-clock timeout (milliseconds) for a single export call. The host aborts the call if it exceeds the budget (epoch-interruption / cancellation on runtimes that support it). When null, no timeout is enforced. Complements `fuelLimit` for runtimes without instruction metering.
WasmModule.name: String

__WasmSource.doc: A fetchable reference to the `.wasm` binary (or `.wat` text) a `WasmModule` runs. Same fetch contract as `KernelSource`: designers work through the web and the AI agent, never a local filesystem, so the binary is uploaded to the platform bucket (preferred) or hosted at a URL/git remote, or carried inline (base64 `.wasm` / literal `.wat`). Codegen downloads it into the service's `wasm/` folder at generation time, verifying `sha256` for url/git origins.

WasmSource.__origin.doc: Where the binary is fetched from. `bucket` (preferred) resolves `ref` as a key in the project's platform bucket — the file the user or AI agent uploaded; it stays inside the platform trust boundary. `url` fetches `ref` over HTTPS. `git` clones the `ref` remote. `inline` carries the content directly in `ref` (base64-encoded `.wasm` bytes, or — when `dest` ends in `.wat` — a literal WebAssembly text the codegen compiles to `.wasm`).
WasmSource.__ref.doc: The locator, interpreted per `origin`: a bucket object key, an HTTPS URL, a git remote (optionally `#ref`), or — when `origin` is `inline` — base64 `.wasm` bytes (default) or literal `.wat` text (when `dest` ends in `.wat`).
WasmSource.__dest.doc: Relative path under the generated service's `wasm/` folder where the fetched binary is written (e.g. `imageOps.wasm`). When it ends in `.wat`, codegen compiles it to a sibling `.wasm` before instantiation. The host loads the module from this path.
WasmSource.__sha256.doc: Hex SHA-256 of the fetched bytes. Required for `url` and `git` origins — codegen verifies it after download and fails generation on mismatch, pinning the supply chain. Optional (but recommended) for `bucket`.
WasmSource.__base64.doc: When true (and `origin` is `inline`), `ref` is interpreted as base64-encoded bytes that codegen decodes before writing to `dest`. Default false (raw `inline` text, e.g. a `.wat`).

__WasmSourceOrigin.doc.#: Where a Wasm module's binary is fetched from during codegen.
__WasmSourceOrigin.doc.bucket: Preferred — resolves `ref` as a key in the project's platform bucket (the file the user or AI agent uploaded); stays inside the platform trust boundary.
__WasmSourceOrigin.doc.inline: Carries the content directly in `ref` — base64-encoded `.wasm` bytes, or (when `dest` ends in `.wat`) a literal WebAssembly text the codegen compiles to `.wasm`.

__WasmExport.doc: One exported function of a `WasmModule`, surfaced to the service library as `LIB.<name>(...)`. Declares the export's `name`, its ordered typed `params`, and its `returns` type. The host binds exactly these exports; the value boundary is flat (Wasm value types plus host-marshalled `string`/`buffer`), so host objects never cross into the guest.

WasmExport.__name.doc: The exported Wasm function name. Must match an export the `.wasm` module actually provides, and is the identifier called from MScript as `LIB.<name>(...)`. Use camelCase (e.g. `add`, `sumF64`, `blurImage`).
