WasmExport.__params.doc: Ordered list of the export's parameters. Each is a `WasmParam` with a name and a Wasm value type (`i32`/`i64`/`f32`/`f64`, or host-marshalled `string`/`buffer`). For a `string`/`buffer` param the host allocates a region in the module's linear memory, copies the bytes in, and passes a (ptr, len) pair to the export per the marshalling contract.
WasmExport.__returns.doc: The Wasm value type the export produces (`i32`/`i64`/`f32`/`f64`, or host-marshalled `string`/`buffer`/`void`). For a `string`/`buffer` return the export writes into a host-allocated out region (or returns a (ptr,len) the host reads from linear memory) per the marshalling contract.
WasmExport.name: String

__WasmParam.doc: A single parameter of a `WasmExport`. The value type is flat so it can cross the host↔guest boundary without host-object marshaling: a Wasm numeric value type (`i32`/`i64`/`f32`/`f64`), a host-marshalled UTF-8 `string`, or a numeric/byte `buffer`. For a `string`/`buffer` the host copies the bytes into the module's linear memory and passes a pointer + length pair to the export.

WasmParam.__name.doc: Parameter name, used in the generated host wrapper signature. Use camelCase (e.g. `a`, `values`, `text`).
WasmParam.__type.doc: The parameter's Wasm value type — a numeric value type (`i32`/`i64`/`f32`/`f64`), a UTF-8 `string`, or a `buffer` (raw/numeric bytes). `string`/`buffer` are host-marshalled through the module's linear memory.
WasmParam.name: String

__WasmValueType.doc.#: A Wasm module's value type for export parameters and returns — the core numeric value types plus host-marshalled `string`/`buffer`/`void`. `string` and `buffer` are marshalled through the module's linear memory per the marshalling contract.
__WasmValueType.doc.string: UTF-8 string, host-marshalled through linear memory.
__WasmValueType.doc.buffer: Raw/numeric byte buffer, host-marshalled through linear memory.

__Calculation.doc: A compute *primitive* — the Tier-1 substrate of the compute layer (docs/ADR-calculation-layer.md §1/§5). A `Calculation` is a single curated math operation over a famous crate/package (FFT a buffer, k-means an array, group-by a dataframe), exposed on the service's library and called from MScript like a function: `LIB.<name>(this.signal)`. It answers within the call — synchronously inline or off-thread — and is meant for small/bounded math that belongs inside a request. Heavy or long-running work is a `ComputeJob` instead. Only valid on rust/python host services (the calculation languages). The `category` selects the algorithm taxonomy bucket whose crate/package set is wired into the build manifest; the `recipe` names a framework-shipped curated consumer (§6), or a `body` supplies author MScript when no recipe fits.

Calculation.__name.doc: The calculation name. Unique within the service library; referenced from MScript as `LIB.<name>(...)`. Use camelCase (e.g. `fftMagnitude`, `kMeansFit`).
Calculation.__category.doc: The algorithm-taxonomy bucket this calculation belongs to (CalculationCategory). Drives the default crate/package dependency set wired into Cargo.toml / pyproject.toml (§5).
Calculation.__recipe.doc: Optional name of a framework-shipped curated consumer (a tested adapter wrapping a famous crate/package behind a stable contract — §6), e.g. `polars.groupByAggregate` or `ndarray.fft`. When omitted, supply `body` instead.
Calculation.__params.doc: Ordered list of typed input parameters. Each is a `KernelParam` (flat value types — scalars, numeric buffers, bytes, UTF-8 string) so the call boundary stays coarse-grained and host-object-free (§10), reusing the NativeKernel param shape.
Calculation.__returns.doc: The value type the calculation produces (a `KernelValueType` flat value type, e.g. `f64[]`).
Calculation.__execution.doc: How the calculation is executed: inline vs off-thread offload, single vs data-parallel, thread budget, and target device (CalculationExecution).
Calculation.__body.doc: Optional author-supplied MScript implementing the calculation when no shipped `recipe` fits. Compiled to native rust/python by the language target.
Calculation.name: String

__CalculationExecution.doc: Execution policy for a `Calculation` primitive (docs/ADR-calculation-layer.md §1/§8). Governs whether the call runs inline on the request thread or is offloaded, whether its internal work is single-threaded or data-parallel, an optional thread budget, and the target compute device.

CalculationExecution.__offload.doc: Where the call runs: `inline` (on the calling thread — only for cheap, bounded math), `offthread` (dispatched off the request thread via the worker pool — rayon spawn_blocking / thread strategy), or `background-job` (escalate to the async job lifecycle). See ComputeOffload.
CalculationExecution.__parallel.doc: Intra-call parallelism: `single` (one thread) or `data-parallel` (work-stealing map/reduce across cores). See ComputeParallel.
CalculationExecution.__maxThreads.doc: Optional upper bound on threads this calculation may use when data-parallel. Bounded by the service's compute pool; unset = pool default.
CalculationExecution.__device.doc: Target compute device: `cpu` (default) or `gpu`. See ComputeDevice. In v1 `gpu` is a scheduling hint only.

__ComputeJob.doc: A compute *workload* — the primary, headline tier of the compute layer (docs/ADR-calculation-layer.md §2/§3). A declared `ComputeJob` generates the full async lifecycle (NOT a synchronous endpoint): a submit Business API that enqueues and returns a jobId, a ComputeQueue, a compute-worker controller that drains it on the bounded compute pool, a result + bucket-backed artifacts, progress/completion events on the outbox, and cooperative cancellation + retry. `type` selects one of the eight curated archetype *specs* (carrying the per-type fields), or `custom` for the bring-your-own-code spec (§12); `executionMode` chooses the async `job` lifecycle (default) or a warm synchronous `serving` endpoint (§11); `implementationMode` makes the library-vs-generate decision explicit (§4). Only valid on rust/python host services; other services *submit* to a compute service over M2M (§7).
__ComputeJobBasics.doc: Defines a compute job's identity, workload type, execution mode and implementation mode. The compute job's scalar identity + lifecycle axes (section): `name`, `type` (the curated workload archetype), `executionMode` (`job` | `serving`), `implementationMode` (the library-vs-generate axis) and `parallel`. Grouped into a section because a chapter is a container of sections, not loose scalar columns.

ComputeJobBasics.__name.doc: The job name. Unique within the service; used to name the generated submit/get/list/cancel Business APIs and the worker handler. Use camelCase (e.g. `rebuildTenantAnalytics`).
ComputeJobBasics.__type.doc: Selects the curated workload archetype (ComputeJobType) — which type-specific spec under `spec` is active and which defaults (category set, libraries, implementation mode, resource profile, result/artifact shape) apply. `custom` lets the designer supply a job whose body is author-provided while still inheriting the lifecycle.
ComputeJobBasics.__executionMode.doc: `job` (default) — the async, queued, observable, cancellable, retryable, artifact-producing lifecycle of §2. `serving` — a warm controller that loads the spec's model/solver/state once and exposes a synchronous, M2M-allowed, bounded-concurrency API with no queue/artifact/retry (§11). In v1 only `job` mode is generated; `serving` is schema-only.
ComputeJobBasics.__implementationMode.doc: The explicit library-vs-generate axis (§4): `libraryWrapped` (mature library does the math; generate only loading/batching/marshaling/lifecycle), `toolOrchestrated` (work done by an external binary like FFmpeg/Tesseract; generate intake/command/artifact capture), `generatedNative` (the structure IS the business logic — a Monte Carlo loop, a constraint problem, a risk formula — generated from the pattern using libraries only for primitives), or `hybrid` (generated orchestration around library-backed heavy lifting).
ComputeJobBasics.__parallel.doc: Intra-job parallelism (§8): `single` or `data-parallel`. `data-parallel` wires rayon (Rust) or a thread/process strategy (Python per §8) sized by the resource profile; deps are wired from the type→categories mapping (§5).
ComputeJobBasics.name: String

ComputeJob.__jobBasics.doc: The job's scalar identity + lifecycle axes (ComputeJobBasics): name, type (the curated workload archetype), executionMode (`job`|`serving`), implementationMode (the library-vs-generate axis, §4), and parallel (§8). Grouped into a section because a chapter is a container of sections, not loose scalar columns.
ComputeJob.__spec.doc: The type-specific payload, keyed by `type` (§3). Because the pattern system has no native discriminated-union type, `spec` is a single ComputeJobSpec wrapper holding all nine typed specs as nullable sub-objects (`aiInference`, `batchTransform`, `indexing`, `mediaProcessing`, `optimization`, `simulation`, `riskCalculation`, `cryptoBatch`, `custom`); the active one is the sub-object matching `type`. Codegen reads only the spec keyed by `type`. Each spec keeps its own schema so per-type codegen has a real shape; presets (ThumbnailJob, DataImportPipeline, …) are field-bundles over a spec, not new patterns.
ComputeJob.__input.doc: Declares the job's input source (ComputeJobInput) — typically a bucket reference to a large dataset/file plus the schema it conforms to. Large inputs cross as bucket references, never inline blobs (§10).
ComputeJob.__result.doc: Declares the job's result shape (ComputeJobResult) — a summary schema (status/metrics, returned in the completion event / job record) plus the artifact format for large outputs stored as bucket references (§2).
ComputeJob.__graphIO.doc: Optional graph I/O capability for this ComputeJob (docs/ADR-graph-database-layer.md §12 — the Graph Intelligence hybrid). Beside the job's existing `input` / `result`, `graphIO` declares a graph INPUT (a GraphQuery by name whose result feeds the recipe) and/or a computed-edge OUTPUT (a projected relationship type written back via the §6 write path). The job keeps its normal `type` / `spec`; `graphIO` only swaps the I/O ends — so 'GraphRecommendationJob'-style ideas are presets of `spec` + `graphIO`, not a new job taxonomy. Leave null/absent when the job does not read from or write to a graph.
ComputeJob.__resourceProfile.doc: The job's ComputeResourceProfile (§9) — cores/memory/timeout/concurrency/preferred language/GPU. Drives the worker pool, the deploy manifest's resource requests, and rejection of impossible jobs. Unset = projectSettings.computeSettings.defaultResourceProfile.
ComputeJob.__retryPolicy.doc: The job's ComputeRetryPolicy (§9) — attempts, backoff, dead-letter. Applies to `job` mode only; `serving` callers own their own retries (§11).

__ComputeJobGraphIO.doc: Graph I/O ends for a ComputeJob (docs/ADR-graph-database-layer.md §12). `reads` feeds a GraphQuery result into the recipe; `writes` persists computed edges back into the graph. Both are optional — a job may read only, write only, or both. So compute produces enriched relationships; the graph persists and serves them (GraphQuery serves top-N at request time, no compute on the hot path).

ComputeJobGraphIO.__provider.doc: Name of the graphProvider this job reads from / writes to (must match a projectSettings.graphProvidersSettings.graphProviders[].name).
ComputeJobGraphIO.__reads.doc: Optional graph input (GraphIORead) — a GraphQuery by name whose result subgraph feeds the recipe (e.g. the VIEWED subgraph for a recommendation job).
ComputeJobGraphIO.__writes.doc: Optional computed-edge output (GraphIOWrite) — a projected relationship type written back via the §6 write path (e.g. `(:User)-[:RECOMMENDED {score}]->(:Document)`).

__GraphIORead.doc: The graph INPUT of a ComputeJob.graphIO (docs/ADR-graph-database-layer.md §12) — names a declared GraphQuery whose result feeds the recipe.

GraphIORead.__query.doc: Name of a service.graphLayer.queries[] entry whose result (the subgraph / rows) is fed to the compute recipe as input.

__GraphIOWrite.doc: The computed-edge OUTPUT of a ComputeJob.graphIO (docs/ADR-graph-database-layer.md §12) — the projected relationship the job writes back into the graph after computing scores/clusters/embeddings.

GraphIOWrite.__relationshipType.doc: The Neo4j relationship type the job writes back, e.g. `RECOMMENDED`.
GraphIOWrite.__from.doc: Source node label of the written edge (e.g. `user`).
GraphIOWrite.__to.doc: Target node label of the written edge (e.g. `document`).
GraphIOWrite.__edgeProperties.doc: Names of the computed properties written onto each edge, e.g. ['score','reason'].

__ComputeJobInput.doc: Declares a ComputeJob's input source. Large inputs cross the submit boundary as bucket references (`type: bucketRef`), never inline blobs (§10). `schema` names the DataObject the input conforms to.

ComputeJobInput.__type.doc: How the input is delivered to the worker. `bucketRef` (a RemoteBucket/DbBucket object key — the default for large inputs), `inline` (small serializable payloads only), or `dataObjectQuery` (a query over the service's own data). Kept as String in v1.
ComputeJobInput.__schema.doc: Name of the DataObject the input rows/records conform to (DataObjectName).

__ComputeJobResult.doc: Declares a ComputeJob's result shape (§2). The `summarySchema` is a small status/metrics summary returned in the job record and completion event; large outputs are written as bucket-referenced artifacts in the `artifact` format.

ComputeJobResult.__summarySchema.doc: Name of the DataObject describing the small result summary (status, metrics, counts) carried in the job record / completion event (DataObjectName).
ComputeJobResult.__artifact.doc: Artifact format for large outputs stored as bucket references (e.g. `parquet`, `csv`, `json`, `png`, `pdf`, `onnx`). Kept as String in v1 — the open artifact-format set is workload-dependent.

__ComputeJobSpec.doc: The discriminated type-specific payload of a ComputeJob, keyed by `ComputeJob.type` (§3). The pattern system has no native one-of/discriminated-union type, so this wrapper holds all nine specs (the eight curated archetypes plus the `custom` bring-your-own-code spec, §12) as nullable sub-objects; exactly the one matching the job's `type` is populated and read by codegen. This mirrors the flat-superset modeling used elsewhere (e.g. BucketProviderConfig reads only the fields relevant to the selected provider). v1 ships codegen for `ai-inference` / `batch-transform` / `media-processing`; the other six carry schema only.

ComputeJobSpec.__custom.doc: Active when `type` is `custom` — the bring-your-own-code escape hatch (CustomSpec, §12).

__AiInferenceSpec.doc: Type-specific spec for `ai-inference` ComputeJobs (docs/ADR-calculation-layer.md, Type-specific specs). libraryWrapped: a mature model library does the math; the compiler generates model load, input normalization, batching, timeout, resource profile, result mapping, and fallback — not the model logic. Configurations of this archetype include EmbeddingJob (`task:embed`), BatchPredictionJob, and ModelServingService (serving mode).

AiInferenceSpec.__model.doc: The model to load (AiInferenceModel) — its source, format, and reference.
AiInferenceSpec.__task.doc: Inference task: `classify|embed|score|detect|transcribe`. Kept as String in v1.
AiInferenceSpec.__batchSize.doc: Number of inputs batched per forward pass.
AiInferenceSpec.__preprocessing.doc: Optional preprocessing recipe/spec applied to inputs before inference (free-form String in v1).
AiInferenceSpec.__fallback.doc: Optional fallback behaviour/model when primary inference fails or times out (String in v1).
AiInferenceSpec.__outputMapping.doc: Optional mapping of raw model outputs onto the result summary schema (String/MScript in v1).

__AiInferenceModel.doc: Locates the model an AiInferenceSpec loads. `source` says where it comes from, `format` its serialization, and `ref` the locator (bucket key / hub id / URL).

AiInferenceModel.__source.doc: Where the model is loaded from: `bucket|hub|hf|url`. Kept as String in v1.
AiInferenceModel.__format.doc: Model serialization format: `onnx|torch|safetensors`. Kept as String in v1.
AiInferenceModel.__ref.doc: The locator, interpreted per `source`: a bucket object key, a model-hub id, a Hugging Face repo id, or an HTTPS URL.

__BatchTransformSpec.doc: Type-specific spec for `batch-transform` ComputeJobs (ETL, imports/exports, data cleaning, report precompute, analytics rebuilds, aggregation over millions of rows). hybrid: the compiler generates the schema map, validation, chunking, parallel exec, progress, error-row capture, and artifact. Presets: DataImportPipeline (`direction:import`), DataExportPipeline (`direction:export`), AnalyticsRebuildJob (aggregate→write).

BatchTransformSpec.__direction.doc: Data-flow direction: `import|export|internal`. Kept as String in v1.
BatchTransformSpec.__sourceSchema.doc: Name of the DataObject describing the input/source records (DataObjectName).
BatchTransformSpec.__targetSchema.doc: Name of the DataObject describing the output/target records (DataObjectName).
BatchTransformSpec.__mapping.doc: Field/transform mapping from source to target (String/MScript in v1).
BatchTransformSpec.__validation.doc: Row-level validation rules applied during the transform (String/MScript in v1).
BatchTransformSpec.__errorRowHandling.doc: What to do with rows that fail validation: `collect|fail|deadletter`. Kept as String in v1.
BatchTransformSpec.__chunkSize.doc: Number of rows processed per chunk for streaming/parallel execution.
BatchTransformSpec.__aggregation.doc: Optional aggregation spec (groupBy + aggregate functions) applied before write (BatchAggregation).
BatchTransformSpec.__writeTarget.doc: Where the transformed output is written (a DataObject, bucket artifact, or external sink — String in v1).

__BatchAggregation.doc: Aggregation spec for a BatchTransformSpec — the group-by keys and the aggregate functions applied over each group before the result is written.

BatchAggregation.__groupBy.doc: Ordered list of field names to group rows by (e.g. ['tenantId','day']).
BatchAggregation.__agg.doc: List of aggregate expressions applied per group (e.g. ['count','sum:amount']). Kept as String entries in v1.

__IndexingSpec.doc: Type-specific spec for `indexing` ComputeJobs — the AI-native-app workhorse: chunk → embed → write index. libraryWrapped + generated pipeline: the compiler generates the loader, chunking, metadata, embed adapter, vector write, dedup, retry, and reindex. Presets: EmbeddingPipeline (chunk+embed+write), DocumentChunkingJob (chunk-only), SearchRebuildJob (`writeMode:rebuild`). v1: schema only.

IndexingSpec.__source.doc: The source of documents to index (a DataObject, bucket, or external corpus — String in v1).
IndexingSpec.__metadataExtraction.doc: Optional metadata-extraction rules attached to each chunk (String/MScript in v1).
IndexingSpec.__embed.doc: How chunks are embedded — delegates to an `ai-inference` embed task or a provider (String in v1; a delegated-spec reference is a later-wave refinement).
IndexingSpec.__indexTarget.doc: Where vectors/index entries are written: `elasticsearch|opensearch|vector`. Kept as String in v1.
IndexingSpec.__dedup.doc: When true, duplicate chunks are de-duplicated before write.

__IndexingChunking.doc: Chunking configuration for an IndexingSpec — how source documents are split into index units.

IndexingChunking.__strategy.doc: Chunking strategy (e.g. `fixed`, `sentence`, `recursive`, `semantic`). Kept as String in v1.

__MediaProcessingSpec.doc: Type-specific spec for `media-processing` ComputeJobs — image resize/thumbnails, PDF→image, OCR preprocessing, audio waveform, transcoding orchestration. toolOrchestrated: the work is done by an external binary (FFmpeg, Tesseract, PyMuPDF); the compiler generates intake, the storage adapter, variant/thumbnail rules, the transcode/OCR profile, and artifact metadata — not the codecs. Presets: ThumbnailJob (`op:thumbnail`), TranscodingJob (`op:transcode`), PdfProcessingJob (`op:pdf-render/ocr`).

MediaProcessingSpec.__op.doc: The media operation: `thumbnail|resize|transcode|pdf-render|ocr|waveform`. Kept as String in v1.
MediaProcessingSpec.__tool.doc: The external tool/binary or library used: `ffmpeg|tesseract|pymupdf|image`. Kept as String in v1.
MediaProcessingSpec.__variants.doc: List of output variants to produce (e.g. thumbnail sizes). Kept as String entries in v1.
MediaProcessingSpec.__transcodeProfile.doc: Optional transcode profile (codec/bitrate/container) for `transcode` ops (String in v1).
MediaProcessingSpec.__ocrProfile.doc: Optional OCR profile (language/engine settings) for `ocr` ops (String in v1).
MediaProcessingSpec.__artifact.doc: Artifact metadata/format for the produced media outputs (String in v1).

__OptimizationSpec.doc: Type-specific spec for `optimization` ComputeJobs — routing, scheduling, allocation, pricing, constraint solving. generatedNative problem + library solver: an OpenAPPL compiler generates the decision variables, constraints, objective, solver selection, and input/solution mapping plus explainability; the solver crate/package does the search. Presets: ConstraintSolverJob (`solver:CP`), PlanningService. v1: schema only.

OptimizationSpec.__decisionVariables.doc: List of decision variables the solver optimizes over. Kept as String entries in v1.
OptimizationSpec.__constraints.doc: List of constraints the solution must satisfy. Kept as String entries in v1.
OptimizationSpec.__solver.doc: Solver backend: `or-tools|scipy|pulp|custom`. Kept as String in v1.
OptimizationSpec.__timeLimit.doc: Wall-clock time limit for the solve (e.g. `30s`). Kept as String in v1.
OptimizationSpec.__inputMapping.doc: Mapping of job input onto the problem's data (String/MScript in v1).
OptimizationSpec.__solutionMapping.doc: Mapping of the solver's solution onto the result summary (String/MScript in v1).
OptimizationSpec.__explainability.doc: When true, an explanation of the solution (binding constraints, sensitivity) is produced.

__OptimizationObjective.doc: The objective of an OptimizationSpec — whether to minimize or maximize, and the expression being optimized.

OptimizationObjective.__sense.doc: Optimization sense: `min|max`. Kept as String in v1.
OptimizationObjective.__expr.doc: The objective expression evaluated over the decision variables (String/MScript in v1).

__SimulationSpec.doc: Type-specific spec for `simulation` ComputeJobs — Monte Carlo, agent/state-step, time-series simulation. hybrid/generatedNative: an OpenAPPL compiler generates the MC/state/time-step loop, seed handling, scenario config, parallel exec, and aggregation. Presets: MonteCarloJob (`method:monte-carlo`), ForecastingJob. v1: schema only.

SimulationSpec.__method.doc: Simulation method: `monte-carlo|discrete-event|agent|time-step`. Kept as String in v1.
SimulationSpec.__model.doc: The state/step body of the simulation (generatedNative MScript/native — String in v1).
SimulationSpec.__iterations.doc: Number of iterations / scenarios to run.
SimulationSpec.__scenarioConfig.doc: Scenario configuration (parameter ranges/distributions) — String in v1.
SimulationSpec.__aggregation.doc: How per-iteration outputs are aggregated into the result (String in v1).

__RiskCalculationSpec.doc: Type-specific spec for `risk-calculation` ComputeJobs — portfolio risk, pricing models, credit scoring, forecasting, actuarial. hybrid/generatedNative: an OpenAPPL compiler generates the risk schema, formula, scenario matrix, MC engine, parallel exec, AUDIT TRAIL (required), and explanation. Presets: PricingEngine (serving mode). v1: schema only.

RiskCalculationSpec.__riskSchema.doc: Name of the DataObject describing the risk inputs (DataObjectName).
RiskCalculationSpec.__formula.doc: The auditable risk formula (generatedNative MScript/native — String in v1).
RiskCalculationSpec.__scenarioMatrix.doc: The scenario matrix over which risk is evaluated (String in v1).
RiskCalculationSpec.__monteCarlo.doc: Optional Monte Carlo configuration — delegates to a `simulation` spec (String in v1; delegated-spec reference is a later-wave refinement).
RiskCalculationSpec.__auditTrail.doc: Whether a full audit trail of inputs/intermediate values/outputs is recorded. REQUIRED for risk-calculation — should be true.
RiskCalculationSpec.__explanation.doc: When true, a human-readable explanation of the risk result is produced.

__CryptoBatchSpec.doc: Type-specific spec for `crypto-batch` ComputeJobs — bulk hashing, signature verification at scale, integrity scanning, secure archive generation. libraryWrapped ONLY — never primitives: an OpenAPPL compiler generates file batching, key/KMS handling, the hash/sign workflow, audit logs (required), and the verification report; the cryptographic primitives are always a vetted crate (ring/RustCrypto/sha2/blake3/argon2), never generated. Presets: FileIntegrityJob (`op:hash/verify`), SignatureVerificationJob (`op:verify`), SecureArchiveJob (`op:encrypt-archive`). v1: schema only.

CryptoBatchSpec.__op.doc: The crypto operation: `hash|sign|verify|encrypt-archive`. Kept as String in v1.
CryptoBatchSpec.__algorithm.doc: The algorithm (e.g. `sha256`, `blake3`, `ed25519`, `argon2`). Kept as String in v1 — resolved to a vetted crate, never generated.
CryptoBatchSpec.__keyRef.doc: Reference to the signing/encryption key (a key store key id). Mutually informative with `kmsRef`.
CryptoBatchSpec.__kmsRef.doc: Reference to a KMS-managed key (cloud KMS key arn/id) when keys are not held locally.
CryptoBatchSpec.__batching.doc: File/record batching configuration for the bulk operation (String in v1).
CryptoBatchSpec.__auditLog.doc: Whether an audit log of every operation is recorded. REQUIRED for crypto-batch — should be true.
CryptoBatchSpec.__verificationReport.doc: When true, a verification report summarizing pass/fail per item is produced.

__CustomSpec.doc: Type-specific spec for `custom` ComputeJobs — the bring-your-own-code escape hatch (docs/ADR-calculation-layer.md §12). The designer (or an AI agent acting as one) supplies their OWN Rust/Python calculation — inline in `body`, or uploaded as a source module fetched at codegen/build time — and the compiler generates the full lifecycle scaffolding around the opaque user function (submit → queue → worker → invoke `entrypoint(inputs)` on the bounded pool → result/artifact → event → cancel/retry). `implementationMode` is `generatedNative`, but here "generated" means the WRAPPER, not the math — the developer owns the calculation. The generated wrapper panic/crash-guards the user code (Rust `catch_unwind`; Python process-pool execution) so a fault fails the job, not the service — but this is NOT a sandbox: custom code runs with service privileges and untrusted/third-party code must be gated by the project (§12). This subsumes the `Calculation` primitive's free-form `body` for the cross-request (job) case.

CustomSpec.__language.doc: Host language of the supplied code: must be `rust` or `python` (ServiceLanguage), and must match the host service — the §7 host guard applies (a `custom` job on a non-rust/python host is a codegen error).
CustomSpec.__computeSourceType.doc: Where the code comes from: `inline` (code in `body`) | `bucket` | `url` | `git`. For `bucket|url|git` the module is fetched at codegen/build time via `source` (a KernelSource, reusing the upload-origin concept — but NOT the kernel FFI machinery: this is native rust/python source, no shim/isolation). Kept as String in v1.
CustomSpec.__source.doc: Fetchable reference to the uploaded source module when `computeSourceType` is `bucket|url|git` (a `KernelSource` — origin/ref/dest/sha256/extract). Reuses the existing KernelSource origin shape (the upload-via-bucket-preferred / url / git pattern), so the upload tooling and supply-chain pinning (sha256 for url/git) are shared. Null when `computeSourceType` is `inline` (code lives in `body` instead). Only the bucket/url/git origins apply here; inline source uses `body`, not `source.origin:inline`.
CustomSpec.__body.doc: Inline author-supplied native source (Rust/Python) when `computeSourceType` is `inline`. The function named by `entrypoint` is invoked by the generated worker on the bounded pool. Null when the code is fetched via `source`.
CustomSpec.__entrypoint.doc: Name of the function the generated worker calls with the marshaled inputs (e.g. `run`, `compute`). Must exist in `body` or the fetched module.
CustomSpec.__dependencies.doc: Extra crates / pip packages the user's code needs, wired into the generated `Cargo.toml` / `pyproject.toml`. Each entry is a package spec string (e.g. `ndarray`, `numpy>=1.26`). Kept as String entries in v1.
CustomSpec.__params.doc: Ordered list of typed input parameters crossing the job boundary. Each is a `KernelParam` (flat value types — scalars, numeric buffers, bytes, UTF-8 string), keeping the marshaled boundary coarse-grained and host-object-free (§10), exactly as `Calculation.params` does.
CustomSpec.__returns.doc: The value type `entrypoint` produces (a KernelValueType flat value type, e.g. `f64[]`). Kept as String in v1 to allow workload-dependent return shapes beyond the flat enum.

__ComputeResourceProfile.doc: The resource envelope of a ComputeJob (docs/ADR-calculation-layer.md §9). Drives the bounded worker pool, the deploy manifest's resource requests, and rejection of impossible jobs. Also used as `projectSettings.computeSettings.defaultResourceProfile` for jobs that don't declare their own.

ComputeResourceProfile.__cpuCores.doc: Number of CPU cores the job may use. Bounds the rayon pool / thread budget.
ComputeResourceProfile.__memoryLimit.doc: Memory ceiling for the job, as a quantity string (e.g. `8Gi`, `512Mi`). Surfaced as the deploy manifest's memory request/limit.
ComputeResourceProfile.__timeout.doc: Wall-clock timeout for the job, as a duration string (e.g. `30m`, `2h`). The worker cancels the job when exceeded.
ComputeResourceProfile.__concurrency.doc: How many instances of this job may run concurrently on a host, within the project-level maxConcurrentJobs bound.
ComputeResourceProfile.__preferredLanguage.doc: Preferred host language for this job (ServiceLanguage) — must be `rust` or `python`. Informs scheduling/marshaling; the actual host service's language is authoritative.
ComputeResourceProfile.__gpuRequired.doc: When true, the job must be scheduled on a GPU-capable host (requires projectSettings.computeSettings.gpuEnabled). In v1 a scheduling flag only.

__ComputeRetryPolicy.doc: Retry policy for a ComputeJob in `job` mode (docs/ADR-calculation-layer.md §9). Governs how many times the worker re-attempts a failed job, the backoff between attempts, and whether exhausted jobs are routed to a dead-letter sink. Not applicable in `serving` mode (the caller owns retries).

ComputeRetryPolicy.__maxAttempts.doc: Maximum number of attempts before the job is considered failed (1 = no retry).
ComputeRetryPolicy.__backoff.doc: Backoff strategy between attempts (e.g. `fixed`, `linear`, `exponential`). Kept as String in v1.
ComputeRetryPolicy.__deadLetter.doc: When true, a job that exhausts its attempts is routed to the dead-letter sink for later inspection instead of being dropped.

__CalculationCategory.doc.#: The algorithm-taxonomy bucket a `Calculation` (or a generatedNative/hybrid ComputeJob's internal composition) belongs to (docs/ADR-calculation-layer.md §5). The category drives the default crate/package dependency set wired into the build manifest.
__CalculationCategory.doc.linear-algebra: Matrix/vector operations, decompositions, solvers (ndarray / nalgebra ; numpy).
__CalculationCategory.doc.statistics: Descriptive/inferential statistics, distributions, hypothesis tests (statrs ; scipy.stats).
__CalculationCategory.doc.signal-processing: FFT, filtering, convolution, spectral analysis (rustfft ; scipy.signal).
__CalculationCategory.doc.image-vision: Image transforms, feature detection, computer vision (image / opencv ; Pillow / OpenCV).
__CalculationCategory.doc.ml-classical: Classical ML — regression, trees, clustering, SVM (linfa ; scikit-learn).
__CalculationCategory.doc.ml-deep: Deep learning inference/training (candle / tch / ort ; torch / onnxruntime).
__CalculationCategory.doc.dataframe-analytics: Columnar dataframe analytics, group-by, joins (polars ; pandas / polars).
__CalculationCategory.doc.geometry-graph: Computational geometry and graph algorithms (geo / petgraph ; networkx).
__CalculationCategory.doc.simulation-montecarlo: Stochastic simulation and Monte Carlo methods (rand / rayon ; numpy / simpy).

__ComputeJobType.doc.#: Selects the curated workload archetype of a ComputeJob (docs/ADR-calculation-layer.md §3) — which type-specific spec is active and which defaults apply.
__ComputeJobType.doc.ai-inference: Classification, embeddings, recommendation/fraud/anomaly scoring, speech/document analysis (AiInferenceSpec).
__ComputeJobType.doc.batch-transform: Imports/exports, ETL, data cleaning, report precompute, analytics rebuilds (BatchTransformSpec).
__ComputeJobType.doc.indexing: chunk → embed → write index; the AI-native-app search workhorse (IndexingSpec).
__ComputeJobType.doc.media-processing: Image/PDF/audio processing, transcoding orchestration, OCR preprocessing (MediaProcessingSpec).
__ComputeJobType.doc.optimization: Routing, scheduling, allocation, pricing, constraint solving (OptimizationSpec).
__ComputeJobType.doc.risk-calculation: Portfolio risk, pricing models, credit scoring, forecasting, actuarial (RiskCalculationSpec).
__ComputeJobType.doc.crypto-batch: Bulk hashing, signature verification at scale, integrity scanning, secure archives (CryptoBatchSpec).
__ComputeJobType.doc.custom: A designer-defined job whose body is author-supplied native/MScript, still inheriting the full lifecycle.

__ImplementationMode.doc.#: The explicit library-vs-generate axis of a ComputeJob (docs/ADR-calculation-layer.md §4).
__ImplementationMode.doc.libraryWrapped: The hard math is a mature library; the compiler generates only loading, batching, marshaling, and lifecycle.
__ImplementationMode.doc.toolOrchestrated: The work is done by an external binary (FFmpeg, Tesseract); an OpenAPPL compiler generates intake, command construction, and artifact capture, and declares the binary as a dependency.
__ImplementationMode.doc.generatedNative: The structure IS the business logic; the compiler generates native rust/python from the pattern, using libraries only for math primitives.
__ImplementationMode.doc.hybrid: Generated orchestration/structure around library-backed heavy lifting.

__ExecutionMode.doc.#: The execution mode of a ComputeJob (docs/ADR-calculation-layer.md §11).
__ExecutionMode.doc.job: Async, queued, observable, cancellable, retryable, artifact-producing lifecycle (default).
__ExecutionMode.doc.serving: A warm, synchronous, M2M-allowed, bounded-concurrency endpoint that loads hot state once; no queue/artifact/retry. Schema-only in v1.

__ComputeOffload.doc.#: Where a Calculation primitive's call is executed (docs/ADR-calculation-layer.md §1/§8).
__ComputeOffload.doc.inline: On the calling thread — only for cheap, bounded math that belongs in a request.
__ComputeOffload.doc.offthread: Dispatched off the request thread via the worker pool (rayon spawn_blocking / thread strategy).
__ComputeOffload.doc.background-job: Escalated to the async ComputeJob lifecycle.

__ComputeParallel.doc.data-parallel: Work-stealing map/reduce across cores (rayon on Rust; thread/process strategy on Python).

__ComputeDevice.doc.#: Target compute device (docs/ADR-calculation-layer.md §9). In v1 `gpu` is a scheduling hint only.
__ComputeDevice.doc.gpu: Run on GPU (requires a GPU-capable host and projectSettings.computeSettings.gpuEnabled).

__PdfTemplate.doc: Defines a PDF rendering template used by `RenderPdfAction` to produce styled PDFs (e.g., invoices, receipts, statements). The body is an EJS template that produces HTML, which is rendered to PDF using the service's PDF rendering layer. Page setup (paper size, orientation, margins), optional header/footer EJS templates, and document metadata are configured per template so every render of the same template is visually consistent. Per-call overrides are supported on RenderPdfAction.

PdfTemplate.__name.doc: The unique name of the PDF template. Used to reference the template from `RenderPdfAction`.
PdfTemplate.__description.doc: A brief description of the template's purpose (e.g., 'Customer invoice with VAT breakdown').
PdfTemplate.__parser.doc: The template rendering engine. Currently only 'ejs' is supported.
PdfTemplate.__bodyTemplate.doc: The main EJS template producing the body HTML of the PDF. Has access to the input data passed by RenderPdfAction.
PdfTemplate.__headerTemplate.doc: Optional EJS template producing repeating page-header HTML. Supports the same template variables as the body, plus two renderer placeholders: `pageNumber` and `totalPages` (e.g. `Page <%= pageNumber %> / <%= totalPages %>`). They are not numbers at EJS time: the renderer turns each one into the Chromium page-number element (`` / ``) that is filled in per page, so use them only for output, never in arithmetic or conditions. They take precedence over an inputData key of the same name. The header is rendered in its own document without the body's stylesheet: use inline styles and set an explicit font-size (the renderer's default is very small).
PdfTemplate.__footerTemplate.doc: Optional EJS template producing repeating page-footer HTML. Same data access as headerTemplate, including the `pageNumber` and `totalPages` placeholders (e.g. `Page <%= pageNumber %> / <%= totalPages %>`), which become Chromium page-number elements filled in per page; like the header it is rendered without the body's stylesheet, so use inline styles and an explicit font-size.
PdfTemplate.__paperSize.doc: Default paper size for this template. Per-call overrides supported on RenderPdfAction.
PdfTemplate.__orientation.doc: Default page orientation for this template. Per-call overrides supported on RenderPdfAction.
PdfTemplate.__margin.doc: Default page margins (millimeters) for this template.
PdfTemplate.__metadata.doc: PDF document metadata embedded in the output file.
PdfTemplate.name: String

__EdgeController.doc: An edge controller defines a fully customized route handled by a developer-defined function. Unlike standard Busines APIs, it gives full control over the request processing by directly calling a function from the service library. This allows advanced operations like database queries, external API calls, or dynamic responses without following the CRUD cycle. Edge controllers are ideal for building special-purpose APIs or custom flows outside the compiler's automatic route generation.

EdgeController.__edgeControllerOptions.doc: Configuration object for the edge controller. It defines which edge function will be executed and whether login is required to access it.
EdgeController.__edgeRestSettings.doc: HTTP settings for exposing the edge controller as a REST API. It allows specifying the URL path and HTTP method that will trigger the edge function.
EdgeController.__edgeKafkaSettings.doc: Kafka settings for exposing the edge controller as a Kafka consumer/producer. It allows specifying the Kafka topics that will trigger the edge function and optionally where to send responses.
EdgeController.__edgeCronSettings.doc: Cron settings for scheduling the edge controller to run at specified intervals. It allows defining a cron expression that will trigger the edge function automatically.

__EdgeControllerOptions.doc: Options that define the execution behavior of the edge controller, including the function to call and login requirement.

EdgeControllerOptions.__functionName.doc: The name of the function defined in the service library that will handle this controller's logic. The function must be an async module under 'edgeFunctions'. RETURN CONTRACT: it returns either a plain value, serialised as JSON with HTTP 200, or a response envelope { status, headers, body } (a numeric status TOGETHER with a body and/or a plain-object headers member), which is honoured verbatim: the status is set, the headers are set, a Buffer or string body is sent raw (binary downloads) and any other body is JSON-serialised. A bare { status: 200, ... } with no body/headers stays a JSON body, so legacy handlers are unaffected. Throwing an error carrying a numeric .status answers that code as problem+json.
EdgeControllerOptions.__M2MAllowed.doc: If true, this edge controller accepts machine callers: a service token sent as `x-m2m-token` (an `Authorization: Bearer` is accepted only when it verifies as a service token) that VERIFIES through the same service-identity verifier the Business APIs use, from a calling service this service admits (`serviceOptions.allowedM2MClients` / `blockedM2MClients`). A token is never accepted for its shape: an unsigned or foreign-key token is 401, and a verified service the lists refuse is 403 M2M_CLIENT_NOT_ALLOWED. With loginRequired:false this is an M2M-ONLY edge route (a user session alone does not pass, 401 M2M_TOKEN_REQUIRED). With loginRequired:true the route accepts a user session OR such a token. Unlike a Business API, where loginRequired:false means public, the edge pair has a real m2m mode. The edge function sees the verified caller as ctx.isM2M / ctx.m2mIssuer.
EdgeControllerOptions.__loginRequired.doc: Whether the caller must be logged in to access this edge route. If true (the default), the generated adapter requires a user session before invoking the function (401 SESSION_REQUIRED), or, when M2MAllowed is also true, a user session OR a verified and admitted service token. False with M2MAllowed:true is M2M-only; false with M2MAllowed:false is a public route.
EdgeControllerOptions.__loadShedTier.doc: Optional shed-priority tier (integer 0-5) this edge controller declares for itself when the owning service runs a `loadShield` (0 = never shed; 5 = first to shed). The per-API counterpart of the shield's central `loadShield.tiers.assignments[]` — same semantics as BusinessApi `apiOptions.loadShedTier`. PRECEDENCE (most specific wins): central action-narrowed assignment > central api-level assignment > this `loadShedTier` > the derived default (edge routes classify by HTTP verb: GET 3, mutating 2). INERT without a declared/enabled shield (byte-identical output; validation warns with LOADSHIELD_TIER_WITHOUT_SHIELD). Only the REST-enabled route is shielded — kafka/cron triggers are structurally outside the shield's path. Values outside 0-5 fail validation (LOADSHIELD_TIER_INVALID).

__EdgeRestSettings.doc: Defines the public REST endpoint for the edge controller. Specifies how the route is exposed via HTTP, including path and method.

EdgeRestSettings.__restEnabled.doc: Set to true if you want your edge function to be called through its own REST API. Default is true.
EdgeRestSettings.__path.doc: The URL path for this controller, RELATIVE to the service's edge mount prefix ('/edge' by default, overridable per deployment with the EDGE_MOUNT_PATH environment variable). It determines where the edge function will be accessible in the REST API (e.g., '/generate-invoice', served at '/edge/generate-invoice'). Never repeat the mount prefix here.
EdgeRestSettings.__method.doc: The HTTP method that will trigger the edge controller. Typical values include GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, etc.

__EdgeKafkaSettings.doc: Defines Kafka consumer/producer settings for the edge controller. Specifies how the edge function will be triggered by Kafka messages and optionally where to send responses.

EdgeKafkaSettings.__kafkaEnabled.doc: Set to true if you want your edge function to be triggered by Kafka messages from the specified request topic. Default is false.
EdgeKafkaSettings.__requestTopic.doc: The Kafka topic name from which messages will be consumed to trigger the edge function. When a message arrives on this topic, the edge function will be invoked with the message payload.
EdgeKafkaSettings.__responseTopic.doc: Optional Kafka topic name where the edge function's response will be published. If not specified, the response will not be sent to Kafka (useful for fire-and-forget scenarios or when using REST for responses).

__EdgeCronSettings.doc: Reserved cron settings of an edge controller. The block is accepted and validated, but NO code generator schedules an edge function today (nodejs emits only the REST and Kafka edge adapters, and the other languages none for cron): an edge controller with `cronEnabled: true` is never triggered by the clock, and validation warns (EDGE_CRON_NOT_SCHEDULED). For scheduled work use a service cron job (`Service.cronJobs[]`, which calls a library function once per tick across replicas) or a Business API cron controller (`ApiCronSettings`).

EdgeCronSettings.__cronEnabled.doc: Reserved: setting it to true does NOT schedule the edge function on any language today (validation warns, EDGE_CRON_NOT_SCHEDULED). Use a service cron job (`Service.cronJobs[]`) or a Business API cron controller (`ApiCronSettings`) for scheduled work. Default is false.
EdgeCronSettings.__cronExpression.doc: Reserved, not read by any code generator today (see `cronEnabled`). Standard cron syntax (e.g., '0 0 * * *' for daily at midnight, '*/5 * * * *' for every 5 minutes).

__BusinessApi.doc:
Defines a Business API, a high-level abstraction representing a specific business operation on a primary data object. It encapsulates intent (e.g., get, create, delete), parameters, trigger mechanisms, and a structured workflow composed of modular actions. Each Business API offers more expressive and decoupled control over behavior and access.

## Field applicability by `apiOptions.crudType`

Most option blocks apply to every crudType, but the data-shaping clauses and the `*Options` blocks are restricted. Populating a block on a crudType that ignores it is a design-time mistake: the codegen silently drops the configuration. The validator emits a `BUSINESSAPI_BLOCK_IGNORED` warning when this happens.

| Block               | create | get | list | update | delete |
|---------------------|:------:|:---:|:----:|:------:|:------:|
| `apiOptions`        |   ✓    |  ✓  |  ✓   |   ✓    |   ✓    |
| `authOptions`       |   ✓    |  ✓  |  ✓   |   ✓    |   ✓    |
| `requestParameters` |   ✓    |  ✓  |  ✓   |   ✓    |   ✓    |
| `dataClauseItems`   |   ✓    |  —  |  —   |   ✓    |   —    |
| `redisParameters`   |   ✓    |  ✓  |  ✓   |   ✓    |   ✓    |
| `restSettings`      |   ✓    |  ✓  |  ✓   |   ✓    |   ✓    |
| `grpcSettings`      |   ✓    |  ✓  |  ✓   |   ✓    |   ✓    |
| `kafkaSettings`     |   ✓    |  ✓  |  ✓   |   ✓    |   ✓    |
| `sseSettings`       |   ✓    |  ✓  |  ✓   |   ✓    |   ✓    |
| `cronSettings`      |   ✓    |  ✓  |  ✓   |   ✓    |   ✓    |
| `internalCallSettings` | ✓   |  ✓  |  ✓   |   ✓    |   ✓    |
| `actions`           |   ✓    |  ✓  |  ✓   |   ✓    |   ✓    |
| `workflow`          |   ✓    |  ✓  |  ✓   |   ✓    |   ✓    |
| `selectClause`      |  ans.  |  ✓  |  ✓   |  ans.  |  ans.  |
| `whereClause`       |   —    |  ✓  |  ✓   |   ✓    |   ✓    |
| `getOptions`        |   —    |  ✓  |  —   |   —    |   —    |
| `listOptions`       |   —    |  —  |  ✓   |   —    |   —    |
| `paginationOptions` |   —    |  —  |  ✓   |   —    |   —    |
| `deleteOptions`     |   —    |  —  |  —   |   —    |   ✓    |

Reader's guide:
- `selectClause` shapes the read projection on `get` / `list`. On `create` / `update` / `delete` (`ans.`) only `selectProperties` is read, as the boundary of the answer: the written row narrowed to the declared properties + `id`, the write itself never projected; `selectJoins` there is ignored.
- `whereClause` locates the target record(s). It applies to every read or mutation that has to identify what to operate on; `create` is excluded because it makes a new record.
- `dataClauseItems` carries the write payload — each entry maps a property name to a value MScript or literal that the framework writes at create / update time. `sessionSettings` and `staticJoin` properties are auto-injected and don't need entries here. Only `create` and `update` mutate fields; a `delete` writes no payload at all — it either archives the row (`isActive: false`) or removes it, and that choice is made by the data object's `objectSettings.basicSettings.useSoftDelete`, NOT by `deleteOptions`.
- `getOptions` / `listOptions` / `paginationOptions` / `deleteOptions` are the four crudType-specific knobs. Each is meaningful for exactly one crudType. `deleteOptions.useSoftDelete` is the one exception that is inert: no generator reads it, so a per-API soft-vs-hard override does not exist; the validator warns (DELETE_OPTIONS_SOFTDELETE_IGNORED) when it contradicts the data object's flag.

When in doubt, consult the per-field doc on each option block — every block whose applicability is restricted repeats the rule in its own `__doc`.

__BusinessApi.useCase.description: Use a BusinessApi to expose a business operation on a primary data object — declaring its crudType, auth, the full request shape via requestParameters, the write payload via dataClauseItems (create/update only), transport bindings, and an optional action workflow. This example is a create API that registers a project, taking the name/slug from the caller and auto-injecting the owner from the session.

apiOptions.name: createProject
apiOptions.apiDescription: Create a new project owned by the current user within their tenant.

requestParameters.name: slug
requestParameters.description: URL-safe unique slug for the project.

BusinessApi.__actions.doc: Represents the available logic actions that can be referenced by the Business API's workflow. Actions include data fetches, validation, permission checks, interservice calls, transformations, and output shaping. Author sparsely: include only the action-type arrays you use — omitted arrays normalize to [] server-side. Every action needs a unique name (its handle in workflow refs); ids are auto-assigned — never write them.
BusinessApi.__workflow.doc:
Defines the logical flow of the Business API, composed of sequenced action names grouped by lifecycle stages. Workflow entries reference actions from the api's action store by NAME (unique within the store); legacy action ids are accepted on input and resolve to the same action, but the stored form is the name. This workflow is generated visually in the architecture UI or programmatically inferred from the API's type. Author sparsely: send only the api's own crudType with only its populated phases; omitted sections are equivalent to empty.

## Ordering — what an action may read

Stages run in the fixed ApiManager pipeline order: `afterStartBusinessApi` (before the login check), `afterReadParameters`, `afterTransposeParameters`, `afterCheckParameters`, `afterCheckBasicAuth`, `afterBuildWhereClause`, `afterFetchInstance`, `afterCheckInstance`, `afterBuildDataClause`, `afterMain<Crud>Operation`, `afterBuildOutput`, then (post-response) `afterSendResponse`, `afterApiEvent`. The key order of the stored JSON is irrelevant — this table is.

WITHIN one stage, actions run in the DECLARATION ORDER of that stage's array. There is no dependency resolution and no topological sort. A workflow write MERGES additively, and `options.replace: true` replaces an array wholesale — it does NOT reorder one; to put a producer ahead of a consumer already listed before it, rewrite the whole array or move the producer to an EARLIER stage.

Two clause slots are evaluated by the framework rather than by an action, and both run BEFORE the stage that shares their name: `query.whereClause` at `buildWhereClause()` (so it may read through `afterCheckBasicAuth`) and `query.dataClauseItems[].value` at `buildDataClause()` (so it may read through `afterCheckInstance`).

An MScript that reads `this.<name>` of a value produced LATER evaluates to `undefined` — it does not throw and it is not a syntax error. In a `shouldBeTrue: false` validation action (`if (result) throw`) that is falsy, so the guard does not fire and the request is answered as though the check had passed. The validator reports it as `ACTION_CONTEXT_READ_BEFORE_PRODUCED` (error for a `validationActions` script or a `dataClauseItems` value, warning elsewhere), naming both the reading action and the producing one.

The SAME rule judges the framework's own MID-pipeline bindings. Most `this.<X>` the framework binds — `this.session`, `this.request`, `this.crudType`, the request-parameter mirrors, the route segments — exists before any action runs and is never an ordering question. Six do not: `this.result` (written by `executeMainOperation()`), its `mainOperation()` aliases `this.data` and `this.dbResult`, and on a CREATE the singular `this.<objectName>` plus `this.createOutcome` (also `executeMainOperation()`) — all available only from `afterMain<Crud>Operation` on — and `this.output`, written by `buildOutput()` and available only from `afterBuildOutput` on. An action scheduled earlier reads `undefined`: a `publishEventActions` message that is an object literal then ships an event whose every key is `undefined` and which serializes as `"data": {}`. A framework step cannot be rescheduled, so the remedy is always to move the READER to the producing stage or later. On a `get`, an `update` or a `delete` the `this.<objectName>` alias is bound by `fetchInstance()` at step 7 instead, which is why only a `create` is judged on it. `this.createOutcome` exists only on a `create`, and it is what separates a real insert from an idempotent replay: `'created'`, `'duplicateStopped'` (an `onDuplicate: 'stopOperation'` unique index matched and NOTHING was written) or `'duplicateUpdated'`. A post-main side effect that must not repeat on a replay is gated with `condition: "this.createOutcome === 'created'"`; read from an earlier stage it is `undefined`, the comparison is false for the GENUINE create too, and the gate suppresses exactly the run it was meant to allow.

The pipeline produces `this.instance` the same way: `fetchInstance()` runs at step 7, so the row is `null` at every stage from `afterStartBusinessApi` through `afterBuildWhereClause` and is loaded only from `afterFetchInstance` on. A check whose expression reads `this.instance.<field>` from an earlier stage therefore compares `undefined` and REFUSES every caller — a 403 with no database read behind it. The validator reports that as `INSTANCE_READ_BEFORE_FETCH` (error on a gate action or the where clause, warning elsewhere); the two fixes are to schedule the check at `afterFetchInstance` or later, or to derive its key from a request-scoped value (`this.<paramName>`, `this.session.<field>`) that is already available at the stage it runs. Only `update`, `delete` and an ownership-gated `get` fetch a row at all; on a `create`, a `list` or a plain `get` there is no `this.instance` at ANY stage.

## Failure semantics — no rollback

A workflow is NOT a transaction. Actions run sequentially, every write commits on its own, and an action that throws (`onActionError: throwError`, the default) aborts the rest of the pipeline WITHOUT rolling back the main operation or anything an earlier action already wrote. Order a write that may legitimately fail into a pre-main stage — `afterBuildDataClause` for `create`/`update`, `afterCheckInstance` for `update`/`delete` — so it fails before the main row is written. The full contract is on the `BusinessWorkflow` page.
BusinessApi.__basics.doc: Core identity and authentication settings for this Business API.
BusinessApi.__parameters.doc: Custom and Redis-derived parameters fed into the workflow context. Optional — omit (or null) when unused; never [].
BusinessApi.__controllers.doc: Transport bindings (REST, gRPC, Kafka, SSE, cron, internal call) that expose this Business API. Optional — omit (or null) when unused; never [].
BusinessApi.__query.doc: Data-access shape: select / where / data / list / pagination clauses. Optional — omit (or null) when unused; never [].

__ApiOptions.doc: Main configuration section for a Business API. This object includes essential attributes such as naming, access control, event handling, input generation, and fallback strategies. In many cases, configuring this section alone is sufficient to define the primary behavior of an API entry point.

__ApiOptions.useCase.description: Use ApiOptions to declare the core identity of a Business API — its target data object, crudType, name, and behavioral flags (events, default-API marking, MCP opt-out with `blockMcp`). This example configures a list API over orders that is marked as the default list endpoint; like every REST API without `blockMcp`, it is also published as a tool in its service's `GET /tools` registry.

example.name: listOrders
example.apiDescription: List orders visible to the current user within their tenant.

ApiOptions.__dataObjectName.doc: Specifies the primary data object that this Business API interacts with. This object is the core target of the API's operation, such as reading, updating, or deleting records. Required even when dataViewName is set — the DataView's mainObject must match this dataObject.
ApiOptions.__dataViewName.doc: Optional. Specifies the name of a DataView defined in the BFF service whose mainObject matches this API's dataObject. The `get` and `list` read operations then answer the VIEW's row (its projection plus its aggregates/stats). How they read depends on the view: for a STORED view (`viewBasics.isStored: true`) they query the view's Elasticsearch index; for a DYNAMIC view they bind at READ TIME - the api reads its object from the DATABASE with its own where machinery exactly as authored (selectBy, fullWhereClause, additionalClauses, tenant and ownership terms; never compiled to an Elasticsearch query) and the view's joins are applied to each returned row per request, so the read is as fresh as any database read. All write operations (create, update, delete) - including the instance fetch performed by update/delete - execute against the database; they do not read from the DataView. The dataObjectName is always required and must match the DataView's mainObject.
ApiOptions.__crudType.doc: Defines the primary operation type for this API. Possible values are `get`, `list`, `create`, `update`, and `delete`. This classification drives the behavior and flow of the API lifecycle.
ApiOptions.__name.doc: A unique, human-readable name for the API, used for referencing in documentation and the UI. This is not a code-level identifier; instead, generated class and function names are derived from this value. Use camelCase formatting, avoid spaces or special characters, and ensure uniqueness within the same service. If you want the API to behave like a default RESTful endpoint, use a verb-noun combination like `createUser`, `getOrder`, or `deleteItem`, which will enforce expected parameters and URL patterns (e.g., `/users/:userId`). This name IS the API's identity: it keys the generated manager class and its file, the api-layer barrel export, the internal-call registry member you call as `API.<name>(params)`, the `targetApi` of an interservice call, and the swagger operationId. Two entries on the same data object that resolve to the same identifier — identical, differing only in case, or differing only by separators (`get_user` vs `getUser`) — are refused at design time (API_NAME_COLLISION). A trailing `ById` on a `get` / `update` / `delete` API affects only the derived ROUTE, which drops the suffix so `getOrderById` mounts at `/orders/:orderId`; the identity keeps the full name, so `unpublishPortfolio` and `unpublishPortfolioById` are two distinct, legal APIs (give at least one of them its own `restSettings.routePath`, or they will share a mount). The name `<serviceName>Service` (any letter case) is refused (SERVICE_MANAGER_NAME_COLLISION): the api's generated manager class would take the name of the service-level base manager `<ServiceName>ServiceManager`, the same clash a DataObject of that name draws.
ApiOptions.__apiDescription.doc: A brief explanation of the API's business purpose or logic. Helps clarify its intent for developers and documentation readers.
ApiOptions.__frontendDocument.doc: A text based information to inform the frontend developer or frontend AI agent about the api specific UX behaviour of the api logic based on user stories and use cases. The format may be either text or markdown(recommended). Write the document as an AI prompt and describe api specific UX behaviours. Note that this document will be given to the AI agent or human developer combined with all technical details that is generated from the business api design,so this document should only focus on data api-specific behavioral UX business logic.
ApiOptions.__testingNotes.doc: Free-text markdown block written by the designer at apply time, describing how this API's happy path should be tested. Read VERBATIM by the api-test-plan-scaffold blueprint as the AUTHORITATIVE happy-case source — overrides the planner's role/body-field inference rule when present. Write down only what the planner cannot statically infer from authOptions + the data-object schema + the route doc: custom validateAction rules (e.g. 'rejects 403 when seller.isActive=false'), sequencing prereqs ('must be called after checkout'), side effects worth asserting (kafka events, related-record writes), auto-populated session fields (sellerId, ownerId, tenantId — keep these out of the request body), conditional status codes (200 vs 201 vs 409). Format: short markdown following the template in the apply prompt — Happy path / Side effects / Custom rules / Skip cases. Empty is allowed (planner falls back to inference) but the validator will warn.
ApiOptions.__raiseApiEvent.doc: Indicates whether the Business API should emit an API-level event after successful execution. This is typically used for audit trails, analytics, or external integrations. Default `false` since patterns 1.93.0: a new api publishes nothing until you set it to `true`, and a stored api that omits the field publishes no route event and declares no route topic (before 1.93.0 an omitted field meant `true`; set it to `true` explicitly to keep such an api publishing). An explicit stored `true` publishes exactly as before. A project consumer of this API's derived route topic, written with or without the project codename prefix, requires `raiseApiEvent: true`; validation reports KAFKA_TOPIC_API_EVENT_DISABLED and names the service and API when it is off. Turn it on for writes another service or an external system listens to; a get or list event carries the whole result (a list event the whole page), so leave reads off unless a consumer needs them. The emitted payload is the unified event ENVELOPE: `{ id, type, source, time, requestId, actor: { userId, sessionId?, tenantId?, roleId? }, data: { _type, ...record }, old? }`. The API's result record rides under `data` (e.g. a `createUser` event carries `payload.data.email`, never `payload.email`), `type` is the domain fact (`user.created`), `source` is the publishing service codename, and update/delete events carry the previous state under `old`. Events NEVER carry a session object, tokens, or HTTP transport metadata — `actor` is the minimal identity, and credential-bearing keys are scrubbed at publish time. Every consumer mapping (agent kafka controllers, event subscriptions, notification triggers, external integrations) must read record fields through `data`. Use the `getKafkaEventPayloadStructure` tool to see the exact per-topic shape.
ApiOptions.__raiseDbLevelEvents.doc: RETIRED: this api-level flag never had a runtime effect and still has none. Db-level events are published by default; an object nobody consumes turns them off with the DataObject setting `objectSettings.basicSettings.publishDbEvents: false` (validation refuses it where a DataView, a subscription, a hub, a notification or another consumer reads them). This flag and is kept only so stored blueprints that carry it stay valid; do not set it. Db-level events carry the unified envelope: the row (stamped with `_type`) under `data`, the pre-change row under `old` (`updated` events only), and a `<object>.<verb>` event `type`; topics are `<serviceCodename>-dbevent-<object>-<verb>`. Use the `getKafkaEventPayloadStructure` tool for exact per-topic shapes.
ApiOptions.__blockMcp.doc: When true, this Business API is left out of its service's public `GET /tools` registry, so mcpbff does not publish it as an MCP tool and the agent hub's discovered tool catalog does not list it. Every REST BusinessApi is in that registry by default; this flag is the only way to remove one (`mcpExposed` is retired). It hides the tool only: the REST route and the other controllers stay mounted with their normal auth, and an agent whose `toolSettings.apiTools` names the API still gets it. Use this for APIs that require frontend-specific flows (e.g., payment with credit card input, 3DS verification) and should not be called by AI agents directly.
ApiOptions.__mcpExposed.doc: RETIRED: no generator reads this flag to decide MCP exposure, so setting it neither adds nor removes a tool. Generated services run no MCP server and serve no `/mcp` or `/mcp-tools` route. Each service publishes a protocol-neutral `GET /tools` registry that mcpbff, the project's only MCP endpoint, reads and projects into MCP tools named `<service>__<api>`. Every BusinessApi with a REST controller is in that registry unless `blockMcp: true`: exposure is opt-out, and `blockMcp` is its only switch. Kept so stored blueprints that carry it stay valid; do not set it. A few design-time checks still read it: `true` reserves the parameter name `accessToken` (MCP_RESERVED_PARAMETER_NAME) and counts as an external exposure in the UNPAGED_LIST_EXPOSED and PUBLIC_MUTATION_AUTHZ_PIPELINE_OFF warnings.
ApiOptions.__isDefaultApi.doc: Marks this API as the canonical API for its crudType on the associated data object. This is a DOCUMENTATION marker, not a codegen switch — no emitter derives a route, a controller or a client from it. Its one realised effect is that the generated project documentation labels the endpoint '[Default <crudType> API]' so a frontend developer or an AI agent picks it over a custom variant. At most one API per crudType per data object should carry it — nothing enforces that today (follow-up). Leaving it unset is fine — readers then fall back to the most general API for the operation.
ApiOptions.__useIdempotencyKey.doc: When true, this API supports idempotent replay. The caller sends any string as `api-idempotency-key` (REST: header, query, or body — header wins; gRPC/MCP: in the request envelope). A repeated key returns the previously stored successful response with the response header `idempotency-key-cache: true` instead of re-running the API; error responses are never cached, so a failed call can be retried with the same key. Reusing a key with a different request payload is rejected with 409 `IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_INCONSISTENCY` — the client must keep a key's request identical across retries. The default is `false`: no replay behavior, every call executes normally.
ApiOptions.__loadShedTier.doc: Optional shed-priority tier (integer 0-5) this API declares for itself when the owning service runs a `loadShield` (0 = never shed — bypasses the shield queue entirely; 5 = first to shed under congestion). The per-API counterpart of the shield's central `loadShield.tiers.assignments[]` (the eventStream `loadSheddingPriority` idiom — a designer states an API's importance where the API is authored). PRECEDENCE (most specific wins): a central action-narrowed assignment > a central api-level assignment > this `loadShedTier` > the derived default by action nature (health 0, auth 1, writes 2, single reads 3, lists/reports 4) — the shield stays the architect's override view. INERT without a shield: on a service with no declared/enabled `loadShield` the property changes nothing (generated output stays byte-identical) and validation surfaces a warning (LOADSHIELD_TIER_WITHOUT_SHIELD). Values outside 0-5 fail validation (LOADSHIELD_TIER_INVALID).
ApiOptions.__includeSoftDeleted.doc: Opt this API OUT of the soft-delete row filter. On a data object with `basicSettings.useSoftDelete: true` every read and scoped write is narrowed with `isActive: true` by default, so archived rows stay invisible. That default makes a RESTORE endpoint inexpressible — an update whose whole purpose is to select an archived row and reactivate it can never match its target (the where clause, the fetch-instance read, and the db-layer update all AND `isActive: true`, so `checkInstance()` 404s). Set `includeSoftDeleted: true` to suppress the filter for THIS api only: no `isActive` term is injected into the where clause, and the generated fetch/get/list/update calls pass `includeArchived: true` down to the db layer. Use it for restore/undelete endpoints and admin or audit reads that must show archived rows — never for ordinary reads, which would leak archived rows. A `crudType: delete` API may not declare it (INCLUDE_SOFT_DELETED_ON_DELETE, error): its main delete selects live rows only, deleting an archived row would re-archive it rather than purge it, and there is no purge operation. The main-object filter is unchanged on an object with `useSoftDelete: false` (no `isActive` column) or a `crudType: create` API (no main where clause); validation warns in both cases. The flag also reaches the workflow child actions whose target object carries `isActive`: a child `UpdateCrudAction`, `DeleteCrudAction` or `FetchStatsAction` passes `includeArchived: true` to their db-layer helper even when the main object has no soft delete (on the stats helper the argument sits after `bucketBy`, so an opted-in api without a bucket emits `(query, stats, undefined, true)`); every other combination keeps the historic call arity byte for byte. Independent of the finer-grained escape hatch: an api whose own query already constrains `isActive` (a `whereClause.fullWhereClause` / `additionalClauses` term reading a declared `isActive` request parameter — `isActive` is framework-managed and cannot be declared as a data property or list filter) always keeps its explicit value; the default is only applied when the clause says nothing about `isActive`.
ApiOptions.__raisedEventTopic.doc: Optional. The EXPLICIT wire-topic suffix for this API's raiseApiEvent event. By default the suffix is DERIVED from the API name by verb inversion (`followUser` -> `user-followed`, `subscribeToPlan` -> `toplan-subscribed`, `processRefundRequest` -> `refundrequest-processed`), which for a non-CRUD verb is rarely the name a spec guesses - and a consumer bound to the wrong spelling receives nothing, with no error anywhere. Set this to publish under a name you choose. An ordinary suffix becomes `<serviceCodename>-<raisedEventTopic>`; a complete topic already starting with `<serviceCodename>-` is used once. Overrides are trimmed and lowercased. Only the complete service prefix followed by a dash counts as already prefixed: a bare service codename, a partial prefix, or another service prefix remains an ordinary suffix. It must satisfy Kafka's topic character class (a-z A-Z 0-9 . _ -) and the composed name must stay within 249 characters. It moves the TOPIC only - the generated publisher class, topic constant and event class are still named from the derived event, so an override can neither rename nor collide generated symbols. Ignored when raiseApiEvent is false. When the derived name is UNGUESSABLE (any non-CRUD verb), validation reports it as the warning KAFKA_RAISED_EVENT_TOPIC_UNGUESSABLE, naming the wire topic and the derivation rule, so the contract is visible at authoring time without a separate getKafkaEventTopicsOfService call; setting this property silences that warning. A CRUD derivation (createOrder -> order-created) is not reported, because a warning on every event would train its reader to ignore the code, and neither is a framework-INJECTED api, whose name the designer did not choose and cannot override.
ApiOptions.__onNotFound.doc: Policy for a missing target row on get/update/delete APIs. `throw404` keeps the ordinary not-found response. `complete` routes a get/prefetch miss and, for update/delete, a zero-row mutation result through workflow.<crud>.afterMissingInstance; the normal after-main branch runs only for a present/successfully mutated row. Both outcomes then rejoin at afterBuildOutput and complete successfully. `complete` is invalid for create/list. TRANSPORT BOUNDARY: `complete` is defined only where the execution path has an explicit completed-miss outcome. Two transports carry one. (1) The ordinary non-streaming REST manager path, where a miss answers 2xx with the miss body instead of 404; an MCP-EXPOSED api counts, because it invokes that same REST route through the generated `/tools` registry — and it is the ONLY MCP exposure there is, since every generated service is MCP-agnostic (docs/ADR-mcp-service-tool-registry.md), so no api is ever refused for `MCP`. (2) A KAFKA controller, where a miss is an explicit CONSUMED NO-OP: `workflow.<crud>.afterMissingInstance` runs, no api event is raised (nothing was written), the handler logs `KafkaCompletedMissingInstance` at info level rather than `ErrorInKafkaMessage`, and it returns normally so the offset commits exactly as it does for an applied message — which is what makes a saga applier idempotent on redelivery. When the api declares a response topic, the miss is published with the envelope `type` `<dataObject>.<crudType>.missed` and the payload carries `_outcome: "completedMissingInstance"` beside whatever `afterMissingInstance` wrote to the response; an APPLIED outcome publishes exactly what it published before, so the ABSENCE of `_outcome` means the operation ran. SSE/streaming, gRPC and cron carry no completed-miss outcome, so declaring `complete` on an api that enables any of them — or that disables the REST controller without enabling a Kafka controller, leaving no supported transport at all — is refused at validation with `API_ONNOTFOUND_TRANSPORT_UNSUPPORTED`, and, if it ever reaches deploy time, by the generator's codegen guard (`[nodejs:onNotFound]`, `[dotnet:onNotFound]`, `[java:onNotFound]`, `[rust:onNotFound]`). EXECUTION-PATH BOUNDARY: two WHOLE-SERVICE shapes carry no completed-miss outcome either, whatever transports the api declares. (a) An api a JobStream targets — the job worker path has no caller to answer a miss to, and `targetApi.keepPublicRoute` does not change that, since it only decides whether the public route survives BESIDE the worker. (b) An api reached through the untyped `serviceLayerCall` adapter, which returns whatever the adapter returns and so cannot state an explicit operation outcome. Declaring `complete` on either is refused at validation with `API_ONNOTFOUND_EXECUTION_PATH_UNSUPPORTED` and, at deploy time, by the same codegen guards (`[nodejs:onNotFound]`, `[dotnet:onNotFound]`, `[java:onNotFound]`, `[rust:onNotFound]`). LANGUAGE PORTS: the Kafka completed-miss outcome is implemented by the nodejs, dotnet and java, rust and golang, and python generators. The dotnet guard composes its transport predicates from the same shared module design-time validation reads (src/patterns/custom/missing-instance-transports.ts); the java and rust guards mirror them. The golang generator emits the Kafka consumed-no-op but carries no codegen refusal of its own, so validation is its only boundary. The python generator emits the Kafka consumed-no-op, the `.missed` envelope and the `_outcome` marker for get, update and delete apis and, like golang, carries no codegen refusal of its own.
ApiOptions.__exposeSecrets.doc: The `isSecret` columns THIS api is allowed to carry in its own response, named one by one. An `isSecret` column is scrubbed from every payload by default, which is right for a credential and wrong for a value whose owner must be able to read it back (a ticket code, a one-time claim link): the owner's own ownership-gated read returned the row with the field silently missing. Naming a column here carries it in this api's response ONLY. Every other surface is unchanged - other apis still scrub it (the allow-list is per-api, not per-column), and the Kafka envelopes, db-event payloads and request/response logs are scrubbed at their own choke points, which this field does not reach at all. Name a column that is not `isSecret`, or not on this api's `dataObjectName`, and validation refuses it: the field has to state facts. A `hashed` column is refused too - that value is a bcrypt digest, not the plaintext anyone wants back - and so is any name that ANY object in the project declares `hashed` (auth's `user.password` included): the scrub matches by name across the whole response, so such a name is never removed from the api's scrub list, whatever validation says. The opened value is this api's response and goes wherever that response goes: an api used as an agent tool hands it to the LLM provider and its conversation checkpoint, and an api with `useIdempotencyKey` stores it in the replay store. This supersedes re-injecting a scrubbed value with an AddToResponseAction, which works but records a deliberate secret exposure as an ordinary response action, invisible to review.
ApiOptions.name: String
ApiOptions.__visitSettings.doc: Makes this BusinessApi a VISIT source (docs/ADR-object-visits-pattern.md): WHICH call counts as a visit of its data object, with which signal, and how it is confirmed. The storage (history table, counter, read state) belongs to the object's `objectSettings.visitTracking`, which must be enabled. The designer knows which api is a real visit: the shop-front product detail is one, the same row fetched by the admin panel, an MCP tool or an internal call is not. Recording runs after the response is sent and never adds latency to the read. This block replaces nothing: the retired GetOptions/ListOptions.setAsRead stay retired. Optional - omit (or null) when unused.

__ApiOnNotFoundPolicy.doc.#: Canonical behavior when a get/update/delete Business API cannot find its target row.
__ApiOnNotFoundPolicy.doc.complete: Run the explicit afterMissingInstance branch and complete successfully.

__ApiRequiredCallerKind.doc.#: WHO may call a Business API, as a demand on the CALLER. The runtime discriminator is `isM2M` — true for a verified machine token, and ALSO true for an end-user identity forwarded on an InterService hop, which carries `x-m2m-token`. Named for the caller rather than for M2M so it cannot be mistaken for `M2MAllowed`, which is what the API declares it tolerates and is true for every caller of an M2M-allowed api.
__ApiRequiredCallerKind.doc.any: No caller-kind demand (default) — the behaviour of every api before this field existed. Whoever the login, role, ownership and permission gates admit, gets through.
__ApiRequiredCallerKind.doc.machine: Machine callers only, WIDE reading: no interactive user session (403 M2M_CALLER_REQUIRED), but an end-user identity FORWARDED on an InterService hop still passes. The maintainer default for "machine-only" — it is the line `isM2M` already draws, and the line real interservice traffic needs.
__ApiRequiredCallerKind.doc.machineWithoutUserIdentity: Machine callers only, NARROW reading: a machine caller carrying NO user identity at all. REFUSES the forwarded InterService hop as well (403 M2M_CALLER_WITHOUT_USER_IDENTITY_REQUIRED). The labelled exception, not the default — declare it only for an api that must never run on behalf of a person.
